title: Vietnam: Strong GDP but rising inflation risks - Commerzbank | FXStreet
body:
Commerzbank Research highlights Vietnam's Q3 GDP growth at 10.0% year-on-year, the strongest since the pandemic, driven by investment and industry. Achieving the government's 10% full-year target would require an unusually strong Q4. September CPI rose to 5.1%, above the 4.5% target on average, with elevated Oil prices and rapid credit growth constraining SBV's room for additional monetary support.

Growth-led but inflation constraints

"Q3 GDP beat expectations, rising 10.0% yoy (Bloomberg consensus: 8.7%) vs 8.8% in Q2, which was revised up from 8.4% initially. This marked the strongest growth since the pandemic, bringing year-to-date expansion to 8.9%. This implies that Q4 has to expand by 12.5% to achieve the government's full-year target of 10%. While growth momentum should remain strong in Q4, achieving the target would require an unusually large further acceleration."

"Nguyen Thu Oanh, the head of the National Statistics Office, stated that "as capital flows into production, investment and consumption, its impact could become more evident in the final months of the year"."

"The strong growth was broad-based but remained heavily driven by investment and industry. It reflects the continued capacity expansion amid the diversification away from Chinese supply chains. Industry and construction grew 12.5% yoy in Q3, while services expanded 9.5%. Manufacturing rose 11.4% yoy vs 10.8% in Q2, contributing 2.8%-points to headline growth. Construction jumped 12.2% vs 8.9% in Q2 due to resilient foreign investment interest."

"Overall, the robust Q3 growth has been largely investment led. Growth momentum should continue in Q4, but this could raise demand-side price pressures. Furthermore, upside risks to inflation are elevated due to higher global oil prices amid the conflict in the Middle East."

(This article was created with the help of an Artificial Intelligence tool and reviewed by an editor. Know more.)

title: Near-term Inflation Expectations Climbed in September -- NY Fed Survey
body:
Consumers' expectations for future inflation rose in the short and medium term last month, according to a New York Fed survey.

Consumers' expectations for future inflation increased to 3.9% at the one-year-ahead horizon and to 3.3% at the three-year-ahead horizon, according to the latest monthly version of the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations. Long-run inflation expectations, or across the five-year horizon were unchanged at 3%.

Officials at the central bank keep a close eye on long-term inflation expectations because the numbers serve as a gauge of the Fed's credibility back to 2%, and because expectations themselves can be self-fulfilling. If consumers anticipate higher prices in the future, they may accelerate purchases or ask for larger raises, moves that make progress back to the Fed's target more difficult.

Wednesday's report from the NY Fed should reassure policy makers inflation expectations in the long-run haven't become unanchored and pose those risks. The small uptick medium run expectations show consumers may think price pressures could persist beyond the near term.

As the conflict in Iran pushes up energy prices, expected price increases over the next year ticked up slightly for gasoline. Additionally, expected price increases rose for food and slightly for medical care.

The report also reflected officials' sentiment that the labor market has remained mostly stable. The mean perceived probability of losing one's job in the next year decreased to its lowest reading since December 2024. In addition, the mean probability that the unemployment rate will be higher one year from now fell.

The survey also showed median one-year-ahead nominal household spending growth expectations increasing to 5.5%, the highest reading since May 2023. The mean perceived probability that the average interest rate on savings accounts will be higher in 12 months rose to 30.3%, its highest reading since October 2023.

title: US stocks, bonds fall on inflation worry as oil rises- Moneycontrol.com
body: A record-breaking run in stocks hit a wall as higher oil prices lifted bond yields, stoking concerns that potential inflationary pressures could trigger Federal Reserve rate hikes. Those worries sent the S&P 500 down from an all-time high and halted the Nasdaq 100's six-day gain. Brent crude hit $102 amid a pickup in Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Treasury 10-year yields hovered near the highest since 2002 before a $39 billion sale of the bonds and minutes of the last Fed meeting. The dollar rose. Bitcoin sank. Investors are demanding greater compensation to hold global bonds as concerns about persistent inflation, government spending and surging corporate borrowing to finance the artificial-intelligence buildout intensify. That sense of unease is being compounded by France's fiscal woes, which are threatening to drag the European Central Bank into the kind of face-off with markets it hasn't seen since the euro area's debt crisis more than a decade ago. Meantime, minutes of the Fed's September gathering could reveal that many policymakers were deeply worried about underlying price trends and expecting to lift rates at least one more time before the end of the year. Money markets see a roughly one-in-four chance of a Fed hike this month. "Persistently high energy prices keep risks to inflation, policy rates, and benchmark bond yields skewed to the upside," said Elias Haddad at Brown Brothers Harriman & Co. "A Fed pause may not bring down long yields if term premiums remain elevated," said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office. "Fixing the curve's long-term problem without fiscal tightening requires two things: productivity-led growth and periods of low real borrowing costs." She recommends positioning for this by staying invested in AI-driven productivity gainers, diversifying across equities and high-quality fixed income, with a preference for shorter- over longer-duration bonds. Equity markets face a genuine rival in bonds for the first time in decades, Bank of America Corp.'s Savita Subramanian told Bloomberg Television. She also cautioned that elevated investor sentiment leaves stocks more exposed to disappointment than upside. With the recent developments in the credit markets, it will be essential that we get another extremely strong earnings season, noted Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. Analysts expect a roughly 25% increase in third-quarter S&P 500 profits from a year earlier, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

title: Nifty, Sensex open in pressure ahead of RBI policy as investors cautious on growth-inflation dynamics
body:
Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 7 (ANI): The domestic equity markets opened under pressure on Wednesday as investors turned cautious ahead of the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) decision and awaited the central bank's view on the emerging growth-inflation dynamics.

The Nifty 50 index opened at 22,690.45, down 85.65 points or 0.38 per cent, while the BSE Sensex opened at 72,965.38, lower by 102.43 points or 0.14 per cent. Soon after opening, both indices fell further.

Banking and market expert Ajay Bagga said the MPC meeting is taking place against the backdrop of a significant shift in macroeconomic conditions.

'The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets today against the backdrop of a significant shift in macro tailwinds,' Bagga told ANI.

He said the RBI has cut the repo rate by a cumulative 125 bps across 2025 to a trough of 5.25 per cent and has kept it unchanged for four consecutive policy reviews. The central bank is now facing a growth-inflation trade-off, he said.

Bagga said a 25 bps rate hike would be the first hike since February 2023. He added that the August MPC minutes had indicated that some members were open to higher rates if inflation broadened.

He pointed to several factors putting pressure on the economy, including CPI inflation rising to 4.82 per cent in August, above the 4 per cent target for a third straight month, while WPI inflation reached 9.92 per cent.

Crude oil is also back above USD 100 per barrel, while the Fed has begun tightening and the rupee is down about 6 per cent this year, he said. The Fed hiked in September to 3.75-4 per cent, while the Bank of Japan has also hiked rates.

Among sectoral indices on the NSE, the Nifty Media index was the only major sector to open in the green, gaining 0.66 per cent. All other sectors opened in the red.

The Nifty Auto index declined 0.52 per cent, Nifty FMCG fell 0.43 per cent, Nifty IT declined 0.51 per cent, Nifty Metal lost 0.59 per cent, Nifty Pharma fell 0.12 per cent, Nifty PSU Bank declined 0.29 per cent, Nifty Private Bank fell 0.29 per cent, and Nifty Oil and Gas declined 0.49 per cent.

Among Nifty 50 stocks, Dr Reddy, Cipla, Bharti Airtel and Coal India were among the top gainers in the opening session. Titan, SBI Life, Asian Paints, M&M and IndiGo were among the top losers.

VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments, said the recent market rally has provided some relief to investors but could face challenges.

'The 558-point rally in the Nifty from last Thursday's low level has come as a relief for investors. But this rally will face headwinds, constraining a sustained up move,' Vijayakumar told ANI.

He said Brent crude is back above USD 101 and there are no signs of a reversal in FPI outflows. At the same time, domestic liquidity and expectations of good Q2 numbers are supporting the market.

'The focus of the market attention today will be on the monetary stance and the message from the RBI Governor,' he said.

Brent crude oil was trading at USD 101.51 per barrel, up more than 1 per cent on Wednesday. Gold prices moderated 0.31 per cent to Rs 1,49,660 per 10 grams for 24 karats, while silver prices declined 0.49 per cent to Rs 2,26,135 per kg at the time of reporting.

In other Asian markets, Japan's Nikkei 225 declined 0.57 per cent to 70,295, Singapore's Straits Times fell 0.07 per cent to 5,624, Hong Kong's Hang Seng declined 0.66 per cent to 24,121, Taiwan's Weighted Index fell 0.27 per cent to 49,689 and South Korea's KOSPI declined 0.83 per cent to 6,882. (ANI)

title: RBI raises repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50% as per market expectations as inflation risks strengthen
body:
Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 7 (ANI): The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday raised its policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent, beginning a rate-hike cycle as rising inflation risks, elevated global yields and resilient domestic growth strengthened the case for tighter monetary policy.

The decision by the Monetary Policy Committee marks a shift from its August policy, when it kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent and retained a neutral stance while seeking greater clarity on the inflation outlook and growth-inflation balance.

In his statement, RBI Governor, Sanjay Malhotra said, "After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial conditions, developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points"

Following the repo rate increase, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands at 5.25 per cent, while the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and Bank Rate are at 5.75 per cent. The MPC stance was changed to a calibrated tightening by a majority.

The decision comes amid rising price pressures. India's CPI inflation stood at 4.82 per cent in August, while economists and research reports have projected inflation to move above 5 per cent during FY27. Inflation is expected to peak around 5.9 per cent in the third quarter, with deficient monsoon conditions and crude oil prices around USD 100 a barrel adding to the risks.

Global financial conditions have also become less supportive. The US Federal Reserve raised its policy rate by 25 basis points in September, while US 10-year Treasury yields have remained elevated at around 5.3 per cent. The rupee was trading at 96.36 per US dollar at the time of filing this report.

Liquidity was evaluated as another key consideration. The RBI's special forex swap facility mobilised USD 132.98 billion through FCNR(B) deposits as of August 31, adding substantial liquidity to the banking system and increasing the need for calibrated absorption.

The RBI's decision also comes against resilient domestic activity. India's economy grew 7.8 per cent in Q1 FY27, while high-frequency indicators have pointed to continued strength in domestic demand, manufacturing and services.

The latest move is expected to set the direction for monetary policy in the coming months, with economists earlier seeing scope for cumulative tightening of up to 75 basis points and the repo rate potentially reaching around 6 per cent by the end of FY27, depending on inflation, oil prices and global financial conditions. (ANI)

title: 10- and 30-year bond yields trading at 24-year highs - AOL
body:
The 10- and 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yields hit 24-year highs during Wednesday morning trading, as the market sell-off persists.

The 10-year note topped 5.36 percent earlier in the day, the highest mark since April 2002. That month, the 10-year bond yield reached a closing peak of 5.48 percent.

The 30-year bond yield, meanwhile, exceeded 5.73 percent, also its highest mark since April 2002. The stock market took a sharp nosedive that year, in the aftermath of a months-long recession.

Both notes dipped slightly from Wednesday's highs and respectively closed at below 5.329 percent and below 5.68 percent. But 10- and30-year bond yields still rose about 1 basis point from closing time Tuesday.

Both notes have dipped slightly from Wednesday's highs and are respectively trading at below 5.32 percent and 5.69 percent as of lunchtime. But 10- and 30-year bond yields both remain about 4 basis points higher than closing time Tuesday.

Bond yields are also up across Europe, as investors have fled the market amid mounting government debt and high oil prices due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Mohamed El-Erian, who chaired former President Obama's Global Development Council, wrote Wednesday on social media that France's 10-year bond yield is "leading a regional rise that increasingly reflects a two-way dynamic with US Treasuries."

Higher interest rates often push up bond yields, which are inversely correlated with prices. Last month, the Federal Reserve hiked rates for the first time since July 2023, as inflation remains above its 2 percent target.

During that meeting, the majority of Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) officials believed another rate hike by the end of this year was "appropriate," according to minutes the central bank released Wednesday.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) pressed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on rising yields Wednesday. In a letter to Bessent, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee asked him how he "plans to address the harm to families and risks to the financial system" from increasing rates.

"Surging Treasury yields carry real consequences for American families," Warren wrote. "Rising Treasury yields increase mortgages, car loans, and credit cards, adding even more costs to Americans' monthly budgets."

Later Wednesday, the Fed will release minutes from the meeting that concluded with the quarter-point rate hike, which raised the federal funds rate to between 3.75 percent and 4 percent.

The FOMC will gather again in the final week of October -- against the backdrop of multiple central bank officials indicating future rate hikes are in store.

Rising bond yields portend higher borrowing costs for Americans on an array of products, including mortgages.

The average 30-year mortgage rate, which closely tracks the 10-year bond yield, is 7.52 percent as of Wednesday, its highest mark since November 2023, according to data from Bankrate.

title: S&P 500 And Nasdaq 100 Slip From Record Highs Amid Pressure From Soaring Treasury Yields -- SPCX, AMD, NVDA, MRVL In Focus
body:
The 30-year bond yield hit its highest level since May 2002 at 5.732%.

* The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.2% lower, the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.7%.

* 10-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since April 2002.

* SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to buy chips from Nvidia, FT reported.

U.S. stock indices ended lower on Wednesday after Treasury yields jumped to levels last seen two decades ago.

The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.2% lower, the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.7%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, lost about 1%.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) slipped 0.2%, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) eased 0.7%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) fell 0.2%.

Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) dropped 1% each, tracking weakness in Nvidia (NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) fell 0.2%.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for QQQ, SPY, and DIA was 'bullish' with 'high' message volumes.

US Market Drivers

Market participants grew anxious as the key 10-year Treasury yield spiked to 5.365% on Wednesday, its highest mark since April 2002. Meanwhile, the 30-year bond yield surged to 5.732%, touching its peak since May 2002.

However, ten-year yields pulled back from session highs following a solid $39 billion auction of 10-year Treasury notes, allowing equities to pare some losses.

"Investors are finding value at these higher rates compared to historical norms over the past two decades, though broader macro dynamics remain at play," Bill Merz, capital markets research lead at U.S. Bank Asset Management, told CNBC, describing the auction outcome as solid.

Elsewhere, Federal Reserve officials expect another hike may be necessary before the year ends, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday, after unanimously voting to raise interest rates at their September meeting.

"Another rate hike is probably coming this year because current policy isn't very restrictive," David Russell at TradeStation told Bloomberg. "With inflation above target and most measures of economic activity strong, price stability is the Fed's dominant mandate."

Key Trending Stocks

SpaceX (SPCX) is in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to buy chips from Nvidia Corp., people familiar with the matter told FT.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) CEO Lisa Su traveled to South Korea on Wednesday to reinforce semiconductor supply chain partnerships and broaden the company's artificial intelligence hardware and software footprint in the region, according to South Korean news outlet The Chosun Daily.

Veteran tech analyst Dan Ives predicts a $4 trillion artificial intelligence spending boom is just beginning, naming Nvidia, Microsoft, Palantir, Apple, and CrowdStrike among his top equity picks.

Investment firm D.A. Davidson has significantly raised its price target on Micron Technology Inc. (MU) to $3,000 per share, up 43% from its previous target of $2,100, while maintaining a 'Buy' rating.

Marvell CEO Matt Murphy remained upbeat after the company's Investor Day, stating that its custom chip goal for 2031 needs only a small slice of the market.

body:

"With the level of rates where they are and the rise that we've seen, I think it's fair to characterize the fact that the margin for error has narrowed as it relates to earnings," Mike Dickson, head of research and quantitative strategies at Horizon Investments, told CNBC Wednesday, adding that earnings could "still carry the market higher."

title: U.S. stocks close lower as Treasury yields touch multi-year highs
body:
NEW YORK, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks closed lower on Wednesday as benchmark Treasury yields touched multi-year highs.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 341.41 points, or 0.66 percent, to 51,179.87. The S&P 500 lost 17.16 points, or 0.22 percent, to 7,801.77. The Nasdaq Composite Index shed 61.20 points, or 0.22 percent, to 27,538.69.

Seven of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the red, with industrials and materials leading the laggards by falling 2.14 percent and 1.53 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, health and consumer discretionary led the gainers by going up 1.06 percent and 0.15 percent, respectively.

U.S. Treasury yields touched multi-year highs before easing after a strong auction. The 10-year Treasury yield reached a high of 5.368 percent, its highest since 2002, but settled near 5.29 percent. The 30-year yield reached a fresh 24-year high before retreating to near 5.67 percent in late trading.

Oil prices settled lower on Wednesday. The West Texas Intermediate for November delivery dropped 1.16 U.S. dollars, or 1.3 percent, to 88.28 dollars per barrel, while Brent crude for December delivery lost 38 cents, or 0.38 percent, to settle at 100.2 dollars per barrel.

In corporate trading, Caterpillar led the Dow lower, dropping 5.75 percent after the Federal Trade Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced a public inquiry into farm-equipment markets. Deere also fell 3.8 percent. Skydance dropped 6.72 percent on its second day of trading since completing its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. ■

title: Wall Street retreats as Treasury yields climb
body:
NEW YORK: Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday, as long-dated US Treasury yields resumed their climb, reviving fears about inflation and mounting debt the day after the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq hit record closing highs.

All three major US stock indices were modestly lower, with the S&P 500 and the Dow snapping four-day winning streaks. The Nasdaq notched its first down day in six.

The small-cap Russell 2000 underperformed its larger cap counterparts, dropping 1.3%.

In the wake of Tuesday's stock market rally, Brent crude settled above US$100 per barrel and long-dated Treasury yields touched a 24-year high.

Iran war-related supply concerns have led to soaring oil prices, which in turn have revived inflation worries and raised the chances of a prolonged central bank rate hiking cycle. Those concerns, combined with mounting corporate and sovereign debt levels, have caused a global bond selloff, which rattled global markets in recent weeks.

Investors "have been looking for some relief on oil, which would drive some relief on rates and that would therefore help the stock market," said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at GLOBALT in Atlanta.

"The third quarter was supposed to be the weak quarter of the year; we were supposed to get a correction," Martin added. "That didn't happen, so it's three cheers and let's take some money off the table."

Stocks pared losses after crude prices turned lower following the International Energy Agency's agreement to speed up the release of oil stocks, prioritizing diesel.

Minutes from the US Federal Reserve's September monetary policy meeting, at which the central bank unanimously approved its first interest rate hike since July 2023, revealed divisions over the rationale of the increase. Some participants saw a hike as necessary to keep the impact of energy price shocks at bay, while others felt the increase was necessary to curb demand-driven inflation.

Financial markets are currently pricing in a 17.2% likelihood that the Fed will implement a second consecutive rate hike at the conclusion of its October meeting, down from 37.6% a week ago, per CME's FedWatch tool.

"The market's Fed expectations are going to seesaw as it gets new bits of data," Martin said. "There's still an expectation for more rate hikes, but it isn't necessarily going to be a hike every meeting and that's what the market is telling you; October will be a pause."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 341.11 points, or 0.66%, to 51,180.17, the S&P 500 lost 17.18 points, or 0.22%, to 7,801.75 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 61.19 points, or 0.22%, to 27,538.69.

Among the 11 sectors in the S&P 500, industrials suffered the steepest percentage drop, while healthcare stocks led the gainers.

Following the upward march of benchmark Treasury yields, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate surged last week to a near three-year high, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Housing and homebuilders slipped 2.3% and 2.9%, respectively.

Chip stocks, which have soared over 80% so far this year, dropped 1.2%.

SpaceX lost 2.5% following media reports that Elon Musk's aerospace firm was seeking $40 billion in financing to fund purchases of Nvidia chips.

Next week, third-quarter reporting season is expected to begin in earnest with a spate of high-profile financial firms expected to post results.

Investors are likely to scrutinise the extent to which massive expenditures on AI technology are beginning to show results, while also watching for clues regarding the health of the US consumer at a time of mounting inflationary pressures.

Analysts currently expect year-on-year S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6%, on aggregate, for the July-through-September period, according to LSEG.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.34-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 115 new highs and 497 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 1,421 stocks rose and 3,371 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.37-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 9 new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 32 new highs and 250 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 16.21 billion shares, compared with the 17.57 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. -- Reuters

title: Gold falls to two‑month low near $4,100 on stronger US Dollar | FXStreet
body:
Fed Minutes showed policymakers backed the September decision to raise interest rates.

Gold price (XAU/USD) tumbles to a near two-month low around $4,110 during the early Asian session on Thursday. A stronger US Dollar (USD) and elevated US Treasury bond yields reduce the appeal of the non-yielding metal. Traders will take more cues from the speeches of Federal Reserve (Fed) officials, including Christopher Waller and Alberto Musalem.

The benchmark US Treasury yields climbed again and are trading near their highest levels since 2002. Meanwhile, the greenback strengthened, making USD-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies. A spike in oil prices also reignited concerns over inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates.

According to the Minutes from the last Fed meeting, policymakers were united in backing their September hike, and most officials assessed that another hike would be appropriate by year-end.

Markets are largely expecting the US central bank to keep interest rates on hold later at its October policy meeting but are still pricing in a 78.3% probability of a December increase, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"I think the message is rates are going to continue to be higher for longer, and that's keeping yields and the dollar underpinned," said Peter Grant, vice president and senior metals strategist at Zaner Metals.

Gold finds support as PBoC buying and ETF inflows offset cta pressure

According to TD Securities, "precious metals come under heavy selling pressure, with CTAs selling gold, silver and platinum," leaving the complex on the defensive as "the yellow metal is on the back foot again this morning amid surging real rates and a stronger Dollar." Even so, the bank argues that "we expect a strong dip buying impulse for gold in particular as longer-term drivers and flows remain supportive," pointing to the fact that "ETF accumulation continues and the PBoC reported a 23rd consecutive month of central bank buying, with another 23 tonnes in September."

TD Securities highlights that "a continued bid from discretionary traders, ETFs, and central banks all combine to provide a strong floor for gold," with the underlying "drivers of these flows" ranging from "geopolitical risk, fiscal concern, Dollar debasement, de-dollarization and stagflation concerns." In their view, "we expect the appetite to be more persistent and ultimately hold firm in the face of surging real rates," and "continue to see the stage being set for gold to disconnect from real rates further and begin a new bull run into 2027."

Fed's Schmid flags AI-driven inflation and signals more short-rate tightening

Fed's Schmid delivers a notably hawkish tone, with an 8/10 FXS Speechtracker score standing above the 7.5/10 historical average, underscoring a stronger-than-usual focus on inflation risks. The emphasis that inflation is "frustrating" and "must be fixed," alongside the assertion that AI is now one of the largest drivers of inflation and that the Fed's credibility is at stake, reinforces a message of persistent price pressures and a readiness to act. The comment that the Fed still has work to do on the short rate despite higher long-term yields signals a bias toward keeping policy tight or tightening further, a backdrop typically supportive of the Dollar and a headwind for risk-sensitive currencies.

The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rose by 0.34 points to 137.91, keeping the gauge firmly in hawkish territory well above the neutral 100 mark. This incremental move higher, aligned with the above-baseline FXS Speechtracker score, confirms that Fed communication is tilting more hawkish at the margin, reinforcing expectations for sustained restrictive policy.

Technical Analysis: Gold remains capped below the 100-day SMA

In the daily chart, XAU/USD remains under clear bearish pressure, as it holds below the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and also below the Bollinger Bands' middle line, keeping the broader trend capped. Price is hovering just above the lower Bollinger Band support, while the Relative Strength Index (14) at 37.09 slips toward oversold territory, hinting at persistent downside momentum rather than an imminent recovery.

On the downside, immediate support is located at the Bollinger Bands' lower band near $4,070, where a sustained break would open the door to further declines toward lower psychological levels. On the topside, initial resistance comes at the Bollinger middle band at $4,250, followed by the 100-day SMA at $4,265; a daily close above these overlapping barriers would be needed to ease the bearish bias, with the upper Bollinger Band around $4,424.82 acting as a higher hurdle for any corrective bounce.

(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more.)

title: Treasury Yields Keep Hitting New Highs. Can Savers Still Cash In?
body:
* The Treasury yields grabbing headlines are on longer maturities, requiring years of holding or an early sale that could erode your return.

* Fortunately, shorter-term Treasurys are also offering strong yields, giving savers a more practical time horizon.

* CD rates are also on the rise, giving Treasurys some competition. But if your state has an income tax, Treasurys could come out ahead.

Treasury yields have been pushing through one high after another, generating a fresh round of headlines each time. But if you haven't acted yet, that doesn't mean you've missed your chance to earn today's high rates on your cash.

The catch is that the most eye-catching yields are attached to long-term Treasurys, which aren't particularly practical for many savers. Fortunately, shorter-term Treasurys, as well as other savings products, are also offering stellar returns right now.

The Treasury Yields Making Headlines Come With a Catch

Today's long-term Treasurys are offering their highest yields in more than 20 years. With the 10-year Treasury closing today at 5.28% and the 30-year offering at 5.67%, yields are near the highest these bonds have offered since 2002.

For savers, the appeal of Treasurys is obvious: Buy an individual T-bill, note, or bond and hold it to maturity, and you can lock in a very attractive yield backed by the U.S. government.

But locking in a 10-, 20-, or 30-year Treasury is a much longer time horizon than most people want to commit to. You can, of course, sell the Treasury before maturity, but you're then subject to its market price at that time, which is impossible to predict. If Treasury yields are higher in the future, your older bond will become less valuable, and vice versa. That means selling early could either add to or erode your total return, though the bond's fixed interest payments won't change while you own it.

For savers rather than long-term bond investors, that makes the newsiest Treasury yields less practical than they first appear.

Shorter-Term Treasurys Are Paying High Rates, Too

Fortunately, you don't have to venture nearly as far out on the Treasury yield curve to earn an attractive return. Shorter-term Treasurys have also surged, even if they haven't reached the historic peaks of their longer-term siblings.

For instance, Treasurys maturing in six months are yielding 4.28% today, while 1-year Treasurys are paying 4.42%. The chart below shows plenty of choices for pairing a compelling yield with a timeline that fits your needs.

In addition to shortening your commitment, shorter-maturity Treasurys also reduce the unpredictability of what you'll get back. When you hold an individual Treasury until it matures, you know exactly what it will pay -- regardless of what happens to market interest rates in the meantime. And if you do need to sell early, shorter-term bonds generally experience narrower price swings than longer-term bonds.

title: Wall Street ends lower as Treasury yields climb
body:
Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday, as long-dated US Treasury yields resumed their climb, reviving fears about inflation and mounting debt the day after the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq hit record closing highs.

All three major US stock indexes were modestly lower, with the S&P 500 and the Dow snapping four-day winning streaks. The Nasdaq notched its first down day in six.

Brent crude settled above US$100 per barrel and long-dated Treasury yields touched a 24-year high.

Iran war-related supply concerns have led to soaring oil prices, which in turn have revived inflation worries and raised the chances of a prolonged central bank rate hiking cycle. Those concerns, combined with mounting corporate and sovereign debt levels, have caused a global bond selloff, which rattled global markets in recent weeks.

Investors "have been looking for some relief on oil, which would drive some relief on rates and that would therefore help the stock market," said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at GLOBALT in Atlanta.

"The third quarter was supposed to be the weak quarter of the year; we were supposed to get a correction," Martin added. "That didn't happen, so it's three cheers and let's take some money off the table."

Stocks pared losses after crude prices turned lower following the International Energy Agency's agreement to speed up the release of oil stocks, prioritising diesel.

Minutes from the US Federal Reserve's September monetary policy meeting, at which the central bank unanimously approved its first interest rate hike since July 2023, revealed divisions over the rationale of the increase. Some participants saw a hike as necessary to keep the impact of energy price shocks at bay, while others felt the increase was necessary to curb demand-driven inflation.

Financial markets are currently pricing in a 17.2 percent likelihood that the Fed will implement a second consecutive rate hike at the conclusion of its October meeting, down from 37.6 percent a week ago, per CME's FedWatch tool.

"The market's Fed expectations are going to seesaw as it gets new bits of data," Martin said.

"There's still an expectation for more rate hikes, but it isn't necessarily going to be a hike every meeting and that's what the market is telling you; October will be a pause."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 341 points, or 0.7 percent, to 51,180, the S&P 500 lost 17 points, or 0.2 percent, to 7,801 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 61 points, or 0.2 percent, to 27,538.

SpaceX lost 2.5 percent following media reports that Elon Musk's aerospace firm was seeking US$40 billion in financing to fund purchases of Nvidia chips.

Next week, third-quarter reporting season is expected to begin in earnest with a spate of high-profile financial firms expected to post results. Investors are likely to scrutinise the extent to which massive expenditures on AI technology are beginning to show results, while also watching for clues regarding the health of the US consumer at a time of mounting inflationary pressures. (Reuters)

title: Treasury Yields Keep Hitting New Highs. Can Savers Still Cash In?
body:
Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise.

Treasury yields have been pushing through one high after another, generating a fresh round of headlines each time. But if you haven't acted yet, that doesn't mean you've missed your chance to earn today's high rates on your cash.

The catch is that the most eye-catching yields are attached to long-term Treasurys, which aren't particularly practical for many savers. Fortunately, shorter-term Treasurys, as well as other savings products, are also offering stellar returns right now.

The Treasury Yields Making Headlines Come With a Catch

Today's long-term Treasurys are offering their highest yields in more than 20 years. With the 10-year Treasury closing today at 5.28% and the 30-year offering at 5.67%, yields are near the highest these bonds have offered since 2002.

For savers, the appeal of Treasurys is obvious: Buy an individual T-bill, note, or bond and hold it to maturity, and you can lock in a very attractive yield backed by the U.S. government.

But locking in a 10-, 20-, or 30-year Treasury is a much longer time horizon than most people want to commit to. You can, of course, sell the Treasury before maturity, but you're then subject to its market price at that time, which is impossible to predict. If Treasury yields are higher in the future, your older bond will become less valuable, and vice versa. That means selling early could either add to or erode your total return, though the bond's fixed interest payments won't change while you own it.

For savers rather than long-term bond investors, that makes the newsiest Treasury yields less practical than they first appear.

Shorter-Term Treasurys Are Paying High Rates, Too

Fortunately, you don't have to venture nearly as far out on the Treasury yield curve to earn an attractive return. Shorter-term Treasurys have also surged, even if they haven't reached the historic peaks of their longer-term siblings.

For instance, Treasurys maturing in six months are yielding 4.28% today, while 1-year Treasurys are paying 4.42%. The chart below shows plenty of choices for pairing a compelling yield with a timeline that fits your needs.

In addition to shortening your commitment, shorter-maturity Treasurys also reduce the unpredictability of what you'll get back. When you hold an individual Treasury until it matures, you know exactly what it will pay -- regardless of what happens to market interest rates in the meantime. And if you do need to sell early, shorter-term bonds generally experience narrower price swings than longer-term bonds.

CDs Are Paying More, Too, But for Some Savers, Treasurys Have a Hidden Benefit

Before you start thinking Treasurys are the only compelling place to put your savings, remember that certificates of deposit (CDs) are having a strong run of their own. Like an individual Treasury, a CD lets you lock in today's rate for a set period, and the best nationwide CD offers have bumped up since the Federal Reserve hiked rates last month. Right now, the top certificates pay 4.50% to 5.00%, depending on the term.

For some savers, CDs may also feel simpler. You can open one directly at a bank or credit union, while buying individual Treasurys is generally bought through a brokerage account or TreasuryDirect.

If you need to cash out early, the downside of CDs is that you'll almost always give up some interest. But the penalty is spelled out in advance, so you can calculate exactly what it will cost. Selling a Treasury before maturity is far less predictable: You could come out ahead or behind depending on its market price at the time.

Still, Treasurys have a tax advantage that can tilt the comparison. CDs generate fully taxable interest, while Treasury interest is exempt from state and local income taxes. So if you live in a state with an income tax, a Treasury yielding slightly less than a CD could still leave you with more after taxes. The higher your state tax rate, the greater that advantage becomes.

title: Asia's US dollar bond market grinds to a halt
body:
HONG KONG: Borrowers in the Asia-Pacific are slowing deals in the US dollar bond market, with the highest yields in more than two years sapping deal momentum.

No issuer from the region has sold a bond in the US currency so far this month in the syndicated market, and debt sales in the third quarter (3Q) slumped 10% to about US$88bil, according to Bloomberg data.

A recent global sell-off in government bonds has made it harder for companies across regions to proceed with deals.

The Asian market has had fewer offerings tied to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, which has driven issuance in the United States.

Alphabet Inc and Amazon.com Inc each priced offerings of US$25bil in their home market in the third quarter, the latest in a spree of such jumbo fundraisers.

Bankers and investors in Asia expect deal volumes in the fourth quarter to be flat or down compared with the same period in 2025, when they were about US$40bil, after yields on the region's dollar notes touched 6.1% earlier this week, the highest since 2024.

Concern about the impact from sustained higher yields on company earnings is also starting to disrupt the relative calm in secondary credit markets globally, with spreads widening to their most since April earlier this month, the data showed.

"It's only folks that have must-do financing that will come to market," said Dhruv Saigal, head of Asia bond syndicate at Barclays in an interview.

"If borrowers have time on their hands, you would want to see rates and market conditions stabilise."

Japanese issuers accounted for almost 40% of dollar-denominated bonds sold from Asia-Pacific in 3Q, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Indian and South Korean issuers ranked second and third, accounting for 16% and 15% of the volume, respectively.

Deals from mainland China, once the mainstay of the market before its housing market meltdown, slumped to fifth place at just under 7%, the data showed.

"A lot of the pick-up in supply in Japan we have seen is because of onshore rates spiking to historically high levels after being quite low," said Barclays' Saigal, who also cited a pick-up in investment by the nation's firms.

The average yield on yen-denominated corporate notes is hovering near its highest in more than a quarter of a century at about 2.8%.

That means for some issuers it is possible to raise funds in the dollar market, with little or no extra cost after the proceeds are swapped back to the Japanese currency.

One of the few large AI-related this year from Asia was SoftBank Group Corp's US$10bil fundraising in the greenback last month.

Together with €1bil (US$1.1bil) of notes sold in the common currency, that deal was a record size for the junk bond market.

In Asia, the syndicated loan market has been the primary source of funding for the AI boom, accounting for US$32.6bil of deals linked to data centres so far this year, according to Bloomberg-compiled data, topping 2025's total of US$21.5bil.

Loans to buy advanced computer chips that will power data centres are also becoming a growing focus for banks and private credit lenders in the region.

Apart from loans, many borrowers from Asia, particularly, in China, can turn to cheaper onshore bond funding versus the dollar. Top-rated Chinese companies can currently sell local-currency bonds at yields of under 1.8% for tenors of seven years or shorter, Chinabond indexes showed.

For now, the use of the dollar bond market in the region to fund data centres has yet to take off, but there are signs of change.

"We are seeing a bit more interest coming to the bond market from data centre companies," said Sheldon Chan, a portfolio manager for Asian and Emerging market credit at T. Rowe Price Group. -- Bloomberg

title: S&P 500 And Nasdaq 100 Slip From Record Highs Amid Pressure From Soaring Treasury Yields -- SPCX, AMD, NVDA, MRVL In Focus
body:
* The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.2% lower, the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.7%.

* 10-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since April 2002.

* SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to buy chips from Nvidia, FT reported.

U.S. stock indices ended lower on Wednesday after Treasury yields jumped to levels last seen two decades ago.

The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.2% lower, the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.7%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, lost about 1%.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) slipped 0.2%, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) eased 0.7%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) fell 0.2%.

Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) dropped 1% each, tracking weakness in Nvidia (NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) fell 0.2%.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for QQQ, SPY, and DIA was 'bullish' with 'high' message volumes.

US Market Drivers

Market participants grew anxious as the key 10-year Treasury yield spiked to 5.365% on Wednesday, its highest mark since April 2002. Meanwhile, the 30-year bond yield surged to 5.732%, touching its peak since May 2002.

However, ten-year yields pulled back from session highs following a solid $39 billion auction of 10-year Treasury notes, allowing equities to pare some losses.

"Investors are finding value at these higher rates compared to historical norms over the past two decades, though broader macro dynamics remain at play," Bill Merz, capital markets research lead at U.S. Bank Asset Management, told CNBC, describing the auction outcome as solid.

Elsewhere, Federal Reserve officials expect another hike may be necessary before the year ends, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday, after unanimously voting to raise interest rates at their September meeting.

"Another rate hike is probably coming this year because current policy isn't very restrictive," David Russell at TradeStation told Bloomberg. "With inflation above target and most measures of economic activity strong, price stability is the Fed's dominant mandate."

Key Trending Stocks

SpaceX (SPCX) is in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to buy chips from Nvidia Corp., people familiar with the matter told FT.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) CEO Lisa Su traveled to South Korea on Wednesday to reinforce semiconductor supply chain partnerships and broaden the company's artificial intelligence hardware and software footprint in the region, according to South Korean news outlet The Chosun Daily.

Veteran tech analyst Dan Ives predicts a $4 trillion artificial intelligence spending boom is just beginning, naming Nvidia, Microsoft, Palantir, Apple, and CrowdStrike among his top equity picks.

Investment firm D.A. Davidson has significantly raised its price target on Micron Technology Inc. (MU) to $3,000 per share, up 43% from its previous target of $2,100, while maintaining a 'Buy' rating.

Marvell CEO Matt Murphy remained upbeat after the company's Investor Day, stating that its custom chip goal for 2031 needs only a small slice of the market.

title: CAC 40 Falls 1.22% to 7,769.21 as Bond Yields and $100 Brent Crude Hit Paris Banks
body:
Paris's benchmark gave back Tuesday's rebound as French 10-year yields climbed toward 4.9%, Brent crude returned above $100 a barrel and Société Générale and BNP Paribas led a heavy sell-off in banks.

CAC 40 Today: Index Closes at 7,769.21, Down 1.22%

The CAC 40 closed at 7,769.21 points on Wednesday 7 October 2026, down 95.86 points or 1.22% from Tuesday's close of 7,865.07, according to Euronext Paris data reported by BFM Bourse and Zonebourse. The index opened at 7,813.08, already 0.66% lower, and never recovered the 7,800 level after the first hour of trade, slipping toward 7,750 during the afternoon before stabilising into the bell.

The fall erased Tuesday's 0.40% gain and left the Paris benchmark about 11% below its 2026 high of 8,755.03 and only around 3.5% above the year's low of 7,505.27. The broader SBF 120 fell 1.20%. Paris nonetheless held up better than several of its neighbours: Frankfurt's DAX 40 lost 1.35% and Milan's FTSE MIB tumbled 2.51%.

Why Did the CAC 40 Fall on 7 October 2026?

The main driver was the bond market. The yield on France's 10-year OAT climbed to about 4.87% during the session, with Italian press reports putting it near 4.93%, close to its highest level in 18 years. French debt was once again singled out among eurozone sovereigns after a brief improvement on Tuesday, and Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin warned that France is in a risk zone on its deficit and that the 2027 budget plan would be important to reassure markets, dpa-AFX reported.

Energy prices added to the pressure. The December Brent contract moved back above $100 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi airports in Jazan and Najran revived concerns about Middle East supply, while a tropical storm in the Gulf of Mexico threatened US output. Deutsche Bank linked the oil rebound to Iranian attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz. John Plassard of Cité Gestion said higher oil and US yields close to 5.3% show that the latest Wall Street records remain fragile, BFM Bourse reported.

Which CAC 40 Stocks Fell the Most?

Banks bore the brunt. Société Générale dropped 5.0% and BNP Paribas fell 3.9% as investors reassessed the risk attached to French sovereign bond holdings and the possibility of tighter financial conditions. Among the heaviest fallers on the SRD list were Legrand (-4.9%), Soitec (-4.6%), Nexans (-4.5%) and Valeo (-4.3%), with technology and electrical-equipment names hit by the same rise in yields that weighed on growth stocks across Europe. STMicroelectronics and ArcelorMittal were also among the weakest index members according to Zonebourse.

Carmakers were the bright spot. Renault rose 3.7% and Stellantis gained 1.6% after press reports suggested Paris and Berlin could push for an easing of EU rules on combustion-engine vehicles. Auto supplier Forvia added 2.2% after Bank of America upgraded the stock from underperform to buy. Pernod Ricard (+2.8%) and Rémy Cointreau (+3.0%) also advanced, offering a rare defensive bid.

What Do the Fed Minutes Mean for French Stocks?

After the European close, the minutes of the Federal Reserve's 15 and 16 September meeting showed that all 19 participants backed September's rate increase and that most expect another hike before year-end, without committing to the 28 October or 9 December meeting. With the US 10-year Treasury yield touching 5.35% earlier in the day, its highest since 2002, the read-across for Paris is a higher global discount rate at a time when domestic fiscal risk is already elevated.

The euro also weakened, losing about 0.6% to near $1.118, which offers some support to exporters such as luxury and aerospace groups but does little for domestically focused banks and utilities that are most exposed to French funding costs.

CAC 40 Technical Levels to Watch

The 7,750 area tested on Wednesday afternoon is the first support, and below that the 2026 low of 7,505.27 is the key line for the bulls to defend. The 5 October intraday low of 7,796.58 has now been broken on a closing basis and turns into near-term resistance. Above it, the 7,900 to 7,930 zone capped rallies on 2 and 6 October and remains the main hurdle, while a sustained move back above 8,000 would probably require a clear easing in French yields.

How Did Other Global Stock Markets Perform on 7 October 2026?

The selling was broad. London's FTSE 100 shed 0.79% to 10,458.50. Germany's DAX 40 dropped 1.35% to 25,104.36. The EURO STOXX 50 blue-chip gauge lost 1.47% to 6,180.29. Milan's FTSE MIB was Europe's weakest major market, sliding 2.51% to around 49,970. The common thread across Europe was a renewed rise in long-dated government bond yields, with French and Italian debt under the most pressure, combined with Brent crude holding above $100 a barrel.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 eased 0.22% to 7,801.77, one day after a record close. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 341.41 points, or 0.66%, to 51,179.87. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.22% to 27,538.69. Toronto's S&P/TSX Composite sank 1.70% to 35,041.86, a one-month low. In Asia, Tokyo's Nikkei 225 fell 0.92% to 70,035.71. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index declined 0.62% to 24,130.50. India's BSE SENSEX lost 0.59% to 72,638.70 after the Reserve Bank of India raised rates. Mainland China's SSE Composite remained closed for the Golden Week holiday, parked at 3,842.19 until trading resumes on 8 October. The Federal Reserve minutes released at 2 p.m. in Washington confirmed that most policymakers expect one more rate increase before the end of 2026, keeping the focus on borrowing costs into Thursday.

Investor Takeaway

The CAC 40's 1.22% drop was driven less by company news than by the price of money. As long as the French 10-year yield sits near 4.9% and Brent stays above $100, banks and rate-sensitive sectors are likely to remain under pressure, while autos, spirits and exporters benefiting from a softer euro may continue to outperform. The draft 2027 budget and any comments from ratings agencies are the next domestic catalysts to watch.

Rising French government bond yields, Brent crude back above $100 a barrel and caution ahead of the Federal Reserve minutes hit the index, with banks such as Société Générale (-5.0%) and BNP Paribas (-3.9%) leading the decline.

Which CAC 40 stocks rose on 7 October 2026?

Renault (+3.7%) and Stellantis (+1.6%) gained on reports of a possible easing of EU combustion-engine rules, while Pernod Ricard rose about 2.8%.

title: Dow Jones (DJIA) Drops 341 Points to 51,179.87 as Caterpillar Slumps and Treasury Yields Climb
body:
The blue-chip average underperformed the S&P 500 and Nasdaq as Caterpillar fell almost 6%, only about a dozen of its 30 members advanced and the 10-year Treasury yield touched its highest level since 2002.

Dow Jones Close Today: 51,179.87, Down 341.41 Points

The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 51,179.87 on Wednesday 7 October 2026, down 341.41 points or 0.66% from Tuesday's close of 51,521.28, according to CNBC and TheStreet. The index fell about 440 points in the first minutes of trading, recovered part of the drop during the afternoon and finished near the middle of its daily range.

The Dow underperformed the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite, which each fell 0.22%. Only around 12 of the 30 Dow components were higher during the afternoon, according to TheStreet. The decline erased Tuesday's gain of 253.38 points and left the index more than 2,600 points below the levels above 53,700 it reached in mid-August.

Why Did the Dow Jones Underperform?

The Dow is price-weighted, which means that a large move in a high-priced stock has an outsized impact. Caterpillar, one of the most expensive stocks in the average at more than $800 a share, fell 5.75% to $813.83. A drop of almost $50 a share in a single high-priced component accounts for a large part of the Dow's daily decline. Industrials as a whole were under pressure amid risk-off sentiment and concerns that higher borrowing costs will hit capital spending.

TheStreet noted that the Dow and the Russell 2000, which fell 1.31%, have been moving in a similar way in recent months, because both are more exposed to economically sensitive companies than the technology-heavy S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Rising rates have been more damaging to those parts of the market.

What Drove Wall Street Lower?

The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.35% in the morning, its highest since 2002, and the 30-year to about 5.72%, a 24-year high, CNBC reported. Oil prices also rose, with Brent at about $102 in the morning after Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and as Tropical Storm Isaias threatened Gulf of Mexico production. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that high energy prices, record public debt and risks linked to the AI investment boom threaten global growth.

The Federal Reserve minutes, published at 2 p.m., showed that all 19 participants backed September's rate increase and that most expect another hike before the end of 2026, though the timing between the 28 October and 9 December meetings remains open.

Which Dow Stocks Rose and Fell?

Besides Caterpillar, losses were widespread among industrial and consumer names. McDonald's slipped about 0.4% in the morning after a federal lawsuit alleged that its AI-enhanced pricing tool for franchisees violated antitrust laws, claims the company said were filled with inaccuracies. Nvidia eased 0.76% after its record run.

Gains in Amgen (+2.6%), Amazon (+1.42%) and Apple (+0.91%) helped cushion the decline. Several healthcare names, including Amgen, Gilead Sciences and Eli Lilly, were among the better performers on the day, consistent with a defensive tilt as yields rose.

Dow Jones Technical Levels

The 51,000 level is the immediate support. A close below it, and then below 50,500, would suggest a deeper correction is under way. On the upside, 51,500 to 51,600, Tuesday's close and intraday range, is the first resistance.

What Is the Dow Jones Industrial Average?

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, first published by Charles Dow in 1896, tracks 30 large US companies and is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices. Unlike the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, which are weighted by market capitalisation, the Dow is price-weighted: each stock's influence depends on its share price rather than its company value, and the sum of prices is divided by a divisor that adjusts for splits and membership changes.

That methodology explains why a single expensive stock such as Caterpillar can move the average significantly. Members span technology, healthcare, finance, retail and industrials, including Apple, Amazon, Nvidia, Amgen, McDonald's and Goldman Sachs. Because of its narrow membership and price weighting, many professional investors treat the S&P 500 as a better gauge of the overall US market, but the Dow remains the most widely quoted barometer of Wall Street sentiment and a useful indicator of how industrial and blue-chip names are faring.

title: Greek Banks Better Protected From Rising Bond Yields
body:
Greek banks have significantly increased their holdings of government bonds in recent years, but they hold the vast majority until maturity, limiting their exposure to the risks created by the recent rise in bond yields, according to an analysis by credit rating agency DBRS on European banks.

The value of government bonds held by Greek banks reached almost 300% of their Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital in June 2026, compared with less than 100% in June 2019.

That figure exceeds the average for banks across the European Union and European Economic Area, where government bond holdings rose to 264% of CET1 from 214% at the end of 2022, reaching their highest level since 2019.

However, Greek banks remain below their counterparts in Portugal, Italy and Spain, whose holdings stood at 367%, 361% and 342%, respectively.

Greek Banks Diversify Government Bond Holdings

The increase in Greek banks' government bond exposure has also coincided with greater participation by other countries' sovereign securities in their portfolios.

Greek government bonds accounted for less than 50% of Greek banks' total government bond portfolios in June 2026, down from more than 60% in June 2019.

Across the EU and EEA, the corresponding share fell to 43%, from a peak of 53% in June 2021.

DBRS said the trend partly reflects banks' search for higher yields and greater diversification opportunities. This diversification could, in turn, weaken the traditionally close interdependence between banks and their respective sovereigns.

Greek Banks Hold Longest-Dated Bonds

Greek banks also hold the highest proportion of government bonds with maturities of more than five years, at 71%.

Across EU and EEA banks, the proportion increased to 46% from 42% in June 2019.

More than 80% of Greek banks' government bonds use amortised-cost accounting, meaning the banks generally hold the securities until maturity. As a result, rising government bond yields do not translate into accounting losses on those holdings.

The corresponding figure for EU and EEA banks stands at 59%.

DBRS also noted that banks' portfolios of long-term bonds held at amortised cost protect their net interest income from greater interest-rate volatility over the medium term.

Greek banks hold only a small single-digit percentage of their government bonds for trading purposes, according to DBRS data.

DBRS Sees Weaker Bank-Sovereign Link

DBRS said the traditional relationship between sovereigns and banks has become less direct as European banks have reduced their focus on domestic government bonds and operate under a stronger supervisory framework than during previous periods of financial stress.

Nevertheless, European banks still maintain significant government bond exposures.

Banks have built larger portfolios of longer-duration securities, making them more sensitive to interest-rate movements if government bond yields continue to rise.

DBRS nevertheless expects the impact on European banks to remain manageable, citing the large share of sovereign debt held at amortised cost, improved earnings generation and stronger balance sheets.

title: Wall Street ends lower, off record highs, as Treasury yields climb
body:
[NEW YORK] Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday (Oct 7), as long-dated US Treasury yields resumed their climb, reviving fears about inflation and mounting debt the day after the S&P 500 Index and the Nasdaq Composite hit record closing highs.

All three major US stock indices were modestly lower, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average snapping four-day winning streaks. The Nasdaq notched its first down day in six.

The small-cap Russell 2000 Index underperformed its larger-cap counterparts, dropping 1.3 per cent.

In the wake of Tuesday's stock market rally, Brent crude settled above US$100 per barrel and long-dated Treasury yields touched a 24-year high.

Iran war-related supply concerns have led to soaring oil prices, which in turn have revived inflation worries and raised the chances of a prolonged central bank rate-hiking cycle.

Those concerns, combined with mounting corporate and sovereign debt levels, have caused a global bond sell-off, which rattled global markets in recent weeks.

Investors "have been looking for some relief on oil, which would drive some relief on rates and that would therefore help the stock market," said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt in Atlanta.

"The third quarter was supposed to be the weak quarter of the year; we were supposed to get a correction," Martin added.

"That didn't happen, so it's three cheers and let's take some money off the table."

Stocks pared losses after crude prices turned lower following the International Energy Agency's agreement to speed up the release of oil stocks, prioritising diesel.

Minutes from the US Federal Reserve's September monetary policy meeting, at which the central bank unanimously approved its first interest rate hike since July 2023, revealed divisions over the rationale of the increase.

Some participants saw a hike as necessary to keep the impact of energy price shocks at bay, while others felt the increase was necessary to curb demand-driven inflation.

Financial markets are currently pricing in a 17.2 per cent likelihood that the Fed will implement a second consecutive rate hike at the conclusion of its October meeting, down from 37.6 per cent a week ago, per CME's FedWatch tool.

"The market's Fed expectations are going to seesaw as it gets new bits of data," Martin said.

"There's still an expectation for more rate hikes, but it isn't necessarily going to be a hike every meeting and that's what the market is telling you; October will be a pause."

The Dow fell 341.11 points, or 0.66 per cent, to 51,180.17, the S&P 500 lost 17.18 points, or 0.22 per cent, to 7,801.75 and the Nasdaq lost 61.19 points, or 0.22 per cent, to 27,538.69.

Among the 11 sectors in the S&P 500, industrials suffered the steepest percentage drop, while healthcare stocks led the gainers.

Following the upward march of benchmark Treasury yields, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate surged last week to a near three-year high, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association.

Housing and homebuilders slipped 2.3 per cent and 2.9 per cent, respectively.

Chip stocks, which have soared over 80 per cent so far this year, dropped 1.2 per cent.

SpaceX lost 2.5 per cent following media reports that Elon Musk's aerospace firm was seeking US$40 billion in financing to fund purchases of Nvidia chips.

Next week, third-quarter reporting season is expected to begin in earnest with a spate of high-profile financial firms expected to post results.

Investors are likely to scrutinise the extent to which massive expenditures on artificial intelligence technology are beginning to show results, while also watching for clues regarding the health of the US consumer at a time of mounting inflationary pressures.

Analysts currently expect year-on-year S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6 per cent, on aggregate, for the July-through-September period, according to LSEG.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.34-to-1 ratio on the NYSE.

There were 115 new highs and 497 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 1,421 stocks rose and 3,371 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.37-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted nine new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq recorded 32 new highs and 250 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 16.21 billion shares, compared with the 17.57 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

title: Stock Indices Fall as Treasury Yields Hit 20-Year High
body:
Stock Indices Fall as Treasury Yields Hit 20-Year High

Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Decline as 10-Year Yield Tops 5.36%, Highest Since 2002

U.S. Treasury yields surged to their highest levels in over two decades, causing the three major New York stock indices to fall simultaneously. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq indices, which hit record highs the previous day, also declined within a single day.

On October 7 (local time), the Dow Jones 30 Industrial Average closed at 51,179.87, down 341.41 points (0.66%) from the previous session. The S&P 500 index fell 17.16 points (0.22%) to 7,801.77, and the Nasdaq Composite Index dropped 61.20 points (0.22%) to 27,538.69.

Treasury yields continued to rise due to inflation concerns driven by rising international oil prices and worries over expanded fiscal spending by the U.S. government. The 10-year yield exceeded 5.36% during trading, marking its highest level since 2002, while the 30-year yield also climbed to 5.73%, the highest in 24 years.

The upward momentum in yields slowed after strong demand was observed in the U.S. Treasury's $39 billion 10-year note auction. The 10-year yield fell to around 5.28%, but the auction's bid rate of 5.3% remained the highest since 2000.

A decline in international oil prices also helped curb further losses in the stock market. Following news that the International Energy Agency (IEA) would accelerate the release of oil reserves, November-delivery West Texas Intermediate crude (WTI) fell $1.16 (1.3%) from the previous session. December-delivery Brent crude closed at $100.2 per barrel, down 38 cents (0.38%).

The Federal Reserve's September Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting minutes, released the same day, indicated a focus on additional rate hikes within the year. Most participants assessed that raising the benchmark interest rate once more by the end of the year would likely be appropriate, though no specific timing was provided.

David Russell, TradeStation's global market strategist, stated, "Given that current monetary policy is not particularly restrictive, the likelihood of additional rate hikes this year is high. With inflation exceeding the target and most economic activity indicators remaining strong, price stability remains the Fed's top priority."

title: Wall Street Retreats From Records as Treasury Yields Climb - [your]NEWS
body:
U.S. stocks closed lower Wednesday as long-term Treasury yields climbed to multi-decade highs, reviving inflation and debt concerns a day after the S&P 500 and Nasdaq finished at record levels.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.

Wall Street pulled back from record highs Wednesday as rising long-term Treasury yields renewed concerns about inflation, government borrowing and the possibility that interest rates could remain elevated longer than investors had hoped.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 341.11 points, or 0.66%, to 51,180.17. The S&P 500 lost 17.18 points, or 0.22%, to close at 7,801.75, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 61.19 points, or 0.22%, to 27,538.69.

The S&P 500 and Dow snapped four-session winning streaks, while the Nasdaq recorded its first decline in six trading days. The small-cap Russell 2000 underperformed, dropping 1.3%.

The retreat came one day after the S&P 500 and Nasdaq reached record closing highs as investors looked ahead to the start of third-quarter earnings season.

Wednesday's losses were driven largely by the bond market.

Long-dated Treasury yields resumed their climb, with the 30-year yield touching its highest level in 24 years. Investors have been demanding higher yields amid concerns about persistent inflation, heavy federal borrowing and mounting corporate debt.

Oil prices added to those concerns.

Brent crude settled above $100 per barrel as the Iran war continued to disrupt energy supplies and raise fears that elevated fuel costs could keep inflation pressures alive.

"Investors have been looking for some relief on oil, which would drive some relief on rates and that would therefore help the stock market," Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at GLOBALT in Atlanta, said.

"The third quarter was supposed to be the weak quarter of the year; we were supposed to get a correction," Martin added. "That didn't happen, so it's three cheers and let's take some money off the table."

Stocks pared some of their losses later in the session after crude prices turned lower following an International Energy Agency decision to accelerate the release of emergency oil stocks, with diesel prioritized.

Investors were also digesting newly released minutes from the Federal Reserve's September meeting.

The central bank unanimously raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, marking its first increase since July 2023. The minutes showed policymakers agreed on the action but differed over the reasoning behind it.

Some officials viewed the rate increase as necessary to keep energy and supply shocks from becoming embedded in inflation, while others believed stronger demand was itself generating inflationary pressure that required tighter monetary policy.

Despite those concerns, financial markets have become less convinced that the Fed will raise rates again at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.

CME FedWatch pricing showed a 17.2% probability of another increase in October, down from 37.6% one week earlier.

"The market's Fed expectations are going to seesaw as it gets new bits of data," Martin said. "There's still an expectation for more rate hikes, but it isn't necessarily going to be a hike every meeting and that's what the market is telling you; October will be a pause."

Higher Treasury yields are already filtering into household borrowing costs.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed U.S. mortgage rose to 7.49% in the week ending Oct. 2, its highest level since November 2023, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association.

Housing-related stocks reflected that pressure Wednesday. The S&P housing index declined 2.3%, while homebuilders fell 2.9%.

Technology shares also weakened after a powerful run earlier in the year.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 1.2% Wednesday after chip stocks had gained more than 80% so far in 2026.

SpaceX shares dropped 2.5% after reports that Elon Musk's aerospace company was seeking approximately $40 billion in financing to purchase Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips. The proposed financing reportedly includes about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt.

Attention is now shifting toward corporate earnings.

Third-quarter reporting season is expected to accelerate next week as major financial companies begin releasing results. Investors are expected to focus closely on whether massive artificial-intelligence spending is translating into revenue and profit growth, while also watching for signs of strain among U.S. consumers facing higher borrowing costs and renewed inflation pressure.

Analysts currently expect aggregate S&P 500 earnings for the July-through-September quarter to rise 30.6% from a year earlier, according to LSEG.

Market breadth was notably weak Wednesday.

Declining stocks outnumbered advancing shares by more than 3-to-1 on the New York Stock Exchange, while 3,371 Nasdaq-listed stocks fell compared with 1,421 that advanced.

The session underscored the tension confronting investors after a strong equity rally: corporate earnings expectations remain robust, but oil above $100, historically high long-term yields and renewed inflation concerns are increasing the cost of capital across the economy.

For now, Wall Street remains near record territory, but Wednesday's retreat showed that rising rates and energy prices can quickly interrupt the momentum.

title: US Dollar Hits 18-Month High as Fed Signals More Rate Hikes
body:
The U.S. dollar climbed to a nearly 18-month high on Wednesday as Federal Reserve minutes signaled another interest rate hike could come before year-end, while weakness in the euro and British pound provided additional support.

The U.S. Dollar Index, which measures the greenback against six major currencies, gained 0.4% to 102.24, hovering around its strongest level since April 9, 2025.

Minutes from the Fed's September meeting showed that most Federal Open Market Committee participants believed another increase in the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by the end of 2026. The Fed unanimously raised rates by 25 basis points in September, its first increase in more than three years.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has also emphasized the challenge of bringing inflation back toward the central bank's 2% target. However, expectations for an October hike remain limited, with markets assigning an approximately 83% probability that rates will remain unchanged.

The euro fell 0.6% to $1.1195 as investors focused on France's worsening fiscal outlook and political uncertainty. France's budget deficit is projected at 5.4% of GDP this year, while public debt is nearing 120% of GDP. The government's 2027 budget proposal seeks €54 billion in spending reductions to bring the deficit to 5%.

French bond yields have surged amid concerns over public finances and political tensions ahead of next year's presidential election, adding pressure to the euro.

Sterling also weakened, falling 0.5% to $1.3213 as Britain's 30-year government bond yield reached its highest level since January 1998. UK officials reiterated their commitment to fiscal credibility amid challenging global financial conditions.

In Asia, the Indian rupee dropped as low as 97.151 per dollar despite the Reserve Bank of India raising its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%. The RBI also shifted its policy stance to "calibrated tightening," but the widely expected hike failed to offset pressure from high crude oil prices and continued capital outflows.
