title: Iranian Oil, a Minor Player and the Limits of US Sanctions
body:
JOHOR STATE, Malaysia -- In early 2024, an aging tanker anchored off Malaysia's coast delivered more than 500,000 barrels of oil that were said to be from Oman, but were in fact from Iran.

The deception was intended to evade U.S. sanctions on Iranian oil, which have long been part of Washington's efforts to choke off revenue for Tehran's military and nuclear weapons program. The ship, the Palau-flagged Reneez, was not on the list of blacklisted entities that the U.S. government maintains online.

Shahul Hamid Ahmad, who owned a small Malaysian shipping agency, said he thought little of taking a job to coordinate repairs and an inspection of the ship. His company, Tefcas Marine, was one of many companies that specialize in arranging port services for ships passing by Johor state.

But halfway through the repairs, the tanker was placed under sanctions for ties to Sa'id al-Jamal, a Houthi financier who previously had been sanctioned by the United States for leading a network that procured "tens of millions of dollars" by smuggling Iranian oil. In late 2024, Tefcas and two other Malaysian companies were hit with sanctions for having "materially assisted" al-Jamal.

The action was part of an expanding effort by Washington to crack down on foreign maritime service providers, which U.S. officials have said facilitate Iran's oil trade.

For Shahul, 62, the outcome felt staggeringly disproportionate. His company's bank closed his accounts and Microsoft locked his company email, which holds records he needs to file taxes.

Tefcas made around $2,500 from the 2024 engagement, according to invoices viewed by The New York Times. But at least nine other entities involved with the Reneez since it began shipping Iranian oil in 2023 went untouched, the Times has found. Among them was a major East Asian oil company that received the cargo.

"We always turned down sanctioned vessels," Shahul said. "I would not jeopardize my company for that money."

The waters around Malaysia have increasingly become the center of Iran's oil trade. It's where tankers transfer the crude to vessels that take them to the eventual customer, mainly Chinese refineries. In August, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sweeping new sanctions to target the shipping facilitators that enable the trade.

But Tefcas's case, experts said, illustrated the limits of Washington's increasing crackdown.

"Sanctioning these small players is a warning shot, but I'm honestly not sure if that warning shot has been heard given this activity continues," said David Tannenbaum, a former official at the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control and the director of Blackstone Compliance Services, a consulting firm.

Since Tefcas was sanctioned, the trade of Iranian oil near Malaysia has only grown, contributing to the 667 million barrels exported by Tehran in 2025, according to data from United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit.

In Malaysia and Singapore, the buyers of Iranian oil have continued to operate with impunity, said Jeffrey Soh, director of Contemporary Logistics, a Malaysian maritime services company.

Soh, whose company owned the floating storage unit into which the Reneez had deposited its Iranian cargo in 2024, said that both his company and the local port authority had failed to screen out the vessel. So did the apparent charterer of the oil, which was a major state-linked oil corporation in China, according to a contract viewed by the Times.

But all three avoided sanctions, Soh said, adding that his company had cut ties with that client, which he believed knew of the oil's Iranian origins. He spoke on the condition that the customer not be named, citing risks of legal retaliation.

"Some companies, it's an open secret that they trade Iranian barrels," he said. "The case with Tefcas was really an injustice."

U.S. sanctions, by design, do not necessarily point to the biggest or most culpable actors, said Erich C. Ferrari, the founder of Ferrari & Associates, a Washington-based law firm.

"The consequences of designating a large trading house or a counterparty in a politically sensitive jurisdiction are weighed at the interagency level," he said.

"OFAC designates to produce an effect," he added, referring to the Office of Foreign Assets Control. "And the effect it wanted here was to deter the service ecosystem around these transfers, which you can do with small agents at very little diplomatic cost."

While some companies deliberately flout sanctions, many others are likely unwittingly exposed. While Soh's firm has spent thousands of dollars to upgrade its screening capabilities, he said not every business has "the financial ability to do that."

Last year, Shahul asked OFAC to reconsider his case. He has not yet heard back. A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment on his case.

Because Shahul has been accused of collaborating with a terrorist, his former clients refuse to settle unpaid invoices, but he still owes various creditors $240,000.

"I think I have under a year to solve this," he said.

But the Reneez has continued to ship Iranian oil, according to satellite data from TankerTrackers.com. It was spotted near Malaysia as recently as May, under a new name and flag.

--

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

title: Carney must hit Iran's Ayatollah with sanctions and legal action, human rights advocates say
body:
OTTAWA -- The Carney government should directly target Iran's leader and his allies with sanctions and legal action to close the "impunity gap" and to ensure that this country doesn't become a safe haven for repression, a coalition of human rights groups and an all-party group of MPs insisted Wednesday.

Speaking on Parliament Hill on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led terrorist attack on Israel that killed an estimated 1,200 people, the human rights advocates warned that more atrocities in Iran are likely if democratic governments don't do more to limit the Iranian government's power.

Irwin Cotler, a former Liberal MP and cabinet minister and now an advocate, told reporters that it's a critical moment in the battle between human rights and the government of Iran. The government killed an estimated 40,000 protesters and critics over two days in January and has since followed with repressive techniques such as controlling mass communications and detentions, disappearances, torture, rape and more executions.

Cotler, who also faced an Iranian assassination plot for his efforts to call out the regime, said the Iranian regime's repression tactics extend to other countries, including Canada.

Shilan Mirzaee, a democracy advocate and former political prisoner, held up a photo at the press conference of a young couple who were arrested a month ago, just a couple of days before they were to be married. He was then executed while she remains in prison.

Despite the U.S.-led attacks on Iran over the last seven months, that country is still governed by the Islamic Republic of Iran. Canada does not have diplomatic relations with Iran and Ottawa has designated its government a supporter of terrorism.

After tens of thousands of Iranians took to the streets earlier this year to protest soaring prices and a weak economy, government soldiers opened fire after demonstrators called for regime change. A widespread brutal crackdown ensued.

Less than two months later, the United States and Israel began large-scale strikes on Iranian facilities, reportedly out of concern about the advance of Iran's efforts to build nuclear weapons. The early attacks in February killed the previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, 86, the current leader's father, who had ruled since 1989.

The attacks and the war, which have led to oil supply problems and rising prices, have not ended.

The advocates in Ottawa, which included the Iranian Justice Collective and the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights, also released a report Wednesday with 12 steps that Canada should take to counter the Iranian regime and stand up for human rights.

Beyond sanctioning the leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, and other senior members of the government, the list includes:

* Passing Bill C-219, a private member's bill to strengthen Canada's ability to fight corruption and human rights abuses. The proposed legislation has passed second reading in the House of Commons and is now being studied by the foreign affairs committee.

* Sanctions against the "shadow" banking, shipping and other networks used to support repression. That could include using sanctions to freeze and forfeit assets to compensate victims and their families.

* Strengthen anti-money laundering efforts, including going after jurisdictions such as Hong Kong seen as money-laundering hubs.

* Support Iranians' access to the Internet, which has been restricted by the government.

title: EU reportedly agrees major expansion of Russia sanctions blacklist
body:
EU member states agreed Wednesday to place more than 1,600 additional individuals and organizations under sanctions over Russia's war in Ukraine, Euronews reported.

The agreement reached by EU ambassadors would add 743 people and 826 entities to the bloc's blacklist over their alleged role in supporting Russia's war.

Another 77 lawmakers are set to face restrictions after standing in September's State Duma election in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, according to the report.

The decision followed weeks of negotiations and legal checks and is due to receive formal approval from EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg on Monday.

Those designated will face asset freezes and travel restrictions, while EU individuals and companies will be barred from making funds available to them, according to the report.

The agreement comes as European governments confront a series of suspected hybrid attacks which they attributed to Russia.

Brussels is also considering further designations following a drone incident at Leipzig airport in Germany.

The latest expansion will bring the total number of names in the EU's Russia-related sanctions list to nearly 4,650, according to the report.

title: EU Council to adopt new sanctions targeting Russian military-industrial complex on Monday 12 October
body:
The Council of the EU is expected to formally adopt new sanctions on Monday 12 October targeting nearly 1,600 people and entities linked to Russia's war in Ukraine (see EUROPE 13947/16).

The Committee of Permanent Representatives of the EU Member States (Coreper) approved legislative proposals to this effect on Wednesday 7 October. The sanctions will have to be formally endorsed on Monday by EU foreign ministers when they meet in Luxembourg. They comprise a series of decisions and regulations concerning restrictive measures in response to actions that undermine or threaten Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence.

The new sanctions target 743 individuals and 826 entities, all linked to Russia's military-industrial complex. In addition, 77 new entries on the EU 'blacklist' were approved following the recent Duma elections, which the EU deemed undemocratic. They include three members of the electoral commission.

In total, nearly 4,500 people and entities will now be subject to EU sanctions for their role in Russia's war. (Original version in French by Lionel Changeur)

title: Iran sends $200 million to Hezbollah for Lebanon war aid amid US sanctions- Moneycontrol.com
body: Iran has transferred around $200 million to Hezbollah to help Lebanese civilians displaced by its war with Israel, with the militant group planning to distribute the money to families worst affected by the conflict. According to two people with direct knowledge of the transfer quoted by Reuters, the funds, received last month, are expected to be used for an initial payment of around $3,000 per family, with priority given to households whose villages have been destroyed or remain inaccessible because of the Israeli occupation. One source estimated that around 50,000 families could qualify for the initial assistance. A Hezbollah official confirmed that the group had secured funds and said a plan for distributing the money would be announced in the coming days, but did not elaborate on the source. The reported transfer comes as Iran faces mounting US economic pressure under Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast", which has tightened sanctions on Tehran and targeted its ability to generate and move revenue from oil exports. Moving the money to Lebanon has also become increasingly difficult, with intermediaries reportedly charging as much as 20% to transfer the funds -- four times the normal fee, according to one source. Iran's foreign ministry, its permanent mission in Geneva, the US State Department and the Lebanese government have not commented on the reported $200 million transfer. Iran's long-standing financial support for Hezbollah The reported payment underscores Hezbollah's continued dependence on Iran, which has provided financial backing to the group for decades despite sweeping US sanctions. The US Treasury Department said Iran transferred $1 billion to Hezbollah in the first 10 months of 2025 alone. Tehran has never publicly acknowledged financing the group. Hezbollah was founded by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 1982 and has long been a key component of Tehran's regional network of allied armed groups. Its reliance on Iranian funding has, however, become increasingly difficult to sustain as US sanctions have intensified and the group has faced severe financial and military pressure following its conflict with Israel. Iran had also promised Hezbollah additional financial support after Tehran reached an interim agreement with Washington in June that allowed it to resume oil sales. That agreement collapsed in July, after which Washington stepped up economic pressure on Iran, including measures aimed at restricting its oil exports. The funding of Hezbollah has also been politically sensitive inside Iran, where Tehran's support for regional proxy groups has previously triggered anger among protesters amid domestic economic hardship. Hezbollah faces pressure to support displaced Lebanese The latest reported transfer comes after Israel's bombardment and ground offensive in Lebanon displaced hundreds of thousands of people from Lebanon's Shi'ite community, which forms much of Hezbollah's support base. Hezbollah entered the wider regional conflict in support of Iran on March 2. The group has since suffered heavy losses and significant damage to its infrastructure, while Israeli attacks have devastated villages in southern Lebanon. Despite the scale of the displacement, Hezbollah has provided little visible assistance to many affected families so far, a sharp contrast with its response after the 2006 war with Israel. At that time, Hezbollah rapidly distributed cash payments to displaced families and helped rebuild parts of Beirut's southern suburbs, its main stronghold. This time, however, reconstruction has been considerably slower. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that rebuilding after the two wars since 2024 could cost more than $27 billion. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a speech last month that the group would contribute to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced by the conflict, using "available resources and donations". US disputes claims The United States, however, has disputed the reported $200 million transfer. US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the money "is not there" and accused Hezbollah of attempting to "save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran". A US Treasury spokesperson separately said Iran was "running out of money and ways to move money", adding that Tehran "does not have money to fund its campaign of terror". Pigott said Washington would continue targeting Hezbollah's finances through sanctions while supporting Lebanon's legitimate government in rebuilding the country's south. On Tuesday, Iran's Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said that while Iran was indeed facing an "economic war" under intense US pressure, Tehran decided to inject $2 billion in currency into the market to send a message directly to US President Donald Trump and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that that the country has no shortage of foreign exchange. According to Hemmati, Iran had supplied about $24.9bn in foreign currency by early October, down about 12 percent from $28bn during the same period last year.

title: UEFA monitoring Man City's legal battle over financial breaches; secondary sanctions may follow
body:
Manchester [UK], October 7 (ANI): Manchester City's off-field legal battle over alleged financial rule breaches could have wider ramifications, with UEFA monitoring the club's appeal against the Premier League's findings and the possibility of secondary sanctions at the European level, according to Goal.com.

Manchester City was found guilty on 114 of 115 charges brought by the Premier League over alleged financial rule breaches. One of the most serious allegations concerned the club allegedly orchestrating artificial sponsorship agreements to boost its revenue by approximately 900 million pounds between 2009 and 2018, a period during which the club emerged as one of the dominant forces in English football and won three Premier League titles.

Following the verdict, the Premier League club officially began its appeal process last week and has continued to maintain its innocence, claiming it has ''irrefutable evidence' that will clear it of the charges.

A three-person independent panel will review Manchester City's appeal, with a resolution expected before the end of the season.

As per a Sky Sports report quoted by Goal.com, UEFA is closely monitoring the legal proceedings and will wait for the outcome of the three-person panel before deciding whether to launch its own investigation into the matter.

If the Premier League's ruling is upheld, it will be uncertain what punishment UEFA will impose on Man City. The prospect of secondary, European-level sanctions looms large over the club and its rich legacy built over the last decade or so.

This is not the first time Manchester City and UEFA have been at loggerheads over financial regulations. UEFA initially banned the English club from European competition for two years in 2020 and imposed a fine of 30 million pounds for Financial Fair Play breaches.

However, the two-year ban was overturned after Manchester City appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). The financial penalty was subsequently reduced to 10 million pounds.

Domestically, the problems awaiting the club look massive, ranging from point deductions to stripping of past major titles to complete ouster from the Premier League, the top-flight English football competition.

After the international break, City, who are currently at the top of the Premier League with five wins from five matches, are scheduled to resume their campaign against Liverpool at Anfield on October 11. (ANI)

title: Govt rolls out digital system for financial sanctions
body:
Move aligns with SASCI guidelines on strengthening public finance IT infra

Srinagar, Oct 7: The Jammu and Kashmir government has approved the operationalisation of the e-sanction and re-appropriation & surrender modules on the Jammu and Kashmir Budget Estimation, Allocation and Monitoring System (JK BEAMS) to digitise the processing of financial sanctions and budget adjustments across the Union Territory.

The Finance Department, through government order no. 310-F of 2026, issued under the Budget Division, said the two modules have been technically completed and will now be implemented across all Administrative Departments, Controlling Officers, Heads of Departments, Drawing and Disbursing Officers (DDOs) and other concerned authorities.

The move has been taken in line with the 2026-27 State Annual Scheme for Capital Investment (SASCI) guidelines issued by the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, particularly the provisions relating to strengthening public finance IT infrastructure in states.

Under the e-sanction module, administrative and financial sanctions will be prepared, processed, approved and issued through a prescribed digital workflow within JK BEAMS.

The government has directed that sanctions issued through the system shall be digitally signed by the competent authority through the e-Sanction Module, replacing the need for conventional physical processing wherever the module applies.

Similarly, proposals relating to budget re-appropriation and surrender will have to be submitted, examined, processed and approved through the newly introduced re-appropriation & surrender module.

The finance department has directed authorities to surrender anticipated savings and reallocate funds through the digital module in a timely manner, in accordance with applicable financial rules and delegated powers.

According to the order, the status of sanctions as well as re-appropriation and surrender proposals will be available online to concerned authorities. Digital records of all cases will also be maintained through the modules for monitoring, verification and audit purposes.

The finance department said the digital system is aimed at reducing dependence on physical files and manual processing while establishing a streamlined workflow and a proper digital audit trail for government financial transactions.

The budget division of the finance department will provide technical support for the rollout and implementation of both modules across Jammu and Kashmir.

The order was issued by the Financial Commissioner (Additional Chief Secretary), Finance Department, Shailendra Kumar, IAS.

title: Ukrainian Sea Drones Set Sochi Ablaze, Hitting Russia Where Sanctions Failed
body:
With 300-Plus Vessels Hit, Ukraine's Drone Fleet Is Enforcing What Sanctions Could Not

A Liberia-flagged crude oil tanker loaded with up to 100,000 metric tons (approximately 110,000 short tons, or about 750,000 barrels) of Russian crude caught fire off the coast of Sochi on Tuesday evening after Ukrainian naval drones struck it in the Black Sea -- the most visible demonstration yet that Ukraine's uncrewed surface vessel campaign is physically enforcing what three years of Western diplomatic sanctions could not. Russia's Transport Ministry confirmed that the Liberian-flagged vessel, identified by open-source trackers as the Aframax Rio, had been attacked by "naval drones" and that crude oil was burning openly in the sea. All 23 Indian crew were rescued. The fire, which broke out around 6 p.m. Tuesday evening, sent towering columns of black smoke over Sochi, a resort city of nearly 500,000 people and the host of Russia's 2014 Winter Olympics. Beaches and waterfront promenades were closed until further notice, and residents in both Sochi and the adjacent Sirius federal territory were told to limit outdoor time and keep windows shut. By Wednesday morning, firefighters had extinguished the blaze and cleanup operations had begun. The Ministry maintained that no oil spill had occurred.

The Aframax Rio strike is not an isolated act of war. It falls within Operation MoLoChKa -- a Ukrainian acronym meaning "Moscow will fall through Crimea" -- a systematic naval drone campaign that Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) launched on July 6, 2026, targeting vessels tied to Russia's sanctions-evading shadow fleet. In the three months since, the operation has struck more than 300 shadow-fleet vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. What began as a series of disabling strikes on river barges and small tankers in the Sea of Azov has escalated into a sustained maritime denial campaign targeting Russia's most economically critical export corridor -- and the Aframax Rio's fire, visible from a major resort beach, marks its most dramatic geographic escalation yet.

What Operation MoLoChKa Has Accomplished

The scale of the campaign is unlike anything previously seen in modern maritime warfare. In just the first 11 days -- from July 6 through July 16 -- Ukrainian drone operators struck 147 vessels in 11 days, including 117 in the Sea of Azov and 30 in the Black Sea. By July 28, the count had reached 201 vessels. By September 22, the USF claimed 300 total strikes, with 285 shadow-fleet vessels hit in the first ten weeks -- 215 in July, 54 in August, and 16 in the first half of September.

USF Commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi -- whose call sign comes from the Ukrainian word for "courage" -- has consistently framed the operation's goal in logistical terms rather than kinetic ones: impose "systemic pressure on the logistics chain," not simply a vessel count. "We turn every self-propelled watercraft into a blind and deaf barge drifting at sea," Brovdi said in a July statement, explaining why his units deliberately avoid hull breaches that would cause oil spills. "The goal is not to pollute the waters with oil slicks."

That doctrine has produced measurable behavioral change. Russia has diverted frontline drone units to commercial shipping protection, deploying up to 200 protection groups from the Rubicon unit, one of the most effective drone warfare units in the Russian military, to escort shadow-fleet vessels. "The occupiers have already understood the level of threat and are now forced to factor in the risk of being struck even before a vessel sets out on its route," USF spokeswoman Olha Meloshyna told LIGA.net. In September 2026, Ukrainian drone footage showed an uncrewed vessel maneuvering under fire from a Russian helicopter before striking the Armada Leader tanker near Sochi -- the helicopter had been assigned specifically to intercept the drone.

The Kerch Strait, Brovdi stated, has been effectively blockaded for an indefinite period. Shipping in the northern and northeastern Black Sea has been "significantly hampered."

How Ukraine's Naval Drones Work: Sea Denial Without a Navy

Ukraine has no conventional Black Sea navy. Russia's Black Sea Fleet drove it from open water in the early days of the 2022 invasion. What Ukraine built instead -- beginning with the first drone-boat attack on Russia's fleet at Sevastopol in October 2022 -- is a class of uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs) that has progressively transferred maritime dominance.

The primary strike system in Operation MoLoChKa is the MAGURA family of naval drones, developed by Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) and UFORCE. The MAGURA V5's range reaches 800 kilometers (500 miles) at a top speed of 42 knots (78 km/h or 48 mph) using a small, high-speed catamaran-hull platform. The MAGURA V7, unveiled May 2025, extends operational range to 800 nautical miles (approximately 1,500 km) using a 270-horsepower diesel engine and 1,200-liter fuel tanks, and can operate autonomously for 48 hours or up to seven days when paired with a generator. In May 2025, MAGURA V7 drones shot down two Russian Su-30SM fighter jets -- the first time an uncrewed surface vessel class downed enemy aircraft in combat.

The operation also uses aerial drone units -- the USF's "Birds" -- that fly over open water, making them harder to intercept than sea-surface vessels and capable of tracking targets that have disabled their AIS (Automatic Identification System) transponders. Shadow fleet vessels routinely switch off their AIS to evade tracking; Ukraine counters with satellite imagery of the vessel (the Aframax Rio was located approximately 11 km off Sochi after its AIS went dark), partisan intelligence networks like Atesh, and commercial vessel-tracking data.

The strategic innovation is the cost exchange: a MAGURA V5 costs a fraction of the crude oil cargo aboard a fully loaded Aframax tanker. The Aframax Rio alone was reportedly carrying 95,000 to 100,000 metric tons of oil -- approximately 750,000 barrels -- valued at well over $50 million at current market prices. Ukraine has demonstrated that a state with no surface fleet can deny a naval adversary's maritime commerce using mass-produced, remote-controlled vessels -- a doctrinal proof of concept that US defense planners, maritime security analysts, and navies worldwide are now studying.

What Is the Shadow Fleet?

Russia's shadow fleet is a clandestine network of aging tankers assembled since 2022 to circumvent the G7's sixty-dollar-per-barrel oil price cap and broader Western export restrictions. The vessels operate outside Western marine insurance systems, frequently sail under flags of convenience -- Liberia (like the Aframax Rio), Panama, Cameroon, Comoros -- change names and registration regularly, and routinely transmit false AIS location data or disable transponders entirely.

By late 2022, the fleet counted over 600 ships; by December 2023, estimates placed it between 1,100 and 1,400 vessels; and the Ukrainian government's sanctions list cataloged 1,337 ships as of February 2026. The fleet carries roughly 70 percent seaborne of Russia's oil exports, according to Kyiv School of Economics data, and evading the price cap earned Russia an extra $9.4 billion in oil revenue through 2024 alone.

The Aframax Rio fits the archetypal shadow-fleet profile. Built in 2004, the vessel carried 80,000 to 120,000 deadweight tons of crude -- the Aframax class is particularly dominant in Russian Black Sea exports because its draft of roughly 14 to 15 meters (46 to 49 feet) suits the port constraints of Novorossiysk and Taman while still allowing passage through the Bosphorus. Shipping records show it regularly transported oil from the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Novorossiysk, and Taman to India, Singapore, and Saudi Arabia between 2024 and 2026. Ukraine sanctioned the Aframax Rio in February 2026 among 91 vessels designated as part of Russia's shadow fleet.

Why the Shadow Fleet Is Also an Environmental Time Bomb

The Aframax Rio fire raises a question that maritime analysts and environmental groups have been pressing since 2024: what happens when a fully loaded shadow-fleet tanker burns or sinks in the Black Sea?

The vessels that make up the fleet are, by design, old, poorly maintained, and uninsured by Western P&I (protection and indemnity) insurers. Two-thirds of ships carrying Russian oil operate with insurers classified as "unknown." In December 2024, two shadow-fleet tankers -- the Volgoneft-212 and Volgoneft-239 -- broke apart in a storm near the Kerch Strait, releasing over 4,000 metric tons (approximately 4,400 short tons) of heavy fuel oil in what Ukraine's Permanent Representative described to the United Nations as the Black Sea's worst-ever spill.

Operation MoLoChKa's explicit targeting doctrine -- disable propulsion without breaching hulls -- was designed partly to avoid replicating that scenario. Russia's Transport Ministry maintained the Aframax Rio fire did not cause an oil spill. But Greenpeace Bulgaria, which painted "NO GAS + OIL" on the abandoned tanker Kairos in Burgas harbor in August 2026, warned that the broader campaign had already produced one maritime environmental disaster: the shadow-fleet tanker Caroline Bezengi, hit off Oman earlier in 2026 with a nearly full 160,000-ton cargo, was reported leaking. Maritime intelligence analyst Michelle Wiese Bockmann has called the entire shadow fleet "a billion-dollar oil spill catastrophe waiting to happen."

Ukraine's Strategic Logic

Ukraine has consistently framed its energy-infrastructure strikes as proportionate retaliation for Russia's nightly drone and missile barrages against Ukrainian cities. "Ukraine says its attacks on Russia's oil infrastructure are fair retribution for Moscow's nightly barrages of its towns and cities," AFP reported Tuesday.

The Sochi strike carries additional strategic weight. Sochi is not an anonymous industrial port. It is Russia's most famous resort destination, internationally recognized as the site of the 2014 Winter Olympics, with a civilian population of half a million. An oil fire visible from its beaches, generating columns of black smoke over its waterfront, carries symbolic reach into Russian domestic perception in a way that a tanker fire off Novorossiysk's industrial harbor does not.

Previous Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure in the region have produced oil slicks, beach closures, and toxic residue from burning petroleum. The pattern is familiar enough to Sochi residents that officials have developed a response protocol. But a burning Aframax tanker at sea -- with crude oil visible on the surface even as Russia denied a spill -- represents a qualitative escalation in visibility and civic disruption.

Both sides have also escalated elsewhere. Russia has struck grain vessels carrying Ukrainian cargo near the coast of EU member Romania, and has begun striking key bridges in Kyiv and conducting daytime drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital -- a new tactic that has disrupted traffic and daily life in the city.

Does Kinetic Sanctions Enforcement Work?

The broader question raised by Operation MoLoChKa -- and by the Aframax Rio fire specifically -- is whether physical disruption of the shadow fleet accomplishes what diplomatic and financial sanctions have not.

The case for effectiveness is behavioral: Russia has diverted frontline military assets to tanker protection, restructured convoy doctrine, and seen vessel availability in the northern Black Sea and Kerch Strait region effectively collapse, according to Brovdi. Former US Navy SEAL Chuck Pfarrer, analyzing the operation's first two months for Kyiv Post, concluded that MoLoChKa achieved "more than 170 vessels struck without Ukraine deploying a single large surface warship" -- a fundamentally asymmetric outcome.

The countervailing concern is legal and environmental. The International Maritime Organization's Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez condemned attacks on commercial shipping in the Black and Azov Seas in July 2026, stating that civilian seafarers should never become casualties of geopolitical conflict. The 23 Indian crew members rescued from the Aframax Rio are a reminder that the vessels carry international nationals whose governments -- particularly India, one of the largest buyers of Russian shadow-fleet oil -- have not endorsed the military targeting of commercial shipping.

What Comes Next

Operation MoLoChKa is ongoing. Brovdi stated after the September 300-vessel milestone that the campaign "will not end" at any particular number. Russia is simultaneously building its own USV fleet -- expected to receive over 150 uncrewed surface vessels in 2026, with a possible order of 230 -- but faces significant technical obstacles in developing communications systems resistant to electronic warfare and accessing satellite connectivity.

For global energy markets, the campaign represents a meaningful tightening of Russia's Black Sea export corridor -- the geographic chokepoint through which Aframax-class vessels move the bulk of Russia's southern crude exports. As insurance premiums for Black Sea tankers rise, vessel availability shrinks, and military escort costs increase, the cost of keeping shadow-fleet oil flowing rises on multiple simultaneous fronts. Whether that cost pressure ultimately registers in Russian export volumes or crude pricing is a question that energy market analysts will be watching closely in the weeks ahead.

What is clear is that Ukraine has demonstrated something new in the history of economic warfare: a state with no surface navy has used mass-produced drones to establish maritime denial of a great-power adversary's commercial shipping. The fire off Sochi is, among other things, the most photogenic proof of concept yet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Operation MoLoChKa and how many ships has it struck?

Operation MoLoChKa -- a Ukrainian acronym meaning "Moscow will fall through Crimea" -- is a drone campaign launched July 6, 2026, by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces targeting vessels in Russia's shadow fleet. As of September 22, 2026, the operation has struck over 300 vessels across the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, including oil tankers, gas tankers, dry cargo ships, ferries, tugboats, and floating cranes. The operation is conducted primarily by aerial drone units and uncrewed surface vehicles, without Ukraine deploying any conventional surface warships.

How do Ukraine's maritime drones locate and strike tankers that have turned off their tracking signals?

Russia's shadow fleet vessels routinely disable their AIS (Automatic Identification System) transponders to evade tracking, making them invisible on commercial vessel-tracking platforms. Ukraine counters this using multiple independent channels: satellite imagery analysis (the Aframax Rio was located by satellite approximately 11 km off Sochi even after its AIS went dark), open-source partisan intelligence networks such as the Atesh network that monitors Russian fleet movements, and commercial vessel-data providers. Ukrainian drone operators then use encrypted satellite communications to guide both aerial and surface drones to verified target coordinates.

What is Russia's shadow fleet and why does it matter for global oil markets?

Russia's shadow fleet is a network of aging tankers -- estimated at 1,100 to 1,400 vessels as of late 2023, with further growth since -- that transport Russian crude outside the Western financial and insurance system, enabling Russia to sell oil above the G7's $60-per-barrel price cap. The fleet carries approximately 70 percent of Russia's seaborne oil exports and is estimated to have earned Russia an additional $9.4 billion in 2024 alone beyond what the price cap would have permitted. Disrupting this fleet directly affects Russia's primary war-financing revenue stream, something diplomatic sanctions have been unable to fully achieve.

Is there a risk of a major oil spill from the Aframax Rio or other shadow fleet vessels struck by drones?

Russia's Transport Ministry stated that the Aframax Rio fire did not cause an oil spill, though the Ministry also confirmed crude oil was "burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea," suggesting some surface burning of leaked cargo. The environmental risk from the broader campaign is significant: shadow-fleet vessels operate with minimal or fraudulent insurance, and the Black Sea has already experienced its largest recorded oil spill in December 2024 when two poorly maintained Russian tankers broke apart near the Kerch Strait. Ukraine's stated operational doctrine specifically targets propulsion and navigation systems rather than hull integrity to reduce spill risk, but a fully loaded Aframax tanker on fire near a resort coastline tests those limits.

title: Carolina Mejía calls for sanctions against Wilson Isidor over remarks about Dominican Republic

title: Carney must hit Iran's Ayatollah with sanctions and legal action, human rights advocates say
body:
OTTAWA -- The Carney government should directly target Iran's leader and his allies with sanctions and legal action to close the "impunity gap" and to ensure that this country doesn't become a safe haven for repression, a coalition of human rights groups and an all-party group of MPs insisted Wednesday.

Speaking on Parliament Hill on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led terrorist attack on Israel that killed an estimated 1,200 people, the human rights advocates warned that more atrocities in Iran are likely if democratic governments don't do more to limit the Iranian government's power.

Irwin Cotler, a former Liberal MP and cabinet minister and now an advocate, told reporters that it's a critical moment in the battle between human rights and the government of Iran. The government killed an estimated 40,000 protesters and critics over two days in January and has since followed with repressive techniques such as controlling mass communications and detentions, disappearances, torture, rape and more executions.

Cotler, who also faced an Iranian assassination plot for his efforts to call out the regime, said the Iranian regime's repression tactics extend to other countries, including Canada.

Shilan Mirzaee, a democracy advocate and former political prisoner, held up a photo at the press conference of a young couple who were arrested a month ago, just a couple of days before they were to be married. He was then executed while she remains in prison.

Despite the U.S.-led attacks on Iran over the last seven months, that country is still governed by the Islamic Republic of Iran. Canada does not have diplomatic relations with Iran and Ottawa has designated its government a supporter of terrorism.

After tens of thousands of Iranians took to the streets earlier this year to protest soaring prices and a weak economy, government soldiers opened fire after demonstrators called for regime change. A widespread brutal crackdown ensued.

Less than two months later, the United States and Israel began large-scale strikes on Iranian facilities, reportedly out of concern about the advance of Iran's efforts to build nuclear weapons. The early attacks in February killed the previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, 86, the current leader's father, who had ruled since 1989.

The advocates in Ottawa, which included the Iranian Justice Collective and the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights, also released a report Wednesday with 12 steps that Canada should take to counter the Iranian regime and stand up for human rights.

title: Two German parties draft resolution on ending aid to Ukraine and lifting Russia sanctions
body:
Two German political parties, Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Alliance for Social Justice (BSW), plan to pass a resolution in the regional parliament of Saxony-Anhalt calling for an end to military and financial aid to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.

Source: European Pravda, citing Der Spiegel

Details: Under the draft resolution, the state parliament (Landtag) should acknowledge that the policy of sanctioning Russia and providing weapons and financial aid to Ukraine has failed. An extraordinary session is to be held to pass the resolution.

The resolution calls on the regional government "to use all available means, including through an appropriate initiative in the Bundesrat, to make efforts to prevent further escalation of the conflict in Ukraine and to implement a policy aimed at establishing peace". According to the draft, the main focus should be on diplomacy. "An immediate ceasefire and the start of peace negotiations with Russia are necessary," the draft resolution states.

The normalisation of economic relations with Russia and the immediate lifting of economic sanctions against the Russian Federation are stated to be among Germany's objectives.

The effect of the resolution would be largely symbolic, as the main authority regarding aid to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia is held by Berlin and Brussels.

AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who intends to run for Minister-President of Saxony-Anhalt in December, said the parties are at last able to increase pressure on Berlin, "forcing it to finally make efforts to end the war rather than prolong it, and to spend billions in taxpayers' money on the people in our country and not weapons for the battlefields in Ukraine".

BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht said Germany should focus on dialogue with Moscow "instead of contributing to an escalation that will sooner or later end in war". She accused German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of travelling to Kyiv with a "suitcase of money".

Background:

* BSW parliamentary group leader Thomas Schulze told the dpa news agency that a peace motion had been one of the party's election pledges: "We are now keeping this campaign promise. Magdeburg is sending Berlin a signal for a policy of peace."

* The extraordinary session of the state parliament is scheduled to take place on 14 October. Under the rules of procedure, such sessions must be convened if requested by a quarter of members.

* On 6 October, the state parliament held its first session in Magdeburg. AfD politician Tobias Rausch became the new speaker.

title: Iran transfers $200 million to Hezbollah despite tightening US sanctions
body:
Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year's war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, the first significant aid from the group to supporters who bore the brunt of the conflict.

Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening U.S. economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, said the people.

Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.

Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.

The Iranian foreign ministry, Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Treasury Department and the Lebanese government did not ⁠immediately respond to requests for comment.

Israel's bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah's Shi'ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2.

But those displaced have so far received little to no assistance from Hezbollah, an armed group founded by Iran's Revolutionary Guards in 1982 which has suffered heavy Israeli blows in two wars since 2024 and is designated a terrorist group by Washington.

Aiding 50,000 families

Hezbollah would use the funds to pay an initial $3,000 per family, and priority will go to those whose villages have been destroyed or are inaccessible due to Israeli occupation, the sources said. These number around 50,000 families, one of the sources said.

Iran has maintained financial support to Hezbollah through years of crippling U.S. sanctions: it transferred $1 billion to the group in the first 10 months of 2025, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.

Tehran has never acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran's policy of funding regional proxies has stirred domestic protester anger against the clerical rulers in the past and could prove particularly sensitive at a time of worsening hardship in Iran.

Iran had promised Hezbollah more funding after Tehran signed an interim deal with Washington in June that allowed Iran to sell ⁠its oil, Reuters reported at the time. That agreement collapsed in July.

Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Iran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade to block Iranian oil exports.

Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a speech last month that the group would soon contribute to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced by the war, using "available resources and donations", without elaborating.

Hezbollah's ability to fund local services and provide post-conflict aid has helped shore up its support in the past. Following a war with Israel in 2006, the group immediately handed out large cash payments to those impacted and moved swiftly to help rebuild Beirut's southern ⁠suburbs, a stronghold.

But this time there has been little sign of reconstruction. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that the total reconstruction costs from the two wars since 2024 could exceed $27 billion.

A costly war

The two sources provided no details on how the money got to Lebanon.

One of them said it was increasingly difficult for Hezbollah to move funds via financial companies that once processed such transfers. Such firms based in Iraq and ⁠Dubai were no longer an option, and they were also now under pressure in Turkey, this source said.

Hezbollah's foes believed money was currently the group's "oxygen", the source added. Despite the difficulties securing funding, the group had not stopped paying its fighters and the family members of those killed in combat, this source said.

In Lebanon, the war has inflicted a heavy price on the Shi'ite Muslim community ⁠from which Hezbollah draws support. Israel has razed villages across a swathe of territory it has seized in the south, saying it aims to shield northern Israel from Hezbollah attack.

title: EU envoys approve more Russia sanctions listings: diplomats
body:
More than half of the measures target Russia's ballistic missile production chain, as Moscow ramps up attacks amid dwindling Ukrainian air defences.

The European Union envoys approved on Wednesday 1,646 new designations under the bloc's sanctions regime for Russia, with the majority focused on the country's military industrial complex, three EU diplomats said.

More than half of the newly added entities and individuals are involved in the chain of production of Russia's ballistic missiles, such as the 9M723 Iskander-M, which can only be intercepted by US-made Patriot air defence systems.

Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors as the US diverts military resources to the Gulf, while Russia has intensified ballistic missile strikes.

Russian politicians also targated

title: New EU Russia sanctions cover about 1,700 items | News.az
body:
The European Union has agreed on a new package of sanctions targeting Russia's defense industry, according to Ukrainian President's Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk.

According to him, the EU will add about 1,700 new items to the sanctions list, Militarnyi reported.

Vlasiuk said about 60% of the package consists of Ukrainian proposals.

In particular, the EU has included the Design Bureau of Special Machine Building, based in the city of Kurgan, in the sanctions package.

It is a leading Russian company specializing in designing, developing, and modernizing light and medium armored vehicles. It has been under Ukrainian sanctions since September.

According to Vlasiuk, the EU is imposing sanctions on individuals and companies involved in Russia's defense industry.

"The core of the package is the missile program and the electronic component base: electronics, capacitors, resistors and semiconductors," the presidential commissioner said.

He also added that the restrictions would apply to manufacturers and suppliers of materials, including those used for machine tools, Lancet drones and ballistic weapons.

"There is electronic warfare, shipbuilding, and explosives. They also threw in repair plants, chemical companies, garment factories and traders," Vlasiuk noted.

European Union ambassadors approved the 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 7. The package is expected to be formally adopted by mid-October.

The EU approved its 21st package of sanctions against Russia in July 2026. The restrictions targeted key sectors of the Russian economy, including finance and energy. Pressure on Russia's "shadow fleet" was also increased.

title: Senators push the Trump administration to act swiftly on Russian sanctions to help Ukraine
body:
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Nearly a month after President Donald Trump signed a sweeping Russian sanctions bill named after Lindsey Graham into law, bipartisan leadership in the Senate is urging the administration to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine .

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio , the senators said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. They also pushed for a halt of Russia's emerging satellite system that Ukraine has warned could prove devastating with real-time bombing attacks this winter.

"Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation," wrote Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The senators note that the bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham's sudden death, with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has been expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose birthday is Wednesday, to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute. Congress backed Ukraine with the Russian sanctions package

The sanctions package had been a year in the making but was suddenly rushed to passage after Graham, the long-serving South Carolina senator, died in July of a likely torn aorta after a whirlwind trip to a NATO summit in Turkey and a stopover in Kyiv.

Senators had been negotiating a bipartisan bill that could win robust support but it was only when Graham received the nod of approval from Trump in the days around the senator's overseas trip that it gained momentum.

Zelenskyy had also been pushing the U.S. to act, and he arrived in the Senate after a visit at the White House late in the evening before a key vote that advanced the package. The House gave final approval to the bill, sending it to Trump's desk, but Democrats in both chambers warned that they doubted the president would use the vast tools available to slap back at Russia.

In the month since, momentum appears to have stalled without public steps from the administration toward the law's implementation. Trump's next moves against Russia are uncertain

With the bipartisan push, Shaheen and Wicker in their letter sent late Tuesday are urging the administration to take several specific steps to impose the sanctions regime. Many of the steps are aligned with goals pushed by the Ukrainians.

The senators, who were both key to the bill's passage, said it's most crucial for the U.S. to focus on the several hundred rogue tankers that are able to "transport Russian oil with impunity and thereby provide the Kremlin a financial lifeline."

It's also, imperative, they wrote, "that the administration paralyze the global financial networks that allow Russia to evade our sanctions."

They said the Kremlin continues to "move billions of dollars through networks that shield it from scrutiny." They urged the administration to focus specifically on overseas bank branches, including in Shanghai, and "a growing network of Kyrgyz financial institutions" they said serve as clearinghouses for sanctioned capital.

"Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice." the senators wrote. "They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia's war. They cannot do both."

They said the Trump administration should work to undermine Russia's "weaponization of space" with its emerging low Earth orbit system. Ukraine has warned that such a satellite system would prove deadly in the coming winter as Russia prepares its attacks.

The senators also noted that the sanctions law bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and handling of sovereign debt. They said it's imperative that the Treasury Department "issue clear regulatory guidance ahead of the October deadline to ensure American financial institutions completely sever these capital pipelines."

Additionally, the senators said the U.S. must stop the flow of dual-use technologies and electronics for Russia's frontline operations, and use the sanctions tools available to "penalize entities feeding Russia's military-industrial complex."

title: Neal Froneman's US sanctions call angers Ramaphosa's office
body:
South Africa's Presidency has said it expects Neal Froneman, the former chief executive of Sibanye-Stillwater, to withdraw from a partnership between business and the government, after he urged Washington to sanction individual South African officials rather than the country's businesses.

Presidency spokesman Vincent Magwenya called Froneman's approach unpatriotic and destructive. "As to his role in the government and business partnership, one would expect he will withdraw his participation now that he is at odds with the government," Magwenya said, BusinessDay reported on Wednesday.

The partnership brings cabinet ministers and senior officials together with business leaders, coordinated through the group Business for South Africa. A joint oversight committee meets with President Cyril Ramaphosa every quarter.

'Don't punish business'

The dispute follows an interview Froneman gave to BizNews, in which he described his recent discussions in Washington. "With my work in Washington and with the United States, we have made it very clear that the private sector and the majority of South Africans are not the problem," he said. "Therefore, don't punish business in South Africa."

Froneman said the United States should target officials who back policies favorable to Russia and Iran, as well as those advancing land expropriation without compensation, which he said had made deals with American companies harder.

The comments have drawn criticism beyond the government, with commentators accusing him of straying into diplomacy at a time of strained relations between Pretoria and Washington.

A Formula One bid at stake

The clash comes as Froneman leads a R6.7 billion plan to build a Formula One circuit in the Swartland region of the Western Cape, with a target of hosting a Grand Prix in 2031. He has acknowledged that South Africa's foreign relations could put the project at risk, but argued that a clear separation between business and government should address concerns at Liberty Media, which owns Formula One.

Froneman ran Sibanye-Stillwater, one of the world's biggest producers of platinum-group metals and gold, until his retirement, and was once among South Africa's best-paid executives. He now chairs US-based PGM Processing and copper miner Copper 360, and chairs Business Against Crime South Africa.

title: Govt sanctions Rs 1,108 cr for Omkareshwara temple under Musi revamp plan | Hyderabad News
body: Hyderabad: The state govt has sanctioned ₹1,108.27 crore for the development of the Sri Omkareswara Swamy temple complex at Manchirevula village in Gandipet mandal, positioning it as a key spiritual and tourism landmark under the Musi rejuvenation project.The metropolitan area and urban development department issued GOs approving ₹948.64 crore for the temple complex and ₹159.62 crore for a six-lane approach road and connectivity infrastructure linking the temple to the surrounding road network.The project is being developed as part of the larger Musi riverfront development initiative, which aims to promote cultural and spiritual tourism alongside urban infrastructure development along Musi river."As part of the project, it is proposed to develop the temple precinct comprising the main Sri Omkareswara Swamy temple, associated with sub-shrines of Sri Veerabhadra and Bhadrakali temple, Sri Lalitha Maha Tripurasundari Devi temple, Sri Bala Ganapathy Swamy temple and Sri Bala Subramanya Swamy temple, together with maha mandapam, Nandi mandapam, prakarams, raja gopurams, yagasala, pushkarini, an iconic Shiva statue and other associated facilities," the GO said.According to the govt, the preliminary estimate includes ₹598 crore for temple architectural works and ₹349 crore for civil and structural works, including mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems and allied facilities.In addition to the temple complex, the Musi Riverfront Development Corporation Ltd has proposed the construction of a 30-metre (100 ft) wide six-lane HMDA master plan road connecting the temple complex with the Musi riverfront road network. The proposed 2.5-km stretch will run from Istana Villas to Keerthi West Wind Villas at Manchirevula and provide connectivity to the temple, adjoining Greyhounds land and the Young India Police School.The estimated cost of the road project, including pavement, drainage, retaining and protection works, culverts, street lighting, road safety measures and related infrastructure, has been pegged at ₹159.62 crore.The govt has also constituted a technical committee to oversee implementation of the project. The committee will be headed by the engineer-in-chief, roads & buildings, while the engineer-in-chief, public health, will serve as co-chairperson. Chief engineer of MRDCL will act as a convener.The committee has been tasked with providing technical guidance and approvals for designs, drawings, DPRs and estimates, finalising rates for specialised temple architecture, stone carving and sculptural works, and examining tendering, execution and any changes in scope during implementation of the project, the GO added.

title: EU envoys approve new Russia sanctions listings, diplomats say
body:
EU Approves Over 1,600 New Russia Sanctions Including Missile Producers

EU Expands Sanctions Targeting Russian Military and Political Sectors

By Julia Payne

Details of the New Sanctions

BRUSSELS, Oct 7 (Reuters) - European Union envoys approved on Wednesday 1,646 new designations under the bloc's sanctions regime for Russia, with the majority focused on the country's military industrial complex, three EU diplomats said.

Focus on Missile Production and Supply Chains

More than half of the newly added entities and individuals are involved in the chain of production of Russia's ballistic missiles, such as the 9M723 Iskander-M, which can only be intercepted by US-made Patriot air defence systems.

Ukraine has virtually run out of these interceptors as the US military diverts resources to the Gulf, and Russia has seized on this vulnerability to ramp up ballistic missile strikes.

Entities Involved in Missile and Drone Manufacturing

The designations include a range of entities involved in missile testing and research as well as the production of solid fuels and rocket engines for Russia's Iskander system. The EU is also targeting producers of specialised textiles and synthetic and carbon fibres used across a range of different missile systems, one of the sources specified.

In addition, the list has drone manufacturers, shipyards that service submarines and 77 Russian politicians who ran for parliamentary seats in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.

Implementation and Broader Impacts

The sanctions will be formally adopted when EU foreign ministers meet on Monday.

Russian Response and Diesel Export Ban

Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week Moscow would not resume diesel exports - currently banned until the end of October - to global markets until sanctions are lifted.

The global diesel market has tightened due to the Iran war, which, combined with the loss of Russian diesel after Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, triggered shortages in Russia.

Sanctions on North Korean Entities

The EU, concerned about strengthening links between Russia and North Korea, also added seven North Korean entities and individuals linked to Moscow's war effort. In July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia struck Ukraine with North Korean missiles for the first time in nearly a year after an apparent stock replenishment.

(Reporting by Julia Payne, Writing by Charlotte Van Campenhout, Editing by Inti Landauro and Gareth Jones)

title: Sports News | UEFA Monitoring Man City's Legal Battle over Financial Breaches; Secondary Sanctions May Follow
body:
Get latest articles and stories on Sports at LatestLY. Manchester City was found guilty on 114 of 115 charges brought by the Premier League over alleged financial rule breaches. One of the most serious allegations concerned the club allegedly orchestrating artificial sponsorship agreements to boost its revenue by approximately 900 million pounds between 2009 and 2018, a period during which the club emerged as one of the dominant forces in English football and won three Premier League titles.

Manchester [UK], October 7 (ANI): Manchester City's off-field legal battle over alleged financial rule breaches could have wider ramifications, with UEFA monitoring the club's appeal against the Premier League's findings and the possibility of secondary sanctions at the European level, according to Goal.com.

Manchester City was found guilty on 114 of 115 charges brought by the Premier League over alleged financial rule breaches. One of the most serious allegations concerned the club allegedly orchestrating artificial sponsorship agreements to boost its revenue by approximately 900 million pounds between 2009 and 2018, a period during which the club emerged as one of the dominant forces in English football and won three Premier League titles.

Also Read | USA vs Namibia Live Streaming Online and Free TV Telecast, ICC Cricket World Cup League Two 2023-27 130th ODI.

Following the verdict, the Premier League club officially began its appeal process last week and has continued to maintain its innocence, claiming it has "'irrefutable evidence" that will clear it of the charges.

A three-person independent panel will review Manchester City's appeal, with a resolution expected before the end of the season.

Also Read | Narendra Modi Stadium Bomb Threat During India U-19 vs Australia U-19 Test Match 2026.

As per a Sky Sports report quoted by Goal.com, UEFA is closely monitoring the legal proceedings and will wait for the outcome of the three-person panel before deciding whether to launch its own investigation into the matter.

If the Premier League's ruling is upheld, it will be uncertain what punishment UEFA will impose on Man City. The prospect of secondary, European-level sanctions looms large over the club and its rich legacy built over the last decade or so.

This is not the first time Manchester City and UEFA have been at loggerheads over financial regulations. UEFA initially banned the English club from European competition for two years in 2020 and imposed a fine of 30 million pounds for Financial Fair Play breaches.

However, the two-year ban was overturned after Manchester City appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). The financial penalty was subsequently reduced to 10 million pounds.

Domestically, the problems awaiting the club look massive, ranging from point deductions to stripping of past major titles to complete ouster from the Premier League, the top-flight English football competition.

After the international break, City, who are currently at the top of the Premier League with five wins from five matches, are scheduled to resume their campaign against Liverpool at Anfield on October 11. (ANI)

title: Israeli banks fear new sanctions over West Bank settlement financing: Report
body:
Israeli banks fear new international sanctions over financing settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, particularly measures planned by Britain, Israeli daily Haaretz reported Wednesday, Anadolu reports.

The newspaper said the Association of Banks in Israel had prepared an assessment warning that anticipated British sanctions could affect Israeli financial institutions.

The measures could target entities involved in settlement construction or financing, extending beyond those implicated in violence by Israeli occupiers, according to the report.

Banks have yet to clarify their position on financing or providing guarantees to construction companies participating in the E1 tenders.

About 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 settlements and 400 settlement outposts across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, according to official Palestinian figures.

The UN has repeatedly affirmed that Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, warning that they undermine prospects for a two-state solution.

body:

EU member states agreed Wednesday to place more than 1,600 additional individuals and organizations under sanctions over Russia's war in Ukraine, Euronews reported.

The agreement comes as European governments confront a series of suspected hybrid attacks which they attributed to Russia.

Brussels is also considering further designations following a drone incident at Leipzig airport in Germany.

The latest expansion will bring the total number of names in the EU's Russia-related sanctions list to nearly 4,650, according to the report.

title: Senators push the Trump administration to act swiftly on Russian sanctions to help Ukraine
body:
By LISA MASCARO, AP Congressional Correspondent

WASHINGTON (AP) -- Nearly a month after President Donald Trump signed a sweeping Russian sanctions bill named after Lindsey Graham into law, bipartisan leadership in the Senate is urging the administration to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. They also pushed for a halt of Russia's emerging satellite system that Ukraine has warned could prove devastating with real-time bombing attacks this winter.

"Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation," wrote Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The senators note that the bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham's sudden death, with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has been expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose birthday is Wednesday, to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.

Congress backed Ukraine with the Russian sanctions package

The sanctions package had been a year in the making but was suddenly rushed to passage after Graham, the long-serving South Carolina senator, died in July of a likely torn aorta after a whirlwind trip to a NATO summit in Turkey and a stopover in Kyiv.

Senators had been negotiating a bipartisan bill that could win robust support but it was only when Graham received the nod of approval from Trump in the days around the senator's overseas trip that it gained momentum.

Zelenskyy had also been pushing the U.S. to act, and he arrived in the Senate after a visit at the White House late in the evening before a key vote that advanced the package. The House gave final approval to the bill, sending it to Trump's desk, but Democrats in both chambers warned that they doubted the president would use the vast tools available to slap back at Russia.

In the month since, momentum appears to have stalled without public steps from the administration toward the law's implementation.

Trump's next moves against Russia are uncertain

With the bipartisan push, Shaheen and Wicker in their letter sent late Tuesday are urging the administration to take several specific steps to impose the sanctions regime. Many of the steps are aligned with goals pushed by the Ukrainians.

The senators, who were both key to the bill's passage, said it's most crucial for the U.S. to focus on the several hundred rogue tankers that are able to "transport Russian oil with impunity and thereby provide the Kremlin a financial lifeline."

It's also, imperative, they wrote, "that the administration paralyze the global financial networks that allow Russia to evade our sanctions."

They said the Kremlin continues to "move billions of dollars through networks that shield it from scrutiny." They urged the administration to focus specifically on overseas bank branches, including in Shanghai, and "a growing network of Kyrgyz financial institutions" they said serve as clearinghouses for sanctioned capital.

"Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice." the senators wrote. "They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia's war. They cannot do both."

They said the Trump administration should work to undermine Russia's "weaponization of space" with its emerging low Earth orbit system. Ukraine has warned that such a satellite system would prove deadly in the coming winter as Russia prepares its attacks.

The senators also noted that the sanctions law bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and handling of sovereign debt. They said it's imperative that the Treasury Department "issue clear regulatory guidance ahead of the October deadline to ensure American financial institutions completely sever these capital pipelines."

Additionally, the senators said the U.S. must stop the flow of dual-use technologies and electronics for Russia's frontline operations, and use the sanctions tools available to "penalize entities feeding Russia's military-industrial complex."

title: EU sanctions list expands with nearly 1,600 individuals and entities
body:
The new EU measures include asset freezes and travel or transit bans targeting individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex.

Brussels, Oct. 7 (SANA) European Union countries agreed Wednesday on a new major package of sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, targeting nearly 1,600 individuals and entities, diplomats said.

According to the diplomats, who spoke to Agence France-Presse (AFP), the sanctions include asset freezes in the European Union and travel or transit bans across EU territory. The measures target 743 individuals and 826 entities, accused of supporting Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The diplomats also said the EU agreed to add 77 new names to its sanctions list following Russia's latest State Duma elections, which Brussels criticized as undemocratic. The new listings include three members of Russia's Central Election Commission.

The measures would bring the total number of individuals and entities sanctioned by the EU over the war to nearly 4,500.

Representatives of EU member states approved the list, which will be formally adopted by foreign ministers at a meeting scheduled for Monday in Luxembourg.

title: UEFA monitoring Man Citys legal battle over financial breaches; secondary sanctions may follow - The Tribune
body:
Manchester [UK], October 7 (ANI): Manchester City's off-field legal battle over alleged financial rule breaches could have wider ramifications, with UEFA monitoring the club's appeal against the Premier League's findings and the possibility of secondary sanctions at the European level, according to Goal.com.

Manchester City was found guilty on 114 of 115 charges brought by the Premier League over alleged financial rule breaches. One of the most serious allegations concerned the club allegedly orchestrating artificial sponsorship agreements to boost its revenue by approximately 900 million pounds between 2009 and 2018, a period during which the club emerged as one of the dominant forces in English football and won three Premier League titles.

Following the verdict, the Premier League club officially began its appeal process last week and has continued to maintain its innocence, claiming it has "'irrefutable evidence" that will clear it of the charges.

A three-person independent panel will review Manchester City's appeal, with a resolution expected before the end of the season.

As per a Sky Sports report quoted by Goal.com, UEFA is closely monitoring the legal proceedings and will wait for the outcome of the three-person panel before deciding whether to launch its own investigation into the matter.

If the Premier League's ruling is upheld, it will be uncertain what punishment UEFA will impose on Man City. The prospect of secondary, European-level sanctions looms large over the club and its rich legacy built over the last decade or so.

This is not the first time Manchester City and UEFA have been at loggerheads over financial regulations. UEFA initially banned the English club from European competition for two years in 2020 and imposed a fine of 30 million pounds for Financial Fair Play breaches.

However, the two-year ban was overturned after Manchester City appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). The financial penalty was subsequently reduced to 10 million pounds.

Domestically, the problems awaiting the club look massive, ranging from point deductions to stripping of past major titles to complete ouster from the Premier League, the top-flight English football competition.

After the international break, City, who are currently at the top of the Premier League with five wins from five matches, are scheduled to resume their campaign against Liverpool at Anfield on October 11. (ANI)
