body:
On Monday in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, German MEP Hildegard Bentele, who chairs the parliament's delegation for relations with Israel, hosted an event honoring the victims of the 7 October 2023 massacre.

The commemorative event featured an exhibition of pictures from the massacre committed by Hamas on 7 October 2023 in the south of Israel as well as as speeches by the Europan Parliament President Roberta Metsola and former Israeli hostage Omri Miran.

During this event, extreme-left French MEP Rima Hassan was filmed throwing to the floor the Israeli and European flags ''to denounce what she called the "ongoing genocide by the Israeli government".

"A member of this house was filmed apparently damaging an exhibition commemorating the victims of the terrorist attack in Israel on October 7th," Metsola said in a statement on the incident.

"The person concerned was seen allegedly throwing the flag of Israel to the ground, dropped a flagpole and the European Union flag was knocked down. Both flags were left lying on the ground before the member left the scene."

"I want to underline that we take this extremely seriously and that all the appropriate steps according to our procedures are being taken, including the right of the person concerned to be heard," she told lawmakers a day after the incident.

The MEP from the hard left ''La France insoumise'' (LFI, France Unbowed) party and a member of the European Parliament's Left group, later admitted to toppling the Israeli flag.

Hassan's staff said in a statement she had explained the events shortly after the incident.

While leaving the exhibition venue, Hassan "removed the Israeli flag from its stand. The European Union flag, attached to the same base, then accidentally fell due to the loss of balance. Neither flag was trampled or damaged," according to the statement sent to French news agency AFP.

"It is entirely possible - as we did with our group - to commemorate the victims of October 7 without associating ourselves with the genocidal Israeli state," Hassan told the EU parliament on Tuesday.

But several MEPs have called on Metsola to sanction Hassan over the unacceptable desecration.

Right wing French deputy Francois-Xavier Bellamy said that her act was "a form of complicity with those who - including within Europe - seek to re-import the antisemitic hatred that marked the darkest chapters of our continent's history."

Centrist French parliament member Nathalie Loiseau said on social media platform X: "Rima Hassan tramples on an Israeli flag at the European Parliament. October 7th is the day after tomorrow. LFI has plumbed the depths of indecency."

European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno accused Hassan of turning the memorial exhibition into a "photo opportunity."

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called it "shameful, outrageous, but sadly not surprising. "The desecration of the exhibition commemorating the victims of October 7 at the European Parliament by radical-left MEP Rima Hassan says above all how little respect she has for the very institution in which she serves," Saar wrote on X.

Israel denied Hassan entry in February 2025, citing her promotion of boycotts and economic sanctions against the Jewish state.

Metsola stressed that ''we cannot have actions that could make people fearful of speaking. We cannot have damage to property. And we cannot have attempts to intimidate rather than to debate.''

"At a time of rising global antisemitism, we owe it to Europe's Jewish community to ensure that when they look to us they see that this is their House too,'' she added.

The incident, captured by the Parliament's surveillance cameras, is now being investigated by the institution's staff and could result in disciplinary action.

Rima Hassan should be at least suspended from the European Parliament

On January 29, 2025, a Polish far-right MEP, Grzegorz Braun, disrupted an annual International Holocaust Remembrance Day moment of silence in the European Parliament in Brussels. He shouted several times: "Let's pray for the victims of the Jewish genocide in Gaza.''

Security guards quickly escorted him out of the parlialment on the orders of European Parliament President Roberta Metsola. Several lawmakers strongly condemned the outburst as antisemitic .

The European Parliament decided suspended Braun from plenary activities for 30 days, stripped him of his daily subsistence allowance and barred him from the next Holocaust commemoration session. Last March 2026, the European Parliament waived his parliamentary immunity and last month, MEPs voted again to lift his immunity over separate Holocaust-denial statements made regarding the gas chambers at Auschwitz-Birkenau and Majdanek.

Why should'nt Rima Hassan get the same sanctions ?

title: UEFA monitoring Man City's legal battle over financial breaches; secondary sanctions may follow
body:
Manchester [UK], October 7 (ANI): Manchester City's off-field legal battle over alleged financial rule breaches could have wider ramifications, with UEFA monitoring the club's appeal against the Premier League's findings and the possibility of secondary sanctions at the European level, according to Goal.com.

Manchester City was found guilty on 114 of 115 charges brought by the Premier League over alleged financial rule breaches. One of the most serious allegations concerned the club allegedly orchestrating artificial sponsorship agreements to boost its revenue by approximately 900 million pounds between 2009 and 2018, a period during which the club emerged as one of the dominant forces in English football and won three Premier League titles.

Following the verdict, the Premier League club officially began its appeal process last week and has continued to maintain its innocence, claiming it has "'irrefutable evidence" that will clear it of the charges.

A three-person independent panel will review Manchester City's appeal, with a resolution expected before the end of the season.

As per a Sky Sports report quoted by Goal.com, UEFA is closely monitoring the legal proceedings and will wait for the outcome of the three-person panel before deciding whether to launch its own investigation into the matter.

If the Premier League's ruling is upheld, it will be uncertain what punishment UEFA will impose on Man City. The prospect of secondary, European-level sanctions looms large over the club and its rich legacy built over the last decade or so.

This is not the first time Manchester City and UEFA have been at loggerheads over financial regulations. UEFA initially banned the English club from European competition for two years in 2020 and imposed a fine of 30 million pounds for Financial Fair Play breaches.

However, the two-year ban was overturned after Manchester City appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). The financial penalty was subsequently reduced to 10 million pounds.

Domestically, the problems awaiting the club look massive, ranging from point deductions to stripping of past major titles to complete ouster from the Premier League, the top-flight English football competition.

After the international break, City, who are currently at the top of the Premier League with five wins from five matches, are scheduled to resume their campaign against Liverpool at Anfield on October 11. (ANI)

title: Iran evades US sanctions to send Hezbollah $200 million - report
body:
Intermediary brokers charged a 20% fee on the transfer, reportedly four times higher than normal

Iran succeeded in evading US sanctions and transferred $200 million to Hezbollah last month, according to a report in Reuters on Tuesday.

The money is expected to be used to support nearly 50,000 families displaced by fighting in Lebanon's south, which translates into about $3,000 per family.

Iran has previously been able to secure large transfers even under US sanctions, with the US Treasury Department reporting nearly $1 billion was transferred in the first 10 months of 2025.

Recent US sanctions and increased pressure on Hezbollah have apparently translated into a significantly higher cost to transfer funds, with Reuters reporting that intermediaries charged a 20% fee on the transfer, reportedly four times higher than normal.

Hezbollah has been starved of funds in recent months, with its sources of funding shut off one by one by a combined US-Israeli effort targeting Hezbollah's economic infrastructure which was used to launder billions of dollars for decades.

Hezbollah's school network showed signs of financial stress when it raised tuition at its schools and offered incentives to parents for paying in dollars, i24NEWS reported in September.

Until the destruction and sanctioning of Hezbollah's bank, the Al-Qard Al-Hassan Association, in 2024 and 2025, the organization could rely on modern money laundering methods; however, since then, Hezbollah has been forced to rely on the informal hawala system which allows brokers to transfer large amounts of money around the world without accessing modern financial systems.

The Hawala system dates back over 500 years and was originally aimed at supporting long-distance traders, in the modern world, it serves as a more secure system in less developed parts of the world as well as allowing users to avoid modern financial scrutiny, although most users and brokers are not involved in terrorism or criminality.

Brokers will often charge fees for the service of cash transfers. The reported 20% charge on transfers to Hezbollah shows that sanctions and pressure have penetrated deep into a system designed to avoid state oversight.

title: At Estonia's request, Russian Solikamsk Magnesium Plant and its chief executive have been removed from EU's main sanctions list, - media
body:
The Russian Solikamsk Magnesium Plant and its chief executive, Ruslan Dimukhamedov, have been removed from the EU sanctions list agreed on 7 October. This was done at the request of Estonia.

Radio Liberty learnt of this from diplomats in Brussels, and confirmation was also received from the Estonian Mission to the European Union, according to Censor.NET.

Why was Estonia asked to exempt the factory from sanctions?

In particular, Estonia requested that the Solikamsk Magnesium Plant and its managing director, Ruslan Dimukhamedov, be removed from the list, on the grounds that the plant supplies strategically important raw materials to the Estonian company NPM Silmet.

"Yes, we have asked for a Russian company and an individual associated with it to be removed from the list of nearly 1,600 entries approved today by the Coreper II ambassadors. The company supplies NPM Silmet, based in Estonia, with materials of strategic importance to Europe," said Kersti Lepik, spokesperson for the Permanent Representation of Estonia to the EU.

According to Lepik, European manufacturers of electric vehicles and wind turbines, as well as the EU's electronics, automotive and aviation industries, are particularly reliant on NPM Silmet's products.

At the same time, she stated that NPM Silmet is actively seeking alternative sources for the materials it imports from Russia.

"Estonia will revisit the issue of adding a Russian company and an individual associated with it to the sanctions list next year," the spokeswoman added.

* NPM Silmet, located in Sillamäe in north-eastern Estonia, specialises in the processing of rare-earth elements and rare metals.

* The Solikamsk Magnesium Plant, for its part, produces rare-earth metal concentrates, as well as products made from niobium, tantalum, titanium and magnesium. From 2023-2024, the plant came under the control of the Russian state corporation 'Rosatom'.

What led up to it

It should be recalled that on 7 October, the ambassadors of the EU Member States agreed to add 743 individuals and 826 companies linked to the Russian defence industry to the sanctions list.

title: Senators push the Trump administration to act swiftly on Russian sanctions to help Ukraine
body:
By LISA MASCARO, AP Congressional Correspondent

WASHINGTON (AP) -- Nearly a month after President Donald Trump signed a sweeping Russian sanctions bill named after Lindsey Graham into law, bipartisan leadership in the Senate is urging the administration to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. They also pushed for a halt of Russia's emerging satellite system that Ukraine has warned could prove devastating with real-time bombing attacks this winter.

"Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation," wrote Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The senators note that the bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham's sudden death, with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has been expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose birthday is Wednesday, to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.

Congress backed Ukraine with the Russian sanctions package

The sanctions package had been a year in the making but was suddenly rushed to passage after Graham, the long-serving South Carolina senator, died in July of a likely torn aorta after a whirlwind trip to a NATO summit in Turkey and a stopover in Kyiv.

Senators had been negotiating a bipartisan bill that could win robust support but it was only when Graham received the nod of approval from Trump in the days around the senator's overseas trip that it gained momentum.

Zelenskyy had also been pushing the U.S. to act, and he arrived in the Senate after a visit at the White House late in the evening before a key vote that advanced the package. The House gave final approval to the bill, sending it to Trump's desk, but Democrats in both chambers warned that they doubted the president would use the vast tools available to slap back at Russia.

In the month since, momentum appears to have stalled without public steps from the administration toward the law's implementation.

Trump's next moves against Russia are uncertain

With the bipartisan push, Shaheen and Wicker in their letter sent late Tuesday are urging the administration to take several specific steps to impose the sanctions regime. Many of the steps are aligned with goals pushed by the Ukrainians.

The senators, who were both key to the bill's passage, said it's most crucial for the U.S. to focus on the several hundred rogue tankers that are able to "transport Russian oil with impunity and thereby provide the Kremlin a financial lifeline."

It's also, imperative, they wrote, "that the administration paralyze the global financial networks that allow Russia to evade our sanctions."

They said the Kremlin continues to "move billions of dollars through networks that shield it from scrutiny." They urged the administration to focus specifically on overseas bank branches, including in Shanghai, and "a growing network of Kyrgyz financial institutions" they said serve as clearinghouses for sanctioned capital.

"Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice." the senators wrote. "They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia's war. They cannot do both."

They said the Trump administration should work to undermine Russia's "weaponization of space" with its emerging low Earth orbit system. Ukraine has warned that such a satellite system would prove deadly in the coming winter as Russia prepares its attacks.

The senators also noted that the sanctions law bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and handling of sovereign debt. They said it's imperative that the Treasury Department "issue clear regulatory guidance ahead of the October deadline to ensure American financial institutions completely sever these capital pipelines."

Additionally, the senators said the U.S. must stop the flow of dual-use technologies and electronics for Russia's frontline operations, and use the sanctions tools available to "penalize entities feeding Russia's military-industrial complex."

WASHINGTON (AP) -- Nearly a month after President Donald Trump signed a sweeping Russian sanctions bill named after Lindsey Graham into law, bipartisan leadership in the Senate is urging the administration to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. They also pushed for a halt of Russia's emerging satellite system that Ukraine has warned could prove devastating with real-time bombing attacks this winter.

"Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation," wrote Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The senators note that the bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham's sudden death, with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has been expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose birthday is Wednesday, to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.

Congress backed Ukraine with the Russian sanctions package

The sanctions package had been a year in the making but was suddenly rushed to passage after Graham, the long-serving South Carolina senator, died in July of a likely torn aorta after a whirlwind trip to a NATO summit in Turkey and a stopover in Kyiv.

Senators had been negotiating a bipartisan bill that could win robust support but it was only when Graham received the nod of approval from Trump in the days around the senator's overseas trip that it gained momentum.

Zelenskyy had also been pushing the U.S. to act, and he arrived in the Senate after a visit at the White House late in the evening before a key vote that advanced the package. The House gave final approval to the bill, sending it to Trump's desk, but Democrats in both chambers warned that they doubted the president would use the vast tools available to slap back at Russia.

In the month since, momentum appears to have stalled without public steps from the administration toward the law's implementation.

Trump's next moves against Russia are uncertain

With the bipartisan push, Shaheen and Wicker in their letter sent late Tuesday are urging the administration to take several specific steps to impose the sanctions regime. Many of the steps are aligned with goals pushed by the Ukrainians.

The senators, who were both key to the bill's passage, said it's most crucial for the U.S. to focus on the several hundred rogue tankers that are able to "transport Russian oil with impunity and thereby provide the Kremlin a financial lifeline."

It's also, imperative, they wrote, "that the administration paralyze the global financial networks that allow Russia to evade our sanctions."

They said the Kremlin continues to "move billions of dollars through networks that shield it from scrutiny." They urged the administration to focus specifically on overseas bank branches, including in Shanghai, and "a growing network of Kyrgyz financial institutions" they said serve as clearinghouses for sanctioned capital.

"Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice." the senators wrote. "They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia's war. They cannot do both."

They said the Trump administration should work to undermine Russia's "weaponization of space" with its emerging low Earth orbit system. Ukraine has warned that such a satellite system would prove deadly in the coming winter as Russia prepares its attacks.

The senators also noted that the sanctions law bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and handling of sovereign debt. They said it's imperative that the Treasury Department "issue clear regulatory guidance ahead of the October deadline to ensure American financial institutions completely sever these capital pipelines."

Additionally, the senators said the U.S. must stop the flow of dual-use technologies and electronics for Russia's frontline operations, and use the sanctions tools available to "penalize entities feeding Russia's military-industrial complex."

title: The UCI must introduce sanctions for in-race safety violations. Enough is enough
body:
Il Lombardia: race of the falling leaves, the season's swansong, its final Monument.

After years of dominance by Tadej Pogačar, the only emotion as Saturday's race nears should be anticipation. All of Remco Evenepoel, Tom Pidcock, and newly-crowned world champion Brandon McNulty are all in outstanding form.

Instead, the build-up has been tarred with trepidation -- with two other Italian warm-up races this week marred by safety incidents, in a year containing too many of them.

In Coppa Bernocchi, held on Monday, a DHL delivery van drove onto the course behind the lead riders with fewer than 30 kilometres left. Thankfully, no riders were hit.

One day later, at Tre Valli Varesine, Pinarello-Q36.5's Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubi were both hit by a police motorbike travelling the wrong way down the course.

"It crashed into two of our guys," said team leader Pidcock, who went on to finish second. "I wanted to stop racing myself. I was mad. The guys all riding in front of me -- for me -- and two of them on the floor."

Camprubi posted a picture of his broken bike on social media. He wrote: "Sad that you have to risk your life to race, one month after a tragic accident."

And this is all the more anger-inducing for what has passed before. In August, British rider Finlay Tarling was killed at the Volta a Portugal after being hit by an unauthorised vehicle driving the wrong way up the course. He was 19 years old. Less than two months on, it is only blind luck that a similar incident has not occurred again.

Last month, Matthew Brennan railed against the lack of action taken since Tarling's death.

"We were watching his funeral yesterday," he told BBC Sport. "I said to my friend: 'It's so sad we've lost someone so special and also nothing has changed.'

"I really think that is disgraceful. Instead of someone somewhere in these organisations saying: 'OK, this should never ever happen again', it feels the world has moved on, nothing has changed, and there are events where cars have been on the course still."

He gets to the heart of a core issue: cycling has repeatedly failed to levy immediate sanctions on races that have resulted in major safety failings.

Coppa Bernocchi and Tre Valli Varesine were both organized by small local cycling associations, respectively, Unione Sportiva Legnanese and SC Alfredo Binda. It is a laudable aspect of cycling's grassroots culture that the sport's biggest names can be attracted to historic, locally-organised events -- but that cannot come at the expense of those riders' safety.

When incidents such as these occur, there needs to be an immediate and transparent disciplinary process which governs the conditions under which future races can take place.

After the Coppa Bernocchi incident, the organizers addressed what happened, telling local media that "For U.S. Legnanese, the safety of athletes, staff, and the public is a tangible priority to which we dedicate personnel, resources, and extensive preparatory work. The security measures in place involved approximately 250 people manning checkpoints, in addition to local police and Carabinieri officers, two unmarked police cars, 16 police motorcycles, four police patrol cars, and 20 motorcycle marshals.

"These figures demonstrate the scale of our commitment, yet they do not erase the need to understand how the van managed to access the course despite the signage and checkpoints."

It could be a requirement to provide further marshalling services, or further guarantees from police over staffing levels. There may be a requirement to move parts or all of the race onto a circuit course, despite the sport's historic resistance to this step, because of the vastly simpler safety situation which it creates. In some cases, it may recommend the cancellation of the race itself -- or at the least, the withdrawal of a licence until minimum standards are met.

Races in Italy appear especially high-risk. Six years ago, seventh-placed finisher Maximilian Schachmann was brought down by an unauthorised car just three kilometres from the race. This was not only a WorldTour race, but a Monument -- one of the five most prestigious one-day events in existence.

This year alone, unauthorized cars have entered the race route at the Volta a Catalunya and the Women's Tour of Britain. Teams quit last year's Etoile de Besseges in protest over a similar situation, while in 2023, both Paris-Nice and the Féminin International des Pyrénées saw cars on the parcours.

Simply put, this is commonplace. A rider has died. When, and how, does it stop?

Cycling's governing body, the UCI, has not publicly announced any repercussions or safety adjustments made after those races. That does not rule out changes having been made, but this is information that should be made transparently -- for the willingness of teams to enter these events, for other events to take note, for failings to be held to account. The Athletic has reached out to the UCI for comment.

Just as commissaires report and sanction riders within a day, races should receive a verdict on safety failings within a week. The UCI has to invest or adapt. As in-race deaths continue to rise, it is a dereliction of their role as a governing body if they continue to wait.

title: Senators push the Trump administration to act swiftly on Russian sanctions to help Ukraine
body:
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Nearly a month after President Donald Trump signed a sweeping Russian sanctions bill named after Lindsey Graham into law, bipartisan leadership in the Senate is urging the administration to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. They also pushed for a halt of Russia's emerging satellite system that Ukraine has warned could prove devastating with real-time bombing attacks this winter.

"Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation," wrote Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The senators note that the bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the House and Senate after Graham's sudden death, with lawmakers urged ahead by Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has been expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose birthday is Wednesday, to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.

The sanctions package had been a year in the making but was suddenly rushed to passage after Graham, the long-serving South Carolina senator, died in July of a likely torn aorta after a whirlwind trip to a NATO summit in Turkey and a stopover in Kyiv.

Senators had been negotiating a bipartisan bill that could win robust support but it was only when Graham received the nod of approval from Trump in the days around the senator's overseas trip that it gained momentum.

Zelenskyy had also been pushing the U.S. to act, and he arrived in the Senate after a visit at the White House late in the evening before a key vote that advanced the package. The House gave final approval to the bill, sending it to Trump's desk, but Democrats in both chambers warned that they doubted the president would use the vast tools available to slap back at Russia.

In the month since, momentum appears to have stalled without public steps from the administration toward the law's implementation.

With the bipartisan push, Shaheen and Wicker in their letter sent late Tuesday are urging the administration to take several specific steps to impose the sanctions regime. Many of the steps are aligned with goals pushed by the Ukrainians.

The senators, who were both key to the bill's passage, said it's most crucial for the U.S. to focus on the several hundred rogue tankers that are able to "transport Russian oil with impunity and thereby provide the Kremlin a financial lifeline."

It's also, imperative, they wrote, "that the administration paralyze the global financial networks that allow Russia to evade our sanctions."

They said the Kremlin continues to "move billions of dollars through networks that shield it from scrutiny." They urged the administration to focus specifically on overseas bank branches, including in Shanghai, and "a growing network of Kyrgyz financial institutions" they said serve as clearinghouses for sanctioned capital.

"Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice." the senators wrote. "They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia's war. They cannot do both."

They said the Trump administration should work to undermine Russia's "weaponization of space" with its emerging low Earth orbit system. Ukraine has warned that such a satellite system would prove deadly in the coming winter as Russia prepares its attacks.

The senators also noted that the sanctions law bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and handling of sovereign debt. They said it's imperative that the Treasury Department "issue clear regulatory guidance ahead of the October deadline to ensure American financial institutions completely sever these capital pipelines."

Additionally, the senators said the U.S. must stop the flow of dual-use technologies and electronics for Russia's frontline operations, and use the sanctions tools available to "penalize entities feeding Russia's military-industrial complex."

title: EU Ambassadors Approve 22nd Russia Sanctions Package - NewsFire.GR | English Version
body:
European Union ambassadors formally approved the bloc's 22nd sanctions package against Russia, blacklisting over 1,500 companies and individuals in the largest single wave since the Ukraine conflict began.

According to TASS / Russia, the package received approval from EU ambassadors and is expected to be ratified by the EU Council before the end of this week. A European source confirmed to the Russian news agency that the sanctions target entities and individuals accused of involvement in the Russian defense sector.

The source stated that the newly sanctioned entities include defense and other companies and individuals from multiple countries, with Brussels alleging these firms produce so-called dual-use goods that can serve both civilian and military purposes.

Largest Designation List to Date

While the new package does not introduce major trade or economic restrictions, it represents the most extensive blacklist imposed in a single action since Russia's special military operation began. Prior to this round, the EU had already sanctioned over 3,000 Russian entities and individuals across more than twenty separate packages implemented over the past four years.

The sanctions carry severe consequences for those designated. Individuals face travel bans preventing entry into the European Union along with asset freezes on any holdings within EU jurisdiction. Legal entities are subject to asset freezes and a complete prohibition on any joint activities or business dealings with EU residents.

Expanding Sanctions Regime

The approval of this unprecedented number of designations signals Brussels' continued commitment to its economic warfare strategy against Moscow, despite questions about the effectiveness of previous sanctions rounds. The EU has progressively expanded its restrictions since February 2022, targeting sectors ranging from energy and finance to technology and defense.

Western sanctions proponents argue that the measures are designed to constrain Russia's military capabilities by cutting off access to critical technologies and components. Critics, however, point to Russia's continued economic resilience and the emergence of alternative supply chains through third countries as evidence that the sanctions have failed to achieve their stated objectives.

The formal adoption by the EU Council is expected to be a procedural formality following the ambassadorial approval, with implementation likely by week's end.

With information from TASS / Russia

title: Vatican Imposes Sanctions on Argentine Bishop for Improper Conduct Reported by Adults
body:
(ZENIT News / Córdoba, Argentina, 10.06.2026).- The Archdiocese of Córdoba, Argentina, announced on October 2 that Bishop Ricardo Seirutti had been removed from his offices as auxiliary bishop and vicar general following a canonical judicial process ordered by the Holy See's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. The case began after two adults reported what the archdiocese described as conduct improper to his episcopal ministry, but the nature of the allegations has not been made public.

The process was conducted by the Interdiocesan Tribunal of Buenos Aires after being ordered by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, and concluded in recent weeks with a ruling that stripped Seirutti of his offices and imposed additional restrictions.

Seirutti, 70, was ordained a priest for the Archdiocese of Córdoba in 1988 and was appointed auxiliary bishop by Pope Francis in 2015. His removal therefore represents a substantial change in the responsibilities he had exercised within the archdiocese, which is led by Cardinal Ángel Sixto Rossi.

The ruling does not, however, amount to a complete prohibition on his sacramental ministry. For five years, Seirutti may not receive formal appointments or new ecclesiastical offices, and he is forbidden to administer the sacrament of penance or reconciliation. The archdiocese specifically referred to Canon 976 of the Code of Canon Law in connection with this restriction. He retains permission to celebrate Mass and administer the other sacraments.

That distinction is important because Catholic bishops do not cease to be ordained simply because they are removed from an office. Canonical penalties can instead restrict what an ordained minister is permitted to do, while leaving other sacramental faculties intact. In Seirutti's case, the ruling has removed him from institutional authority and sharply limited one particular sacramental ministry without eliminating his ability to celebrate Mass or administer the remaining sacraments.

The public information about the case remains deliberately limited. The archdiocese has not identified the two adults who made the accusations, nor has it disclosed what the alleged conduct consisted of. Consequently, the published decision does not provide a basis for drawing conclusions beyond the facts it has made public. What is clear is that the accusations were considered serious enough for the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith to order a formal canonical process rather than leaving the matter solely to local ecclesiastical authorities.

For the moment, the limits of the public record are as important as the penalty itself. The Church has announced the outcome of a canonical process, but not the underlying allegations in detail. That leaves the central facts clear -- the offices lost, the five-year restrictions imposed and the sacramental functions retained -- while avoiding conclusions that the published information does not support.

title: EU ambassadors agree to largest-ever expansion of Russia sanctions list, targeting more than 1,500 people and organizations -- Meduza
body:
EU ambassadors have agreed to add more than 1,500 individuals and organizations to the bloc's Russia sanctions list, Euronews reported.

The additions will include 743 people and 826 organizations that the EU believes support Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The investigative project Sistema previously reported that the sanctions would target defense industry organizations, their executives, and their employees. For some organizations, the EU will expand existing sanctions.

According to Sistema, all the organizations on the new sanctions list appear on a nonpublic list of defense enterprises compiled by Russia's Ministry of Industry and Trade and published by the Dossier Center in 2025.

EU foreign ministers are expected to formally approve the new sanctions list at a meeting in Luxembourg on Monday, October 12.

title: EU to approve 1,646-entry sanctions list against Russia on 12 October
body:
European Union ambassadors have agreed on two new EU-wide packages of sanctions regarding Ukraine's territorial integrity, which EU foreign ministers are set to formally approve at a meeting on 12 October.

Source: European Pravda, citing several EU diplomats familiar with the discussions

Details: A total of 1,646 new listings on the sanctions lists against Russia will be approved at a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council on 12 October.

Quote from a European Pravda source: "Today, Coreper agreed on new packages of listings under the sanctions regime regarding Ukraine's territorial integrity. They will be formally approved by ministers at the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting on Monday."

This will be the largest amount of sanctions approved all at once, containing the previously announced 1,569 sanctions listings targeting 743 individuals and 826 legal entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex.

Separately, EU ambassadors agreed on another 77 listings related to the so-called elections to Russia's State Duma. This package includes, in particular, candidates who ran for seats in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as several representatives of electoral bodies.

Background:

* On 16 September, the European External Action Service (EEAS) presented a new proposal for a package of individual sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex comprising 1,576 listings.

* On 22 September, the Council of the EU decided to extend the restrictive measures against those responsible for undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine for another 36 months, but removed Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.

title: EU agrees largest-ever expansion of Russia sanctions list, adding 1,646 names
body:
The European Union has agreed to add 1,646 people and entities to its Russia sanctions blacklist in the largest single expansion of the list to date, Euronews reported on Oct. 7.

The deal, reached by EU ambassadors in Brussels, covers 743 individuals and 826 entities accused of supporting Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. A further 77 Russian lawmakers will be sanctioned for standing in September's State Duma election in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.

EU foreign ministers are expected to formally approve the listings in Luxembourg on Oct. 12, after which the names will be made public.

Those targeted will face travel bans and asset freezes, while EU persons and companies will be prohibited from providing them with funds.

The additions will bring the EU's Russia sanctions blacklist to almost 4,650 names.

Euronews reported that member states were keen to finalize the agreement amid a recent series of hybrid attacks, some attributed to Russia. Work has already begun on further listings in response to the drone incident at Leipzig airport in Germany.

title: Foreign Ministry: EU Preparing Biggest Sanctions Package Against Russia
body:
EU sanctions could target more than 1,500 Russian individuals and legal entities, including representatives of Russia's defence industry and State Duma deputies.

The European Union is preparing its largest sanctions package against Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. EU ambassadors have already agreed a preliminary deal.

This was announced by Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi during a briefing.

According to him, the new package предусматривает sanctions against more than 1,500 individuals and companies. Among them are 743 individuals and 826 legal entities.

In particular, Russia's military-industrial complex has been targeted by the restrictions. The sanctions list is also proposed to include 77 State Duma deputies elected from Ukraine's occupied territories.

Separately, the EU plans to extend sanctions against those involved in Russia's use of chemical weapons. The restrictions will apply to 31 individuals and six legal entities.

Tykhyi noted that the EU plans to give final approval to the new sanctions package next week.

title: Prevalence of malaria in the United Villages region, Northern Khartoum State, during armed conflict
body:
We're sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Malaria remains a major public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa, where under-resourced health systems and environmental conditions continue to facilitate transmission. In Sudan, the situation has been further aggravated by the ongoing armed conflict that began in April 2023, which has disrupted healthcare services, population movement, and vector control programs. This study was carried out based on data collected amid aggravated war situations in the United Villages region, Northern Khartoum State, to draw a picture of malaria transmission and burden. This retrospective cross-sectional study included 509 patients from two resource-limited centers (Alfaki Hashim and Algaalyn) in the United Villages region with clinical complaints of fever and headache from August 1, 2025, and December 1, 2025. Variables included age, gender, and the result of the thick blood film for malaria. Of 509 patients analyzed, 487 (96%) tested positive for Plasmodium infections by microscopy, while 22 (4%) were negative. The study population comprised 335 females (66%) and 174 males (34%). Plasmodium falciparum (P. falciparum) was overwhelmingly dominant, accounting for 454 of 487 confirmed infections (93.2%), followed by Plasmodium vivax (P. vivax) (26/487; 5.3%) and mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infections (7/487; 1.4%). Positivity rates were similarly high in both females (96%) and males (95.4%), with no statistically significant gender difference (p > 0.9). Across age groups, the highest positivity rate was observed in patients aged 25-64 and 15-24 years (97%); age-related differences in positivity did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.096). Species distribution did not differ significantly by gender (p = 0.1) or age group (p = 0.3). This study demonstrates a high prevalence of malaria among febrile patients in the United Villages region during the ongoing armed conflict. The findings highlight the substantial impact of disrupted healthcare systems and environmental conditions on malaria transmission and emphasize the urgent need for strengthened surveillance, diagnostic capacity, and vector-control interventions in conflict-affected areas of Sudan.

title: EU Approves Record Sanctions Expansion Targeting 1.6K Russian Citizens and Entities
body:
The European Union has agreed to blacklist more than 1,600 people and entities in the single largest expansion of its sanctions regime against Russia since the beginning of the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, diplomats said Wednesday.

The new listings target 743 individuals and 826 entities primarily linked to Russia's defense industry, according to Euronews.

More than half are concentrated on missile production, Reuters reported Tuesday.

The 22nd package also targets 77 political figures and election officials in connection with last month's parliamentary elections held in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

Several other Russia-related listings were approved under the EU's separate North Korea sanctions framework.

The sanctions entail travel bans, asset freezes and prohibitions on receiving EU funding.

EU foreign ministers will formally approve the expanded sanctions list in Luxembourg on Monday, per Reuters, AFP and Euronews. The bloc last approved its 21st sanctions package in July.

The agreement follows backlash over the recent removal of oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, concessions made to prevent all other EU listings from lapsing. Usmanov's removal was linked to the release of a French prisoner in Azerbaijan.

title: Mahama orders sanctions for officials who fail to enforce building safety rules - Adomonline.com
body:
President John Dramani Mahama has directed the Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, to ensure that officials who fail to enforce building safety regulations are held accountable when structural failures occur.

According to the President, officials responsible for issuing building permits and monitoring compliance must be identified and sanctioned if their failure to perform their duties contributes to a building collapse.

He made the call on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, at the National Conference on Housing Finance, where he stressed the need for stronger enforcement of building regulations at the district assembly level.

President Mahama expressed concern over the continued construction of buildings despite stop-work orders issued by local authorities.

He questioned why such directives are often ignored, warning that failure to enforce them could have fatal consequences.

"More often than not, you see red paint stop work, and yet the work continues. And you wonder what's happening," President Mahama said.

He said the consequences of such failures become evident when structurally unsafe buildings eventually collapse.

"And one day they are working, and the whole house comes tumbling down. You ask, who gave the permit for that building?"

President Mahama said authorities must establish responsibility whenever a building collapses, particularly in cases where regulatory officials failed to carry out their mandated duties.

"These are things that the Ministry of Local Government should take very seriously. If a house collapses, we must see whose duty it was to ensure that that house was safe, and that person must be sanctioned for it," he said.

He therefore tasked the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs with strengthening oversight at the district assembly level, where building permits are issued and compliance with safety standards is monitored.

The President's comments come amid growing concerns over building safety and structural failures across the country.

More than 75 building collapses are estimated to have been recorded across Ghana over the past five years, while an estimated one to three multi-storey building failures occur annually.

Beyond building safety

President Mahama also called for broader measures to improve housing conditions and address challenges confronting residents in underserved communities.

He identified overcrowding in slums, insecure land tenure, poor sanitation and inadequate access to basic utilities as some of the issues requiring urgent attention.

"We must also ensure that the homes we build are safe, accessible and connected to jobs and essential services," he said.

He stressed that Ghana's housing agenda must go beyond simply increasing the number of homes and focus equally on safety, accessibility, proper planning and the availability of essential services.

title: VexPay as a New Link in A7: Western Fintech Expertise in the Architecture of Russian Sanctions Evasion
body:
British payments specialist Michael Donald, who previously served on the board of Visa UK and worked at a number of major Western financial companies, has emerged at the center of an investigation into the Kyrgyz payment platform VexPay. According to documents obtained by the Financial Times, the platform was developed with the active involvement of representatives of the A7 network -- a financial infrastructure created with the participation of Russia's Promsvyazbank and fugitive Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor, which the United States has linked to large-scale sanctions evasion.

At an August 12, 2025 meeting in Moscow, Shor introduced VexPay's new management and named Donald as one of the platform's executives. Donald confirmed to the Financial Times that he attended the meeting, but categorically denied that he had been an employee or director of VexPay or had agreed to head the company. According to Donald, he was advising Kyrgyz state-owned Processing KG on international payments, card acceptance, Apple Pay and engagement with Visa.

This discrepancy is central to assessing Donald's role. The appearance of his name in A7 meeting records does not prove that he agreed to work for VexPay or that he was aware of any potential use of the platform to circumvent sanctions. At the same time, the confirmed presence of a British payments specialist at the Moscow meeting, and the nature of the consulting work he acknowledges, illustrate how the creation of alternative financial infrastructure depends not only on technology but also on Western expertise in Visa, international acquiring and digital payments.

VexPay May Be Part of A7's Evolution Rather Than a Standalone Fintech Project

Formally, VexPay is linked to Kyrgyz state-owned Processing KG rather than A7. The Kyrgyz side denies any external control over the project. However, minutes, correspondence and other documents obtained by the Financial Times covering the period from March to August 2025 indicate substantially deeper involvement by A7 representatives.

According to those materials, Shor and A7 employees participated in discussions concerning VexPay's structure, the opening of bank accounts, staffing, the location of call centers, legal arrangements and technical architecture. The project itself was presented to Kyrgyz officials as an alternative international payment channel capable of operating outside the traditional SWIFT infrastructure.

This makes it possible to view VexPay within the broader evolution of Russia's adaptation to sanctions.

After Russian banks' access to Western financial infrastructure was restricted, Moscow began building not a single alternative to SWIFT but a multilayered ecosystem combining banks, payment companies, crypto-assets, intermediary firms and third-country jurisdictions.

In such a system, shutting down or sanctioning one operator does not dismantle the entire network. Transactions can be rerouted through another company, bank, token or jurisdiction.

A7 Is Evolving into a Transnational Shadow Payment Infrastructure

On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury took a significant step by designating the A7 Network as a significant transnational criminal organization.

According to the U.S. Treasury, A7 uses a network of intermediary companies in third countries that disguise transactions as ordinary trade payments. The bank accounts and web resources of such companies may in practice be controlled by A7 personnel, while access to financial accounts can be conducted through specially created VPN infrastructure that conceals the operators' actual locations.

Of particular importance, the U.S. assessment extends well beyond Russian sanctions evasion. Washington has linked A7 to financial operations benefiting Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other sanctioned entities.

A7 therefore increasingly resembles not simply a Russian sanctions-evasion mechanism but an exportable financial infrastructure that could potentially be used by a range of sanctioned actors.

It is in this context that VexPay becomes particularly significant.

Kyrgyzstan Provides A7 with a Necessary Gateway

For Russia's sanctions-evasion system, Kyrgyzstan offers several advantages: geographic proximity, substantial trade with Russia, the integration of post-Soviet financial systems and, at the same time, the ability of local banks and payment companies to interact with external financial infrastructure.

This makes it possible to construct a fundamentally different model from a direct payment originating from a sanctioned Russian bank.

A Russian client or entity can be separated from the international financial system by several layers of intermediaries: Russia → A7/affiliated operator → intermediary company → Kyrgyz payment infrastructure → local or foreign bank → international payment system → final counterparty.

The greater the number of layers, the more difficult it becomes for a correspondent bank to establish the original source of funds, the real party ordering the transaction and its underlying economic purpose.

This is why U.S. regulators are increasingly focusing not only on A7 itself but also on its sub-agents -- companies that may formally appear independent of the Russian network.

Michael Donald's Significance Lies Primarily in His Expertise

The available evidence does not support a conclusion that Donald knowingly helped A7 circumvent sanctions. His professional profile does, however, explain why the involvement of a specialist with his background could have been valuable to the project.

Donald has more than 30 years of experience in the payments industry, having worked at MBNA, Bank of America and other financial institutions, and served on the board of Visa UK. His own company, ImageNPay, specializes in digital payment products and virtual cards.

According to Donald, his consulting work for Processing KG concerned precisely the components that are critical to integrating a new payment operator into the international system: card acceptance, Visa, Apple Pay and international payments.

The principal value of a Western consultant to such a project therefore does not necessarily lie in formally managing the company. Potentially more important are knowledge of international payment-system rules, technical requirements, compliance procedures, acquiring, and the mechanisms for integrating a local fintech platform with global financial infrastructure.

ImageNPay's Russia Links Predate VexPay

The fact that Donald and ImageNPay's contacts with the Russian market did not begin in 2025 adds further significance to the case.

As early as 2020, ImageNPay participated in the Soft-Landing Programme of Russia's Skolkovo innovation center. Donald publicly described Russia and the CIS countries as important future markets for the company and said it was using a team of Russian programmers.

Corporate records for the British company ImageNPay UK Limited also show that Dmitry Kuptsov owned 27.2% of the company in 2020. At the same time, the Russian origin or business connections of an individual shareholder do not in themselves constitute evidence that ImageNPay was controlled by Russian entities or participated in sanctions evasion.

The claim that ImageNPay served as a "cover for Russian capital" therefore requires a substantially stronger evidentiary basis.

The West's Main Vulnerability Is Not SWIFT, but Access Points to the Global Financial System

The VexPay case indicates that the sanctions confrontation is gradually shifting.

Initially, the Western strategy focused on disconnecting Russian banks from SWIFT, blocking correspondent accounts and freezing assets.

Russia's response has been to create alternative routes in which a sanctioned entity may not appear at all at the first layer of a transaction visible to a Western bank.

Instead of a direct route -- Russian bank → SWIFT → Western bank -- a more complex chain emerges: Russian client → shadow payment network → intermediary company → financial institution in a third country → fintech → international payment infrastructure.

The critical resource is therefore no longer SWIFT itself, but the ability to gain access to international acquiring, correspondent banks, Visa/Mastercard, digital wallets and other global payment interfaces.

Western Expertise May Be a Distinct Vulnerability in the Sanctions Regime

The VexPay case highlights another potential problem: Russia's technological isolation can be partly offset by recruiting specialists who have spent years working inside Western financial infrastructure.

Their value lies not only in personal contacts.

They understand how payment systems are structured, which technical and compliance requirements must be met, how financial institutions are onboarded, how international acquiring works and which criteria banks and payment systems use to assess risk.

Regulators should therefore focus not on a consultant's nationality or the mere fact of working in a third country, but on the nature of the services provided, the project's ultimate beneficiary, its source of financing, and whether the expertise supplied enables sanctioned entities to regain access to prohibited financial services.

The Risk to Visa, Apple Pay and Western Banks Is Different in Nature

The argument concerning a direct risk of secondary sanctions also requires qualification.

The mere use of Visa, Mastercard or Apple Pay technologies does not mean that those companies are participating in a sanctions-evasion scheme. The risk arises when a payment operator, bank or fintech company fails to identify a concealed sanctioned participant or continues to service transactions after such a connection has been established.

A7 therefore creates, above all, an attribution problem.

When several formally independent companies are positioned between the Russian originator of a payment and a Western financial institution, identifying the transaction's ultimate beneficiary becomes substantially more difficult.

The new U.S. pressure model is directed precisely at this problem: targeting not only A7's core structure but also its international sub-agents.

Key Judgment

The VexPay case points to a qualitative evolution in Russia's sanctions-evasion system. Moscow is no longer merely attempting to build its own isolated alternative to SWIFT. A more effective model is the construction of a distributed network that uses public and private entities in third countries as gateways to the global financial system.

In this model, A7 provides the financial flows and network of intermediaries; third-country jurisdictions provide the legal and banking shell; fintech platforms create the technological interface; and Western payments expertise can potentially help integrate this infrastructure with international services.

VexPay is an important case because it illustrates a possible transformation of sanctions evasion from a Russian "shadow banking system" into an international fintech architecture.

Michael Donald's role, however, must be assessed separately from A7's. The available documents confirm his presence at the Moscow meeting and his consulting work for Processing KG, but do not establish that he agreed to lead VexPay, controlled the platform or knowingly facilitated unlawful sanctions evasion.The distinction between confirmed professional involvement and unproven knowing participation in sanctions evasion is therefore critical to any legally robust assessment of the case.

title: Do 'bullish' Man City have 'a few cards up their sleeve'? Cult hero Paul Dickov talks 115 charges, possible sanctions and 'bolshy' stance after 'sham' statement
body: Manchester City, despite having 115 Financial Fair Play (FFP) charges hanging over their head and a damning "sham" statement from the Premier League ringing in their ears, remain unwavering in their belief that no rules have been broken and their name will be cleared. Cult hero Paul Dickov has delivered his take on the long-running saga to GOAL, with there still the potential for game-changing "cards" to be pulled out of collective sleeves.

title: 'Tariff-Based System' -- The Sanctions Rival Premier League Clubs Want Man City to Face
body:
Premier League clubs want "reparations" for the nine years in which Manchester City breached the competition's financial rules, with additional limitations in future seasons, a new report has revealed.

City were found guilty by an independent commission over charges spanning almost a decade from 2009-10 until 2017-18. The club continues to vehemently deny wrongdoing, refusing to accept the verdict -- going as far as calling it an "opinion" -- and already lodging an appeal.

Should that process be unsuccessful and the original verdict upheld, rival teams appear keen for sanctions to be wide ranging, according to BBC Sport. That said, when the times comes the decision will solely lie with the original three-person panel who found the club guilty.

Not all clubs are desperate for City to be stripped of titles, but that is the opinion of some. However, they are not necessarily seeking to claim the spoils for themselves -- Manchester United and Liverpool were runners-up to City during the league campaigns in question. Rather, it would be to primarily "take honors away," at which point they would remain vacant. At least one club is concerned the "credibility of the Premier League would be lost" if City keep their titles.

Another club considers it "obtuse" if City are allowed to be active during the January transfer window, even if the process remains ongoing and sanctions have not been applied. The deadline for this appeal verdict to be passed down is Jan. 23, 2027, but City could continue to escalate it up the chain if unsuccessful, suggesting the end is not exactly near.

Retrospective Financial Reparations

In terms of retrospective punishment, one possibility that has been floated is an alteration of City's Premier League finishes during the nine seasons in question via historic points deductions. By essentially applying a "tariff" to City's points tally in each season, it would have the effect of rewriting the final Premier League table each time.

That does more than potentially strip titles, but could also be used as a way to then compensate other clubs who might have finished higher up the table and have been entitled to greater prize money had it not been for the financial cheating judged to have taken place.

It's not only important for seasons in which City finished as Premier League champions. For example, Manchester United were marginally knocked down into fifth place and missed out on Champions League qualification in 2015-16 after finishing level on points with City, but with an inferior goal difference. It would be less likely to affect teams who finished near the bottom of the table, but would of course depend on the severity of each season's deduction.

Man City Premier League Finishes, Points Tallies During Financial Cheating

Single-Season Points Deduction Insufficient

Sky Sports notes that "sympathy is in short supply" among the others clubs, who "do not expect City to be in Premier League next season" if the appeal is unsuccessful.

The Premier League cannot strictly demote the club by one division -- or even two or three -- because the EFL is a separate entity and doesn't have to accept them. The far more severe punishment would be expulsion from the Premier League and an application to join a league much lower down the English soccer pyramid. Such a fate is usually reserved for teams who fall on hard times, go out of business and re-emerge as phoenix clubs with a similar name.

Relegation into the EFL could happen with a stern enough points deductions, which is the clearest way to ensure that City remain punished in future seasons, beyond just historic losses. But, as the BBC report explains, "at least four" Premier League clubs believe a single-season deduction would be "insufficient punishment given the severity."

Applying anything north of a one-off 60-point deduction would be a massive, record-breaking sanction that would almost certainly condemn City to relegation. However, there is an expectation that relegation in that scenario would result in immediate promotion.

FALLOUT ON MAN CITY CHARGES VERDICT

* Man City Punishment Timeline: How Long Will Appeal Take, When Will This End?

* Seven Takeaways From Official Report Into Man City's Nine Years of Cheating

* Premier League Stun Man City With Scathing Official Guilty Verdict

* Man City Charges: The Premier League's Multi-Year Investigation Explained

* The Potential Punishments Facing Man City for 115 Premier League Charges

Given that City players are not believed to have relegation clauses in their contracts, there could be no undervalued poaching of stars like Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki against the club's will, increasing the chance of keeping them for a year in the EFL Championship and bulldozing the second tier at a canter.

With swift promotion, City could be free of punishment sooner rather than later, which feels unfair when the rule-breaking took place over nine years.

The tougher sanction would be spreading a points deduction, which could mathematically be in excess of 450 given the number of charges and the previous sanctions applied to Everton and Nottingham Forest for comparatively minor financial breaches, over multiple years.

Starting season after season on minus points would likely result in repeated failure to qualify for UEFA competition and serve to severely suppress revenue for as long as it is in place. The added consequence of that is City losing appeal for both existing and prospective future players. It is not something that could so easily be cleared and washed away.

title: President Mahama calls for sanctions against officials over building collapses
body:
President John Dramani Mahama has directed the Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, to ensure that officials who fail to properly enforce building safety regulations are identified and sanctioned.

He said officials responsible for inspecting buildings, issuing permits and ensuring compliance with safety regulations must be held accountable when they neglect their duties.

Speaking at the National Conference on Housing Finance on October 7, 2026, Mahama said the enforcement of building regulations must be strengthened, particularly at the district assembly level.

He stressed that whenever a building collapses, authorities must establish which officials were responsible for ensuring its safety and take appropriate action where negligence is established.

"These are things that the Ministry of Local Government should take very seriously. If a house collapses, we must see whose duty it was to ensure that that house was safe, and that person must be sanctioned for it," he said.

President Mahama imposes sanctions on appointees who failed to declare their assets

Mahama also expressed concern about the continued construction of buildings despite stop-work orders issued by local authorities.

"More often than not, you see red paint stop work, and yet the work continues. And you wonder what's happening. And one day they are working, and the whole house comes tumbling down. You ask, who gave the permit for that building?" he stated.

He said the responsibility for enforcing building safety standards cannot end with the issuance of permits, insisting that district assemblies must ensure that developers comply with approved requirements.

Beyond structural safety, Mahama called for measures to address overcrowding in slums, insecure land tenure, poor sanitation and inadequate access to utilities.

"We must also ensure that the homes we build are safe, accessible and connected to jobs and essential services," he indicated.

title: Ukrainian Lawmaker to Stand Trial for Soliciting $250,000 Sanctions Deal
body:
A Ukrainian lawmaker and her assistant will soon stand trial for allegedly offering to arrange National Security and Defense Council (RNBO) sanctions against business competitors for $250,000.

Ukraine's anti-graft agencies, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), said on Wednesday that the investigation was completed in June and the case has been sent to the court.

Earlier reports in December 2025, when the investigation was publicized, identified the lawmaker as Anna Skorokhod, a sitting member of the Verkhovna Rada. Skorokhod denied the charges.

The two agencies said a "criminal group" offered the sanction package, while Skorokhod, unnamed in the agencies' reports, served as a guarantor.

However, Skorokhod is said to have taken $125,000 - half of the amount - and failed to find an RNBO official willing to enact the proposed sanctions.

"According to the investigation, the money was promised to be transferred to officials of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine [RNBO] as payment for the sanction decision," NABU wrote in its Wednesday press release.

"After receiving $125,000, the 'customer' was assured that this part would be transferred to RNBO officials. In reality, the money remained with the attackers, as they were unable to find a person who would agree to commit illegal actions," it added.

The agencies added that one member of the criminal group became a witness by taking a plea deal, under which he was sentenced to 5 years in prison and exempted from serving the sentence by a probationary period.

In addition, the person made a transfer of Hr.700,000 ($15,614) to support the Ukrainian military via the United 24 fund.

title: US formalises removal of three Pakistan-linked men from sanctions list
body:
Rahnuma;US formalises removal of three Pakistan-linked men from sanctions list

Washington, Oct 7 (IANS) The United States has formally published the removal from its sanctions list of three Pakistan-linked men who had been designated more than two decades ago in cases involving terrorism and narcotics trafficking, according to the Treasury Department records.

The three are Mohammed Tufail, Sher Afghan and Nasir Ali Khan.

The removals were originally made by the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control on July 27 as part of a broader effort to modernise its sanctions lists. They were formally published in the Federal Register on Wednesday.

Treasury said the July action removed 84 individuals and entities and updated other entries as part of an effort to keep US sanctions targeted, effective and current.

Those removed included individuals and entities no longer considered US national-security or foreign-policy priorities, including some deceased people, defunct entities and targets sanctioned more than 20 years ago. Treasury did not publicly specify which rationale applied to each of the three Pakistan-linked individuals.

Tufail, also identified as S M Tufail and Sheik Mohammed Tufail, had been designated under US terrorism sanctions.

When his assets were blocked in December 2001, the Treasury Department identified him as an industrialist and one of three key directors of Ummah Tameer-e-Nau, or UTN, an organisation founded by Pakistani nuclear scientists.

Treasury said at the time that UTN directors and members had met Osama bin Laden, al-Qaeda leaders and Taliban leader Mullah Omar and discussed the development of chemical, biological and nuclear weapons.

The other two men were designated under US narcotics sanctions.

Sher Afghan, also identified by aliases including Shir Afghan, Mohammad Aziz and Abdullah Khan, was born in Pakistan and was added to the sanctions list in June 2001 under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act.

Nasir Ali Khan, born in Pakistan in 1955, was also placed under narcotics sanctions in June 2001.

A State Department report covering Pakistan's counter-narcotics efforts in 1996 said the country's caretaker government had arrested a major trafficker named Nasir Ali Khan who was wanted in the United States on drug charges. The report also said an American extradition request was pending.

The available records do not establish in the sanctions-removal notice why each of the three men was taken off the list in July.

OFAC said its broader sanctions-modernisation exercise was intended to remove outdated entries and improve the accuracy of its lists while ensuring removals did not undermine US national-security or foreign-policy interests.

title: EU ambassadors approve largest-ever sanctions list against Russia - source
body:
Today, at a meeting of EU member states' representatives in the COREPER II format, ambassadors approved the largest-ever sanctions package against the aggressor state.

A source in diplomatic circles familiar with the meeting told this to Ukrinform.

The diplomat explained that this includes a large package of 1,569 listings proposed by EU High Representative Kaja Kallas last month, concerning 743 individuals and 826 entities.

He added that the lists would also include another 77 entities linked to elections to Russia's State Duma, including candidates who ran for seats in the temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine, as well as several election commission officials.

"These listings will be formally approved at the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting next week," the source said.

As is known, the EU Foreign Affairs Council will meet in Luxembourg on October 12.

As reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that in response to the lifting of European sanctions on Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov, Ukraine would add 20 more Russian oligarchs to its sanctions lists.

title: Rubio Says Iran Has 'Lost Complete Control' Of Strait Of Hormuz As Sanctions Bite
body:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Wednesday that Iran has "lost complete control" over the strategic Strait of Hormuz, asserting that maritime oil traffic through the critical waterway is returning toward normal operating levels.

Speaking during an official visit to Greece, Rubio said commercial oil shipments are currently moving through the passage at volumes very close to what was seen before the launch of Operation Epic Fury. The secretary attributed the shift to intensified American naval operations and economic measures, arguing that ongoing U.S. sanctions have plunged Tehran's economy into a "total and complete free fall."

Rubio also reiterated Washington's stance regarding Tehran's nuclear ambitions, stating that the Iranian government has repeatedly passed up opportunities to negotiate a deal with the United States and maintaining that Iran will never be permitted to develop a nuclear weapon.

The remarks come amid conflicting claims over the status of Iran's energy sector.

Former Iranian oil minister Mohsen Paknejad pushed back against assertions made by U.S. President Donald Trump, who suggested the minister stepped down because Iran had run out of oil. In statements reported by Iran International English, Paknejad disputed that characterization, stating that his departure was due entirely to "personal reasons" and emphasizing that domestic "oil production and exports continued even under sanctions and a blockade."

Maritime security analysts noted that while commercial shipping has found viable paths, risks throughout the passage remain elevated. Mark Chandler, a former senior U.S. defense intelligence official, explained in a televised interview that tanker traffic has rebounded to between 75% and 90% of pre-conflict levels on peak days.

Most outbound tankers have relied on southern navigation corridors hugging the Omani coastline while turning off transponders to avoid detection, even as sporadic drone and missile attacks on commercial vessels persist.
