title: EU agrees on new sanctions against Russia
body:
BRUSSELS - European Union (EU) countries on Wednesday agreed a major new raft of sanctions on Russia, targeting nearly 1,600 individuals and entities over the war in Ukraine, diplomats said.

Officials said those being blacklisted were mainly linked to the Russian military and arms industry, and that EU foreign ministers will formally adopt the measures at a meeting on Monday.

In addition, diplomats said 77 new listings were agreed over recent Duma elections in Russia decried as fixed by Brussels, including three members of the electoral commission.

This wave will take the number of individuals and entities subjected to visa bans and asset freezes over the war to some 4,500 in total.

Meanwhile, the EU is mulling whether to launch work on another wide-ranging package of broader sanctions on the Russian economy, despite fears it is running out of targets it can agree on.

Diplomats say that Brussels could, going forward, break up its sanctions into smaller batches in the hope that they will be easier to get through.

title: Mahama wants sanctions for officials over building safety failures - The Herald ghana
body:
President John Dramani Mahama has directed the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs to hold officials accountable for failures to enforce building safety regulations.

He said officials responsible for ensuring that buildings comply with safety requirements must be identified and sanctioned when their failure to perform their duties contributes to structural failures.

President Mahama made the call at the National Conference on Housing Finance on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, while urging district assemblies to strengthen the enforcement of building regulations.

He expressed concern about developers continuing construction despite stop-work orders issued by local authorities.

"More often than not, you see red paint stop work, and yet the work continues. And you wonder what's happening," he said.

The President questioned how a building could be allowed to continue after authorities had ordered construction to stop, only for the structure to eventually collapse.

"And one day they are working, and the whole house comes tumbling down. You ask, who gave the permit for that building?" he said.

President Mahama said the responsibility of officials involved in approving and monitoring construction must be established whenever a building collapses.

"These are things that the Ministry of Local Government should take very seriously. If a house collapses, we must see whose duty it was to ensure that that house was safe, and that person must be sanctioned for it," he said.

He said district assemblies must take enforcement seriously, particularly in the issuance of building permits and monitoring compliance with safety requirements.

The call comes amid concerns over building collapses across the country, with more than 75 incidents reportedly recorded over the past five years.

President Mahama also urged authorities to address other housing challenges, including overcrowding in slum communities, insecure land tenure, poor sanitation and inadequate access to basic utilities.

He said efforts to improve housing must also ensure that residents have access to safe homes, jobs and essential services.

title: Mahama orders sanctions for officials who fail to enforce building safety rules
body:
President John Dramani Mahama has directed the Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, to ensure that officials responsible for enforcing building safety regulations are held accountable when structural failures occur.

He said officials tasked with ensuring the safety of buildings must be identified and sanctioned if they fail to properly enforce the relevant regulations.

President Mahama made the remarks on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, at the National Conference on Housing Finance, where he called for stronger enforcement of building regulations at the district assembly level.

He expressed concern about buildings continuing to be constructed despite stop-work orders issued by local authorities, insisting that such directives must be enforced.

"More often than not, you see red paint stop work, and yet the work continues. And you wonder what's happening," President Mahama said.

"And one day they are working, and the whole house comes tumbling down. You ask, who gave the permit for that building?"

The President said accountability must be established whenever a building collapses, particularly where regulatory officials failed to perform their duties.

"These are things that the Ministry of Local Government should take very seriously. If a house collapses, we must see whose duty it was to ensure that that house was safe, and that person must be sanctioned for it," he said.

President Mahama said the issue must be addressed at the district assembly level, where building permits are issued and compliance with safety requirements is monitored.

His comments come amid concerns over structural failures in Ghana, with more than 75 building collapses estimated to have been recorded across the country over the past five years, while an estimated one to three multi-storey building failures occur annually.

Beyond building safety, President Mahama called for broader measures to improve housing conditions, including tackling overcrowding in slums, insecure land tenure, poor sanitation and inadequate access to utilities.

"We must also ensure that the homes we build are safe, accessible and connected to jobs and essential services," he said.

title: World Space Week: How Iran built an independent, world-class space program under sanctions
body:
Iran's space program has evolved from its modest 2009 satellite launch into an increasingly independent capability spanning Earth observation, security satellites, launch vehicles, orbital maneuvering, and geostationary communications infrastructure.

On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a 58-centimeter aluminum sphere, into orbit around Earth. In doing so, it opened an era in which human beings would, for the first time in history, cross beyond the shore of the sky itself and begin the long work of making space a domain of human activity.

World Space Week, observed annually from October 4 to 10 in commemoration of that launch and, a decade later, the signing of the Outer Space Treaty, offers an occasion to trace that arc - from a single radio-beeping sphere in 1957 to a field in which, today, Iran counts itself among a small group of nations capable of designing, building, and independently launching its own satellites.

The first man beyond the sky

Less than four years after Sputnik's launch, the Soviet Union achieved a milestone that no unmanned payload could match: on April 12, 1961, cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human being to travel into orbit, completing a single 108-minute circuit of Earth aboard Vostok 1 before returning safely to the planet.

The significance of Gagarin's flight extended far beyond the technical achievement of keeping a human being alive in the vacuum of space.

For the first time, it demonstrated that the boundary separating Earth from the cosmos was not an absolute limit on human presence, but an engineering problem that could be solved. And it did so under the flag of a nation that, within living memory, had been a largely agrarian society devastated by war.

Gagarin's flight transformed the abstract possibility of human spaceflight into demonstrated fact. In doing so, it reset the terms against which every subsequent spacefaring power would be measured.

A race decided by desperation and improvisation

Gagarin's flight, coming on the heels of Sputnik, placed the United States in a position of profound technological humiliation. Washington had been outpaced by Moscow at nearly every major milestone of the early space age - first satellite, first animal in orbit, first human in orbit - and American planners understood that competing with the Soviet space program on its own terms, incrementally matching each Soviet first one step behind, was a contest the United States was structurally positioned to keep losing.

The American response drew on a resource acquired in the closing days of the Second World War: German rocket scientists recruited from the defeated Nazi regime, chief among them Wernher von Braun, who had developed the V-2 ballistic missile for Hitler's Germany and was brought to the US under the classified postwar program known as Operation Paperclip.

Von Braun and his colleagues became an important part of the technical foundation of the American rocket program. Under this German-American leadership, the United States made the decisive strategic choice of the space race: rather than continuing to chase the Soviet Union through a series of incremental firsts, Washington would leapfrog the competition by committing to land a human being on the Moon - a technical undertaking of such scale and complexity that it would force the United States to develop capabilities far beyond those required for orbital flight and, in effect, change the terms of the contest.

That bet culminated on July 20, 1969, when Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface and spoke the words that would become the defining phrase of the space age: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

The Moon landing closed the first chapter of the space race. But the underlying lesson of how it was won - that a competitor unable to match a rival step for step can instead change the terms of the competition entirely - would echo far beyond the Cold War and far beyond the two nations that fought it.

A field still closed to most of the world

More than six decades after Sputnik, the ability to operate independently in space remains far more exclusive than satellite ownership alone might suggest. More than 80 countries operate satellites of one kind or another, but most of them commissioned their spacecraft from foreign manufacturers or rely on foreign launch providers to reach orbit.

The far narrower circle consists of the countries that have demonstrated the ability to design, build, and launch satellites into orbit using their own indigenous capabilities.

Iran joined that circle in 2009, alongside countries including the United States, Russia, China, Japan, India, France, the United Kingdom, North Korea, and Israel. Of those nations, only three - the United States, Russia, and China - have independently conducted crewed orbital missions.

That distinction matters because satellite ownership and space-launch sovereignty are not the same achievement. A nation can purchase a satellite from a foreign manufacturer and pay another country to launch it, but it remains dependent on foreign providers for access to orbit.

A nation capable of designing, building, and launching its own spacecraft possesses something more consequential: an independent pathway to space.

Omid: Iran enters the circle

Iran crossed that threshold on February 2, 2009, coinciding, fittingly, with the 30th anniversary of the Islamic Revolution. On that day, it launched its first domestically built satellite, Omid ("Hope"), aboard the indigenous Safir carrier rocket, becoming the ninth country to place an independently developed satellite into orbit using its own launch vehicle.

Iran's achievement followed the Soviet Union in 1957, the United States in 1958, France in 1965, Japan and China in 1970, the United Kingdom in 1971, and India in 1980.

Geoffrey Forden of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology described the achievement at the time as a "technological tour de force," underscoring the significance of Iran's entry into an exclusive group of countries capable of reaching orbit despite international opposition and extensive sanctions intended, among other things, to restrict its access to advanced aerospace technology.

Rasad-1: Iran's first eye in orbit

Iran's second satellite, Rasad-1 ("Observation"), launched aboard a Safir carrier on June 15, 2011, becoming the country's first domestically built imaging satellite and successfully transmitting photographic data to ground stations.

According to specifications released by the Iranian Space Agency, Rasad-1 incorporated many of the core subsystems required for an operational satellite platform, including power-management systems, solar cells, attitude control, a payload, GPS, onboard data and command management, receiver and transmitter systems, a ranging transmitter, and thermal-control systems.

Its attitude-control system used a passive gravity-gradient method based on a deployable boom.

As Iran's first step toward an indigenous Earth-observation capability, Rasad-1's camera offered a resolution of approximately 150 meters - a modest capability by modern imaging standards, but an important milestone in the development of Iran's domestic satellite technology.

Navid and Fajr: Building toward maneuverability

Iran's third satellite, Navid ("Promise"), was launched from the Semnan Space Center at approximately 3:30 a.m. local time on February 3, 2012. It was followed by Fajr ("Dawn"), launched aboard an upgraded Safir-1B carrier on February 2, 2015.

Fajr represented a further step toward greater spacecraft autonomy. It was designed with an orbital-transfer capability, allowing it to adjust its orbit from an elliptical path of roughly 250 to 450 kilometers to a circular orbit at approximately 450 kilometers.

The maneuver was enabled by a cold-gas propulsion system and was intended to extend the satellite's operational lifetime to roughly 18 months.

Payam-1: A near miss

Not every Iranian launch reached orbit successfully. Payam-1, launched aboard the Simorgh carrier rocket in January 2019, failed to achieve the velocity required to enter a stable orbit. Iranian officials said the satellite fell short of the required velocity by approximately 150 meters per second before ultimately re-entering and falling into the Indian Ocean.

The narrow margin was a reminder of the unforgiving precision demanded by orbital mechanics - and of the technological gap that can separate a successful launch from failure. It also demonstrated how Iran's ambitions were increasingly moving beyond simply placing small satellites in orbit toward developing larger and more capable launch vehicles and spacecraft.

The Noor constellation: Iran's military satellites take shape

On April 22, 2020, the IRGC's Aerospace Force successfully placed Iran's first military satellite, Noor-1, into an orbit roughly 425 kilometers above Earth using the indigenous Qased carrier rocket, launched from Iran's central desert.

The reaction from Washington offered its own measure of the launch's significance. Then-US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo condemned the launch within hours, claiming it demonstrated that Iran's space program was "neither peaceful nor entirely civilian" and calling for Iran to be "held accountable" under UN Security Council Resolution 2231.

The unusually sharp and immediate diplomatic reaction underscored how seriously Washington regarded the scientific capability Iran had demonstrated.

Iran followed with Noor-2, launched aboard the Qased into an orbit of approximately 500 kilometers and equipped with an imaging payload. Noor-3 followed on September 27, 2023, entering a roughly 450-kilometer orbit with an imaging mission and an announced ground resolution of approximately five meters. The progression represented a substantial improvement in Iran's indigenous military-imaging capability within a single generation of satellites.

Khayyam: Iran's sharpest eye

On August 9, 2022, at 10:31 a.m. Tehran time, Iran's most capable Earth-observation satellite, Khayyam, was launched aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

Khayyam is designed for high-resolution remote sensing, with an advertised ground resolution of approximately one meter - by far the sharpest imaging capability publicly associated with Iran's satellite fleet. Weighing roughly 600 kilograms and operating at an altitude of approximately 500 kilometers, the satellite completes an orbit of Earth roughly every 90 minutes.

The satellite was named in honor of Omar Khayyam, the Iranian mathematician and astronomer whose work on calendrical reform produced the exceptionally accurate Jalali calendar nearly a millennium ago.

As a remote-sensing platform, Khayyam has been associated with six principal application areas: agriculture, environmental monitoring, natural-disaster response, urban change detection, water-resource monitoring, and mineral exploration. Its significance, however, extends beyond those civilian applications. High-resolution Earth observation provides a state with a persistent means of monitoring changes on the ground without relying entirely on foreign imagery providers.

Soraya and the Qaem-100: A breakthrough in solid-fuel propulsion

On January 20, 2024, Iran launched the Soraya satellite aboard the IRGC's Qaem-100 carrier rocket. The Qaem-100 is a multistage launch vehicle based primarily on solid-fuel propulsion, a choice that offers important advantages in storage, readiness, and operational simplicity compared with conventional liquid-fuel systems.

One of the most significant features demonstrated by the Qaem-100 was the ability to terminate thrust from its solid-fuel upper stage after achieving the desired velocity. Conventional solid-fuel motors are substantially less flexible than liquid-fuel engines because their propellant cannot simply be throttled in the same manner once combustion begins.

The ability to control the termination of thrust therefore represents an important advance in Iran's solid-propellant launch technology, particularly for achieving more precise orbital insertion.

The achievement mattered for a reason extending beyond the Soraya mission itself: increasingly precise control over a launch vehicle's final velocity translates directly into greater flexibility in placing satellites into their intended orbits.

Chamran-1: Proving orbital maneuvering

The Ministry of Defense's research satellite Chamran-1, designed and built by Iran Electronics Industries' space division in cooperation with the Aerospace Research Institute and private knowledge-based companies, launched aboard the Qaem-100 on September 14, 2024, successfully reaching an orbit approximately 550 kilometers above Earth.

Chamran-1's primary mission was to demonstrate orbital-maneuvering technology - the ability of a spacecraft to actively modify its orbit - alongside secondary objectives involving a cold-gas propulsion system and the evaluation of navigation and attitude-control technologies.

By the second half of November 2024, Iranian officials reported that Chamran-1 had completed a sequence of orbital maneuvers, including lowering and raising its altitude and conducting a rendezvous maneuver with the upper-stage remnants of its own carrier rocket.

Such capabilities are significant because controlled proximity operations are a prerequisite for more sophisticated activities in space, including satellite inspection, rendezvous, and, potentially, future servicing missions.

Jam-e Jam 1: Iran's first geostationary broadcast satellite

On February 12, 2026, the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting organization's first geostationary communications satellite, Jam-e Jam 1, also designated Iran DBS, was launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan aboard a Russian Proton-M rocket.

The mission represented Iran's entry into a substantially more demanding class of space infrastructure: geostationary communications satellites.

Jam-e Jam 1 is intended to occupy an orbital position at approximately 34 degrees east longitude after completing the necessary orbital-transfer maneuvers. Its principal purpose is to provide broadcast and communications infrastructure for Iran's state broadcasting system.

Unlike conventional direct-to-home television satellites, Jam-e Jam 1 is intended primarily as professional broadcast infrastructure, with its signals designed for reception by ground stations and specialized equipment rather than ordinary household satellite receivers.

The satellite was launched alongside the Russian meteorological satellite Elektro-L No. 5, using the Proton-M launch system and its DM-03 upper stage.

Why space matters - and why it matters most in a crisis

The case for why a nation should bear the enormous cost of developing an indigenous space program is, at its foundation, a case about strategic independence.

A country that cannot build or launch its own satellites remains dependent on foreign manufacturers, launch providers, and satellite operators for access to capabilities that can become critical national infrastructure. That dependence becomes particularly consequential when the country in question is the target of illegal and crippling sanctions and unprovoked wars.

Iran's space program, developed over more than two decades under extensive international sanctions and technology restrictions, is therefore significant not merely because of the individual satellites it has placed in orbit, but because of the technological ecosystem it represents. Iran has progressively developed domestic capabilities in satellite manufacturing, launch vehicles, remote sensing, communications, propulsion, guidance, and orbital operations, areas in which access to foreign technology has frequently been restricted.

The security dimension of this capability is equally important. A high-resolution Earth-observation satellite can provide persistent surveillance of military installations, transportation networks, infrastructure, and changes in force deployment without requiring physical access to the territory being observed. Khayyam's approximately one-meter-class imaging capability provides a level of situational awareness that is strategically valuable.

The same principle applies to communications and navigation. Modern military operations depend on resilient positioning, navigation, timing, and communications infrastructure. But it is important to distinguish between satellite imagery and satellite navigation.

Measured against that backdrop - a space program developed from a relatively modest starting point, under sustained international sanctions and deliberate restrictions on access to advanced technology - Iran's progression from Omid's modest 2009 debut to the Noor satellites, Khayyam's meter-class Earth observation, the Qaem-100's increasingly sophisticated launch technology, and Chamran-1's orbital maneuvering represents a significant trajectory in the development of an indigenous space capability.

title: Officials seize $2.8M in fuel destined for Cuba in 'sanctions-evasion scheme'
body:
Federal officials seized fuel shipments valued at $2.8 million that were suspected of being "unlawfully exported to Cuba," they said in a news release.

Officials said they intercepted 90 shipments of biodiesel-blended middle distillate bound for a "sanctioned Cuban entity" as part of a scheme to evade sanctions.

Agencies involved in the seizure include Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS).

Authorities are expected to discuss the seizure in a news conference at 9:30 a.m. at the Homeland Security Investigations Miami field office.

On Friday, the U.S. Coast Guard announced it had interdicted a vessel trafficking fuel to Cuba. Officials tell NBC6 the seizures are not related.

title: Railway Minister sanctions Amrit Bharat Express and two Haridwar services for Rajasthan
body:

Union Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has approved the operation of three new train services for Rajasthan following an initiative by Chief Minister Bhajan Lal Sharma. The move is set to strengthen regional connectivity across the state and provide passengers in several districts with enhanced transportation facilities.

The approved services include the Bhuj-Barauni Amrit Bharat Express, which will cover approximately 2,532 kilometres, linking Gujarat, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. In Rajasthan, this tri-weekly service will pass through Kota, Sawai Madhopur, Gangapur City and Bharatpur, creating vital connections across four states.

The other two sanctioned services, the Haridwar-Okha Express and Haridwar-Veraval Express, will operate through Rajasthan via Alwar, Jaipur, Ajmer and Abu Road. These routes will provide passengers from these cities with additional rail connectivity to Haridwar in Uttarakhand as well as Gujarat and other major parts of western India.

The Bhuj-Barauni Amrit Bharat Express is scheduled to depart from Bhuj at 5:30 PM and reach Barauni at approximately 4:05 AM on the fourth day, completing the journey in nearly 58 hours and 35 minutes. The approval is also significant for passengers from Kishangarh and surrounding areas who will benefit from improved long-distance connectivity options.

title: Safety in an era of geopolitical risk
body:
Geopolitical developments, particularly conflict zones, are significantly affecting aviation. At the World Safety and Operations Conference, an executive panel discussed how the industry and its people can adapt to rapidly changing conditions while maintaining safe airline operations.

Although each organization faces distinct challenges, it is also affected by industry-wide issues. The panel agreed that a key trend is the shift from managing local disruption to addressing systemic problems. Geopolitical risk is greater than ever and has become a permanent feature of aviation operations.

This affects airline personnel. Repeated crises give them extensive experience, but the resulting pressure and its effects on fatigue and morale must not be underestimated. Training can help, but people must apply what they learn to make the right decision at the right time. Organizational resilience is part of the safety management system, with people remaining central to decision making.

The right culture is essential, making strong safety leadership critical. Leaders must ensure their teams have both the ability and confidence to speak up. The panel identified trust within organizations and with industry partners as the key quality. A crisis rarely affects one organization alone but can involve airports, air navigation service providers, passengers, and many other stakeholders. Everyone must understand that safety comes first.

Technology and standard operating procedures are valuable tools, but their effective use ultimately depends on trust in the organization.

The discussion also addressed attracting young talent. As the workforce ages, the industry is losing experience, making it urgent to transfer knowledge before experienced employees leave.

Reliable information was another key topic. Airlines must decide whether it is safe to fly on limited or outdated data even as they seek to shift from a reactive to a proactive approach. One concern is that information sharing is declining in an increasingly fragmented, populist world, even though safety depends on shared data and real-time intelligence.

Insurance is a rarely discussed aspect of a dynamic operating environment. Every aircraft departure already represents substantial exposure for insurers. Even a low-probability event, such as an accident, can be catastrophic and drive up premiums. The panel noted that the rising risk profile is pushing prices even higher.

Insurers find it difficult to assess safety culture and resilience, though both are recognized as important. Airlines effectively sell their risk to insurers, so a better insurer understanding of that risk benefits airlines. Insurers use risk modifiers IOSA is an obvious example to adjust premiums accordingly.

The panel concluded that maintaining safety in a turbulent world requires flexibility without compromising safety as the top priority. The industry is learning every day. If there is an upside to its many challenges, it is that the industry is becoming more adaptable and resilient.

The Panel

Ahmet Olmutur, CEO & Member of the Executive Committee, Turkish Airlines

Rachel Barrie, Group Chief Executive, Global Aerospace

Marcus Schnabel, CEO, SunExpress Airlines

Florian Guillermet, Executive Director, EASA

Nick Careen, SVP, Operations, Safety and Security, IATA

Moderator: Katherine Kaczynska, IATA Corporate Communications

title: EU ambassadors wave through largest-ever list of Russia sanctions
body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium -- EU ambassadors unanimously approved nearly 1,600 sanctions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex on Oct. 7, paving the way for them to be formally adopted by EU foreign ministers on Oct. 12 in Luxembourg.

The list, previously seen and reported by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 21, targets a wide range of defense industry players, from shipyards and aviation companies to electronics manufacturers, armored vehicle repair facilities, and aerospace companies.

It is the largest single list of new sanctions put forward for EU consideration, with the total list of entities and individuals sanctioned as a result of Russia's war on Ukraine currently standing at roughly 3,000.

Once adopted, the EU intends to move towards a more agile approach of adopting smaller lists of sanctions on a rolling basis rather than bundling them into a single package.

In practice, that change has already taken effect, with separate decisions taken in recent weeks to sanction Russian citizens involved in barring the opposition Yabloko party from parliamentary elections, abducting Ukrainian children, and spreading propaganda in Europe.

Another list of sanctions against those who rigged Russia's September election, and against candidates who ran in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory, is also being prepared.

title: EU Backs Record Sanctions List of 1,646 Russian Targets
body:
EU ambassadors on Wednesday, Oct. 7, approved proposed sanctions against approximately 1,650 individuals and entities, primarily targeting Russia's military-industrial complex and those involved in elections held in occupied Ukrainian territories.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty Europe Editor Rikard Jozwiak said the ambassadors had given the "green light" to sanctions against 743 individuals and 826 entities connected to Russia's defense industry.

The ambassadors also approved listings against 77 people purportedly elected to Russia's State Duma from Ukrainian territories occupied by Moscow.

The measures are not yet legally final. They are expected to be submitted to EU foreign ministers for formal adoption on Monday, Oct. 12, Reuters reported.

Largest wave of listings since 2022

The package would represent the EU's largest single set of sanctions designations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

According to Reuters, approximately 1,570 of the proposed listings cover individuals and organizations involved in Russia's military-industrial complex. More than half are associated with missile production.

The sanctions are intended to restrict Russia's ability to manufacture weapons and obtain the equipment, financing, and technology needed to continue its war.

People added to the EU sanctions list generally face asset freezes and travel bans throughout the bloc. EU citizens and companies are also prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to listed individuals and organizations.

The EU already has sanctions in place against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities associated with Russia's invasion, occupation of Ukrainian territory, and efforts to circumvent international restrictions.

Sanctions target occupation elections

The proposed list also includes 77 people who were purportedly elected to the Russian State Duma from occupied regions of Ukraine.

Russia held State Duma voting on Sept. 18-20, including in Ukrainian territories under Moscow's control. Ukraine and the EU do not recognize the vote conducted in those regions as legitimate.

The European External Action Service had proposed sanctions against the 77 candidates before the election results were finalized.

Their inclusion would target individuals involved in extending Russia's political system into occupied Ukrainian territory and attempting to legitimize Moscow's control over the regions.

Chemical weapons sanctions extended

EU ambassadors also agreed to extend a separate sanctions framework targeting the use and proliferation of chemical weapons.

That regime currently applies to 31 individuals and six entities. It includes Russian officials, scientists, and institutions accused of involvement in prohibited chemical weapons programs.

In July, the EU added six Russian individuals allegedly connected to the poisoning and death of opposition leader Alexei Navalny. The bloc said the listings included researchers and officials associated with Russia's chemical weapons infrastructure.

The restrictions include asset freezes, bans on providing funds to listed parties, and travel prohibitions for sanctioned individuals.

The latest move follows the EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia, adopted in July after weeks of internal disagreements. That package targeted Russian banks, oil revenues, military suppliers, and companies helping Moscow evade existing restrictions.

title: US toughens sanctions against sanctions-busting payments operator | The Bell
body:
This week the US Treasury designated A7, a major payments system that helps Russia and Iran evade sanctions, a "transnational criminal organization". The tougher sanctions likely stem from the fact that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard uses the operator.

* А7 is the biggest organization helping Russian businesses evade international sanctions. It was created by state-owned Promsvyazbank, which specializes in financing and serving the Russian defense industry, and Moldovan businessman Ilan Shor, a professional money launderer and one of the architects of a scheme that siphoned $20 billion out of Russia in the 2010s. Promsvyazbank itself estimates that nearly 12% of Russia's foreign trade flowed through A7 in 2025.

* The Russian core of A7 has been under U.S. sanctions since Aug. 2025, yet payments are specifically routed through foreign firms. According to FinCEN, accounts are held at approximately 435 banks in 83 countries. Since the start of 2025, they have processed more than $17 billion in dollar-denominated payments. FinCEN will not publish a complete list, but it will share it with banks via a secure channel.

* FinCEN has also proposed banning US financial institutions from processing any transfers involving subagents of the network created by A7. This refers to shell companies in the UAE, Hong Kong, Turkey and other countries which A7 uses to transfer funds. Their role is to conceal payments linked to sanctioned sectors and individuals as ordinary commercial activity -- for example, the FT reported on a scheme that listed thermal imaging sights as "tempered glass" on invoices -- and pay foreign suppliers on behalf of Russian clients.

* At the same time, constant corporate regeneration is part of A7's DNA. The company has a team dedicated entirely to creating new shell companies when its existing ones are busted.

Why the world should care

The cat-and-mouse game between US financial authorities and Russian sanctions-busting experts will continue. It is impossible to categorically defeat professional money launderers.

title: Ukraine's Anti-Corruption Bureau takes $250,000 sanctions extortion case against MP Skorokhod to trial
body:
The case involving an offer of $250,000 to arrange for Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) to impose sanctions on a company involves a sitting member of parliament and her accomplices, with an indictment against them sent to court, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) said Wednesday.

According to the investigation, members of the group offered a representative of the company to arrange for the NSDC to adopt a sanctions decision for $250,000, and planned to transfer the funds received to council officials as payment for securing the decision. To conceal the agreement and guarantee payment, the company representative was offered to formalize the transfer of the money as a loan. After receiving the first part of the amount of $125,000, he was assured that the funds would be handed over to NSDC officials. In reality, however, the money remained with the group members because they failed to find anyone willing to carry out the promised illegal actions.

"In December 2025, NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), in cooperation with the Main Directorate of Internal Security of the Security Service of Ukraine, notified a sitting member of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine and her accomplices that they were suspected of committing a crime. In June 2026, the investigation in the case was completed. One of the members of the criminal group entered into a cooperation agreement with the prosecution. Under its terms, he provided incriminating testimony against the other accomplices," NABU said.

The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) sentenced him to five years in prison, releasing him from serving the sentence on probation. In addition, he transferred UAH 700,000 to support the Armed Forces of Ukraine through the UNITED24 fundraising platform.

As reported, in July the HACC approved a plea agreement concluded between a prosecutor from SAPO and a citizen who, along with others, was exposed for soliciting the provision of $250,000 in an unlawful benefit in exchange for resolving the issue of imposing NSDC sanctions.

The criminal group's activities were organized by a member of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, who became the "guarantor" of this agreement. The statement did not explicitly name the lawmaker. Based on the details of the case, it appears to be referring to Anna Skorokhod.

title: EU ambassadors agree on 22nd package of anti-Russian sanctions
body:
Ambassadors of the European Union (EU) member states have agreed on the 22nd package of anti-Russian sanctions, which envisages the blacklisting of more than 1,500 legal entities and individuals affiliated with the Russian defense sector.

These restrictive measures will apply to defense enterprises of a number of countries and their associated persons, which, according to Brussels, are engaged in the production of dual-purpose goods.

This package does not contain fundamentally new large-scale trade and economic restrictions, but it will be the largest in the last four years, simultaneously increasing the number of persons blacklisted, effectively one and a half times the total sanctions list; previously, there were a little more than 3,000 facilities on this blacklist.

title: Sanctions in February, handshakes in September: EU's flip-flop Iran policy is putting lives at risk
body:
Why would the European Union list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation in February, and then, seven months later, have its top diplomat sit down with the foreign minister of the government the Guard Corps defends?

At the UN General Assembly last month, EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas met Abbas Araghchi, who served in the Guard Corps during the Iran-Iraq war.

Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten met president Masoud Pezeshkian, who in 2019 joined fellow parliamentarians in wearing the Guard Corps uniform to protest Washington's terrorist designation of it. France, Italy, and Norway held meetings of their own.

These talks came less than nine months after Iranian security forces, on 8 and 9 January, killed protesters on a scale without precedent in the country's modern history.

The human rights group HRANA has verified more than 7,000 deaths, and the UN special rapporteur warned that the toll may exceed 20,000.

In September, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that the crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity. Nor has the killing stopped: Iran Human Rights counted at least 532 executions in the first eight months of this year, including protesters arrested in January.

After a massacre, a foreign policy guided by European values should pursue one aim above others: making a repetition more costly for those who would order and carry it out.

Naming and shaming raises the reputational cost of repression, targeted sanctions raise its material cost, and delegitimisation raises the political cost of staying loyal to the regime.

They work only in combination, since sanctions without delegitimization tell the regime's elite that their assets are at risk, but their standing is not.

EU vs US sanctions

Europe has used the first two instruments. The EU listed the Guard Corps in February and sanctioned additional Iranian officials for human rights abuses.

However, these measures target assets and individuals, while the government that presided over the killing keeps its seat at the top table.

The UNGA in New York showed how little the third instrument has been used.

The terrorist listing freezes the Guard Corps' funds. Neither Araghchi nor Pezeshkian is on an EU sanctions list.

Yet it leaves a question unanswered: how far should the logic of a terrorist designation extend to the government that funds and publicly defends it?

Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union requires the Union's external action to be guided by human rights and to be consistent.

Branding the Guard Corps a terrorist organisation in Brussels while posing for photographs with the government it defends in New York sits uneasily with that obligation.

This inconsistency is costly. In a study in foreign policy analysis, my co-authors and I examined how Iranians reacted to US sanctions. Comprehensive sanctions produced a rally around the government, even among reformists.

The 2019 designation of the Guard Corps, by contrast, produced almost no rally outside the regime's hardliner core. Thus, targeted pressure on the security apparatus does not drive Iranians into its arms.

Handshakes, on the other hand, may give the apparatus exactly what targeted sanctions are meant to withhold: international legitimacy.

The photographs from New York reach two audiences.

The first sits inside the state: an officer deciding whether to fire on a crowd, or to step aside, weighs one question above most others, namely whether the regime will survive, and each of those photographs suggests an answer.

The second audience is the families of those killed, executed, and blinded since January. For them, the message is that Europe has moved on after eight months.

A picture is worth a thousand words

I am not against diplomacy. Kallas raised the sharp rise in executions with Araghchi, and Jetten raised human rights and Iranian actions on Dutch soil with Pezeshkian. Channels on shipping, detained Europeans, and de-escalation should stay open.

My objection concerns the level and the format: a meeting between leaders, photographed at the General Assembly with no public conditions attached, is not a technical channel.

Concerns voiced in private do not travel as far as the photograph, which signals normal relations with a government that has done nothing to earn them.

Four steps would help.

First, the Council should agree on a common line: contact at the technical and envoy level, and leader-level meetings only on public conditions, beginning with a halt to protest-related executions.

Second, human rights sanctions should move up the chain of command, to those who answer politically for the security forces.

Third, member states should invest in accountability that does not depend on Tehran, such as universal jurisdiction cases and evidence-sharing with the UN mission.

Finally, Europe should engage openly with Iran's democratic opposition.

The EU has already decided, in law, what the Guard Corps is. Its leaders have yet to act accordingly. A massacre answered with sanctions in February and handshakes in September does not raise the cost of the next one. It lowers it.

title: Case involving "Servant of People" MP Skorokhod regarding attempted "sale" of NSDC sanctions has been sent to court, - NACB
body:
Member of Parliament Anna Skorokhod, along with other individuals implicated in the case -- who, for $250,000, offered to arrange for the National Security and Defense Council to impose sanctions against one of the companies -- will stand trial.

This was reported by the press service of NABU, according to Censor.NET.

Details

"According to the investigation, the money was to be given to officials of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine as payment for a decision on sanctions.

"To cover up the scheme and ensure payment, the company representative was told to write a receipt for a supposed loan," the statement reads.

After receiving $125,000, the "client" was assured that this portion would be transferred to officials at the National Security and Defense Council. In reality, however, the money remained with the perpetrators, as they were unable to find anyone willing to carry out the illegal actions.

In December 2025, the member of the Verkhovna Rada and her accomplices were notified of the charges against them, and in June 2026, the investigation was concluded.

At the same time, one of the members of the criminal group reached a plea bargain with investigators.

"In accordance with the terms of the agreement, he provided incriminating testimony against the other accomplices. The High Anti-Corruption Court sentenced him to 5 years in prison but suspended the sentence with a probationary period."

"In addition, the individual transferred 700,000 hryvnias to the United 24 fund in support of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," the NABU added.

The Case of People's Deputy Skorokhod

* Previously, the NABU used hidden camera footage to document the transfer of a portion of the funds to the member of parliament and her representative. The amount in question is $125,000.

* The footage later also shows a receipt, though it is not clear what it says. From the context, it is clear that this "document" specifies a specific amount and the transfer of a portion of the funds so that all participants in the "arrangements" can "sleep soundly."

* On December 5, the Security Service of Ukraine, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) uncovered a criminal group in Kyiv that was led by Ukrainian People's Deputy Anna Skorokhod.

* She is accused of forming a criminal group that offered a businessman $250,000 to arrange for the National Security and Defense Council to impose sanctions on a competitor's company.

* On December 7, Skorokhod's accomplice in this case was ordered to remain in custody, with the alternative of posting bail in the amount of 4,542,000 UAH.

* On December 8, the High Anti-Corruption Court imposed a preventive measure on an aide to People's Deputy Anna Skorokhod in the form of a 1.514 million hryvnia bond.

* The High Anti-Corruption Court of Ukraine imposed a pretrial measure on Member of Parliament Anna Skorokhod in the form of bail in the amount of 3 million 28 thousand hryvnias.

title: Australians Call for Sanctions on Israel
body:
IQNA - On the third anniversary of the start of the Israeli regime's genocidal war on Gaza, pro-Palestinian demonstrations and solidarity vigils were held in several Australian cities on Wednesday, with Muslim groups calling on the Australian government to impose sanctions on the Tel Aviv regime.

During the demonstrations, Palestinian flags were displayed across the grounds of the State Library of Victoria in Melbourne. A cutout depicting Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu holding a sign reading "War Criminal" was also displayed.

The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 on allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The court continues to list Netanyahu as being at large.

Australian media have reported that further pro-Palestinian rallies will be held across Australia on Sunday.

The Australian Muslim Alliance (AAM) and the Australian National Imams Council (ANIC) said in a statement that three years of Israeli attacks had brought "killing, destruction, displacement, starvation and immense suffering" to Palestinians.

The groups called on the Australian government to impose "meaningful sanctions" on Israel and establish "a comprehensive two-way arms embargo" against the regime. They also called on Australia to ensure that it does not contribute, "directly or indirectly," to violations of international law.

The two groups further called for unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza and support for the reconstruction of civilian infrastructure.

The demands come amid criticism of Australia's military ties with Israel. The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on cooperation in the defense industry in 2017, while annual strategic defense talks began in 2018.

Australia also participates in the global supply chain for F-35 fighter jets used by Israel, with more than 70 Australian companies having supplied components for the program. However, the Australian government claims that it does not directly provide weapons or ammunition to the regime.

The Muslim groups said Australia's recognition of the State of Palestine in September 2025 was an important step, but that it should be followed by concrete political and diplomatic action.

title: T Govt Sanctions Rs 1,108 Cr For Omkareshwara Temple
body:
The Telangana Government on Wednesday issued orders to release Rs 1,108.27 crore for the development of the Omkareshwara Swamy temple complex at Manchirevula, along with the construction of a six-lane road as part of the Musi Riverfront development project.

Hyderabad: The Telangana government on Wednesday has issued administrative sanctions worth Rs 1,108.27 crore for the development of the Omkareshwara Swamy temple complex at Manchirevula and the construction of a six-lane road as part of the Musi Riverfront Project development works. The orders were issued through G.O.Rt.No.928.

The government has allocated Rs 948.65 crore for the temple complex development at Manchirevula. Structures such as rajagopurams (temple gateway towers), a yagashala (sacrificial hall) and a pushkarini (temple tank) will be built in the complex. A further Rs 159.62 crore has been allocated for the six-lane road, which will be 30 metres (100 feet) wide and about 2.5 km long, running from Istana Villas to Kirti Westwind Villas. The road will connect to the Greyhounds and Young India Police School areas, and will also give the temple complex better connectivity to the Musi Riverfront road network.

In another key development, the State government has constituted a technical committee for the development of the Omkareshwara temple, which will provide technical guidance for the Rs 700 crore temple project, with key responsibilities covering designs, DPRs (detailed project reports), rates and tenders. The government has issued G.O.Rt.No.929 in this regard.

The R&B (Roads and Buildings) Engineer-in-Chief will chair the committee, with the Public Health Engineer-in-Chief as co-chairman and the MRDCL (Musi Riverfront Development Corporation Limited) Chief Engineer as convener. The members will be the Endowments Chief Engineer, temple architecture expert Dr. E. Sivanagireddy, and the Additional Secretary of the Finance Department.

title: Major Spanish property portal faces sanctions over rental adverts that may mislead tenants
body:
A complaint from consumer group CECU has put a major property website under investigation, and it's the portal itself, rather than the landlords posting on it, that could end up paying. It's a test of who's responsible when renters see adverts that don't give the full picture.

A major portal is now the one under investigation

Spain's consumer ministry has opened sanctions proceedings against a major property website over rental adverts that may have misled people looking for a home, with the portal itself, rather than the landlords posting on it, now in the firing line.

The ministry hasn't named the portal. Its General Directorate of Consumer Affairs launched the case after a complaint from consumer federation CECU, and it's examining possible unfair commercial practices against users. Reports so far don't say exactly how the portal is alleged to have broken the rules, and the ministry hasn't shared details of the adverts involved, so the picture could change as the case moves forward.

Consumo (the consumer affairs department) says it's the first time it has taken this step against a platform over its own conduct. If the case ends in a penalty, the fine could reach €100,000, or four to six times any illicit profit the portal made.

It follows other action by the department this year, including a May investigation into a large rental company accused of imposing payment insurance and disproportionate late fees on tenants.

Why this goes further than January's warnings

Back in January, the government warned that Spain's rules on rental adverts would be enforced, and portals were quick to argue that responsibility for what's in an advert lies with whoever places it.

That argument is now being tested. Until now, the spotlight has been on landlords and agents who list homes above the legal limit or leave out what they should disclose, whereas this case asks whether the platform carrying those adverts shares the blame.

The law behind that warning, the Customer Service Law, took effect on Saturday December 27 2025, and Pablo Bustinduy, the minister responsible for consumer affairs, said anyone trying to make money by dodging the law at the expense of citizens was 'going to pay for it'.

Now the ministry's approach is moving on from warnings and contact with the industry to formal proceedings that could end in a sanction.

What rental adverts are now meant to show

Adverts are meant to display the reference price index for the area (the official benchmark for what a rent should roughly be), plus the rent paid under the previous contract in the last five years. In zones where rents are capped, they should also show the legal limit and say whether the landlord is a large property owner. The requirement is meant to apply across Spain, not just in rent-capped areas, so it could change what renters see in listings from Alicante to Zaragoza, if the portals comply.

The idea is that renters can compare what they're being asked to pay against those figures and spot an unjustified increase before they sign.

What renters should do while the case plays out

How long the new advert rules stay in place will depend on the next housing decree's journey through parliament, where the government's housing measures have had a bumpy couple of weeks. Consumo hasn't said when the case against the portal will be resolved either, so renters shouldn't expect an overnight change in the listings they see.

For now, it's worth checking whether an advert shows the previous rent and the cap for the area, and if it doesn't, asking the landlord or agent directly before you hand over a deposit.

title: EU ambassadors approve new sanctions package against Russia: Report
body:
The EU ambassadors have approved a new sanctions package against Russia targeting its military-industrial complex and some elected members.

As reported by TASS, Russian news state agency, and cited by a European source, the EU envoys have given the green light to a 22nd round of sanctions targeting over 1,500 individuals and companies tied to Russia's defense industry.

"The ambassadors approved blacklisting over 1,500 companies and individuals," the source said.

The package also targets 743 individuals and 826 military-industrial organizations in Russia. The sanctions also concern 77 individuals "elected to the Russian State Duma from the occupied territories of Ukraine."

In a recent move, European Union ambassadors voted to extend sanctions targeting 31 individuals and 6 organizations in response to Russia's use of chemical weapons on the battlefield.

The package is expected to be approved by the EU Council and come into force by the end of this week. The EU's last combined package, its 21st, was adopted in July.

title: EU ambassadors have approved largest package of sanctions against Russia
body:
Ambassadors from EU member states agreed to add 743 individuals and 826 companies linked to the Russian military-industrial complex to the sanctions list.

Radio Liberty reports on this, according to Censor.NET.

What is known?

It is noted that this is the EU's longest sanctions list.

These are personal sanctions imposed under the regime established in response to actions that undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence of Ukraine.

The initial draft called for the inclusion of 744 individuals and 827 legal entities. In the version approved on October 7, the list was reduced by one individual and one legal entity.

The companies mentioned are included in the list of enterprises in the Russian military-industrial complex compiled by the Russian government and, on that basis, are eligible to receive government subsidies.

"Individuals were added to the sanctions list as the heads of these companies, who, according to the EU's assessment, are thereby supporting the Russian military-industrial complex."

Among the enterprises whose executives were involved in the project are companies in the military shipbuilding and submarine sectors, the rocket and space industry, aviation instrument and engine manufacturing, artillery production, the military automotive industry, radio electronics, navigation and semiconductor systems, as well as the chemical industry and organizations involved in ammunition production," the publication notes.

A separate, large group consists of companies associated with the Russian submarine fleet. The project included Mykhailo Budnichenko, head of Sevmash; Igor Vilnit, CEO of the Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Technology; Vladimir Dorofeev, head of Malakhit; as well as the heads of the Admiralty Shipyards, the Zvezdochka Ship Repair Center, and a number of other major enterprises in the Russian defense-industrial complex.

Also listed are executives from the United Rocket and Space Corporation, the Russian Corporation for Rocket and Space Instrumentation and Information Systems, the Kazan Engine-Building Production Association, the Motovilikha Plants, KamAZ subsidiaries, and a number of radio-electronic and chemical enterprises.

"The Chosen Ones"

EU ambassadors also agreed on sanctions against 77 individuals who were "elected" to the Russian State Duma from the occupied territories of Ukraine.

The EU plans to extend sanctions against 31 individuals and 6 organizations for the proliferation and use of chemical weapons.

What will the sanctions entail?

Once the formal procedure in the Council of the EU is completed and the relevant acts are published in the Official Journal of the European Union, the restrictions will include the freezing of assets in the EU and a ban on providing funds or economic resources to sanctioned individuals and companies.

Individuals are also prohibited from entering the European Union or transiting through its territory.

title: Trump official: 'anti-Semitic' European countries risk US sanctions for boycotting Israeli settlements
body:
European countries that impose boycotts on Israel are 'anti-Semitic' and risk retaliatory sanctions from the United States, a senior Trump administration official has declared.

Speaking in Washington DC, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon criticised countries including the UK, France and Norway over measures targeting goods produced in Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

Dhillon, who leads the Civil Rights division at the Department of Justice, said: 'What we call this in the United States is the BDS movement. It is anti-Semitism. And I think every country that is doing that is going to risk, while President Trump is in power, retaliatory or corresponding sanctions potentially.'

She added: 'I think the President has said words to that effect. In the United States, there was an attempt to start trying to do this at the corporate level as well, and it's quickly been shut down overwhelming opposition from well-meaning people in our country... But I do consider BDS, and I think most people in my government consider it to be a form of anti-Semitism, and we call it as such.'

'I think every country that is doing that is going to risk... retaliatory or corresponding sanctions'

Dhillon's comments mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration's on-the-record response to measures taken by the UK and other European countries against Israeli settlements. While the policy has been publicly attacked by the US Ambassador to Israel, when President Trump was asked about Ed Miliband's policy by reporters at the UN General Assembly last month, he did not respond. Instead, he left Andy Burnham to defend the decision.

Speaking to The Spectator and a small group of European reporters, Dhillon did not provide details of what retaliatory measures might involve.

The Assistant Attorney General also warned that the UK and Europe should adopt Trump-style 'hard tactics' to curb illegal migration, which she argued was contributing to anti-Semitic, anti-Christian and anti-western attacks.

Dhillon, who was confirmed by the US Senate in April last year, said: 'It has been politically unpopular in this country to close our borders and yet I think most Americans like the result of less chaos, disruption and fear in our community. Our President is absolutely correct to stop unchecked migration from our southern border particularly because people are pouring in from all over the world and we don't know who they are or where they're coming from.'

title: How a Small Business Got Entangled in U.S. Sanctions on Iranian Oil
body:
In early 2024, an aging tanker anchored off Malaysia's coast delivered more than half a million barrels of oil that were said to be from Oman, but were in fact from Iran.

The deception was meant to evade U.S. sanctions on Iranian oil, which have long been part of Washington's efforts to choke off revenue for Tehran's military and nuclear weapons program. The ship, the Palau-flagged Reneez, was not on the list of blacklisted entities that the U.S. government maintains online.

Shahul Hamid Ahmad, who owned a small Malaysian shipping agency, said he thought little of taking a job to coordinate repairs and an inspection of the ship. His firm, Tefcas Marine, was one of many companies that specialize in arranging port services for ships passing by Johor state.

But halfway through the repairs, the tanker was placed under sanctions for ties to Sa'id al-Jamal, a Houthi financier who previously had been sanctioned by the United States for leading a network that procured "tens of millions of dollars" by smuggling Iranian oil. In late 2024, Tefcas and two other Malaysian companies were hit with sanctions for having "materially assisted" Mr. al-Jamal.

The action was part of an expanding effort by Washington to crack down on foreign maritime service providers, which U.S. officials have said facilitate Iran's oil trade.

For Mr. Shahul, 62, the outcome felt staggeringly disproportionate. His company's bank closed his accounts and Microsoft locked his company email, which holds records he needs to file taxes.

Want to stay updated on what's happening in Iran and Malaysia? Sign up for Your Places: Global Update, and we'll send our latest coverage to your inbox.

Tefcas made around $2,500 from the 2024 engagement, according to invoices viewed by The New York Times. But at least nine other entities involved with the Reneez since it began shipping Iranian oil in 2023 went untouched, The Times has found. Among them was a major East Asian oil company that received the cargo.

"We always turned down sanctioned vessels," Mr. Shahul said. "I would not jeopardize my company for that money."

The waters around Malaysia have increasingly become the center of Iran's oil trade. It's where tankers transfer the crude to vessels that take them to the eventual customer, mainly Chinese refineries. In August, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sweeping new sanctions to target the shipping facilitators that enable the trade.

But Tefcas's case, experts said, illustrated the limits of such an approach.

"Sanctioning these small players is a warning shot, but I'm honestly not sure if that warning shot has been heard given this activity continues," said David Tannenbaum, a former official at the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control and the director of Blackstone Compliance Services, a consulting firm.

Since Tefcas was sanctioned, the trade of Iranian oil near Malaysia has only grown, contributing to almost 667 million barrels exported by Tehran in 2025, according to data from United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit.

In Malaysia and Singapore, the buyers of Iranian oil have continued to operate with impunity, said Jeffrey Soh, the director of Contemporary Logistics, a Malaysian maritime services firm.

Mr. Soh, whose company owned the floating storage unit into which the Reneez had deposited its Iranian cargo in 2024, said that both his company and the local port authority had failed to screen out the vessel. So did the apparent charterer of the oil, which was a major state-linked oil corporation in China, according to a contract viewed by The Times.

But all three of them avoided sanctions, Mr. Soh said, adding that his company had cut ties with that client, which he believed knew of the oil's Iranian origins. He spoke on the condition that the customer not be named, citing risks of legal retaliation.

"Some companies, it's an open secret that they trade Iranian barrels," he said. "The case with Tefcas was really an injustice."

U.S. sanctions, by design, do not necessarily point to the biggest or most culpable actors, said Erich C. Ferrari, the founder of Ferrari & Associates, a Washington-based law firm.

"The consequences of designating a large trading house or a counterparty in a politically sensitive jurisdiction are weighed at the interagency level," he said.

"OFAC designates to produce an effect," he added, referring to the Office of Foreign Assets Control. "And the effect it wanted here was to deter the service ecosystem around these transfers, which you can do with small agents at very little diplomatic cost."

While some companies deliberately flout sanctions, many others are likely unwittingly exposed. While Mr. Soh's firm has spent thousands of dollars to upgrade its screening capabilities, he said not every business has "the financial ability to do that."

Last year, Mr. Shahul asked OFAC to reconsider his case. He has not yet heard back. A Treasury spokeswoman declined to comment on his case.

Because Mr. Shahul has been accused of collaborating with a terrorist, his former clients refuse to settle unpaid invoices, but he still owes various creditors $240,000.

"I think I have under a year to solve this," he said.

But the Reneez has continued to ship Iranian oil, according to satellite data from TankerTrackers.com. It was spotted near Malaysia as recently as May, under a new name and flag.

title: Following massive attack, Sybiha called on partners to strengthen sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex and provide Ukraine with more air defense systems
body:
Following the Russian attack on the night of October 6, Foreign Minister Andriy Sibiga called on partners to tighten sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex. He also called for Ukraine to be provided with the necessary air defense systems and energy assistance ahead of winter.

This was reported by Censor.NET, citing the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Sibiga called on partners to impose additional restrictions on the Russian defense-industrial complex, particularly on companies that manufacture ballistic missiles and the "Rassvet" satellite system.

The foreign minister called the new Russian attack a "gift" from Vladimir Putin to himself for his birthday.

"But his biggest gift will be a cell in The Hague. We are preparing a Special Tribunal on the crime of aggression against Ukraine for its launch as early as next year," Sybiha said.

According to him, during the nighttime attack, Russia struck residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Kremenchuk, and Pryluky.

Sibiga also stated that Russia had lost 1.6 million military personnel -- killed or wounded -- without achieving the strategic objectives of its full-scale invasion.

"Putin is not winning this war and never will. He has lost 1.6 million military personnel -- killed or wounded -- without achieving any of the strategic objectives of his invasion," the minister emphasized.

Intense shelling on October 7, 2026

* As reported, the enemy attacked Ukraine with missiles.

* Russian forces struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles: two people were killed, and a warehouse and a garage cooperative were damaged.

* A strike on a residential area in the Poltava region has been reported: high-rise buildings have been damaged.

* In the Kirovohrad region, one person was killed as a result of a Russian strike.

* Russia struck a high-rise building in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast. There are fatalities and injuries.

* As a result of the hostilities and Russian shelling of energy infrastructure, some consumers in the Vinnytsia, Kharkiv, Kherson, Poltava, and Chernihiv regions are temporarily without power.

title: Video. Browder: Dropping oligarchs from sanctions sets 'bad precedent'
body:
Bill Browder, once Russia's largest foreign investor, said sanctions are the "worst thing" that can happen to Russian oligarchs, adding that they are "scheming and trying to come up with ways of getting off the sanctions list".

The EU recently renewed its sanctions against Russia while removing businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.

Browder believes the only way the war will end is if sanctions inflict "enough economic damage" on Russia that it can no longer "afford the war". Russian President Vladimir Putin "is ready to starve his whole country completely", Browder said, calling for "more sanctions" against Moscow until Putin can no longer "physically afford to carry on the war".

title: EU envoys to approve largest batch of Russia sanctions since 2022 - Reuters
body:
EU envoys are due to approve around 1,650 new designations under the EU's Russia sanctions regime on 7 October, most of them linked to Russia's military-industrial complex.

Source: European Pravda, citing Reuters

Details: EU diplomats told Reuters that the package, proposed by the European External Action Service (EEAS), will be the largest batch of individuals and entities added to the sanctions list since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Following approval by EU ambassadors, the package will be forwarded to EU foreign ministers on Monday 12 October for final adoption.

About 1,570 of the listings are entities and individuals linked to Russia's military-industrial complex, more than half of them involved in missile production.

The main EU regulation on sanctions against Russia currently contains just over 3,000 entities subject to EU travel bans, transaction restrictions and asset freezes.

The remaining new entities and individuals are also connected to Russia but fall under other legal frameworks, including several that are subject to EU restrictions on North Korea.

Background:

* On 16 September, the EEAS presented a proposal for a new sanctions package targeting Russia's military-industrial complex. The package covers 1,576 individuals and entities.

* On 22 September, the Council of the EU adopted a final decision to extend sanctions against individuals and entities responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for a further 36 months, but removed Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.

Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

title: Unification Minister Responds to Reports of Clash with Foreign Minister over N. Korea Sanctions
body:
Unification Minister Chung Dong-young has responded to reports that he clashed with Foreign Minister Cho Hyun over North Korea at a recent National Security Council(NSC) meeting, saying differences of opinion among government ministries are to be expected.

Chung made the remark Wednesday during the parliamentary audit of the unification ministry, when asked by People Power Party lawmaker Park Choong-kwon whether Chung opposed Cho's proposal to impose unilateral sanctions against North Korea for its cyber activities, put forward at the NSC meeting on Thursday last week.

Chung responded by asking what those sanctions had to do with responding to the recent land mine explosions.

Asked whether the blasts were an unfortunate accident or a North Korean provocation, Chung said the government was still verifying the circumstances and that he understood the United Nations Command had yet to determine North Korea's intentions.

The minister stressed that hostility and hatred between the two Koreas were the root cause of the incident and resolving them is the fundamental solution.

He also said it's too early to determine whether placing the land mines there constituted an intentional attack on South Korean troops.

Chung said the government is demanding an apology from North Korea, adding that the two Koreas have different views on the military demarcation line and that his ministry considers unilateral cyber sanctions inappropriate as a response to the land mine blasts.

title: South seeks UN sanctions exemption to send $6.75 million in medical equipment to North
body:
The United Nations Security Council sanctions committee approved the exemption on May 22, putting the government's tentative shipping deadline at Nov. 22.

The South Korean government sought a United Nations sanctions exemption to provide North Korea with medical equipment worth about $6.75 million and is working to send the shipment as early as next month.

The government requested an exemption from the UN Security Council sanctions committee on North Korea to send medical equipment to Kangdong County Hospital in Pyongyang through the Korea Foundation for International Healthcare (Kofih), according to documents submitted by the Ministry of Unification to People Power Party Rep. Kim Dai-sik, a member of the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee, on Wednesday.

Kofih is a public institution under the Ministry of Health and Welfare that provides health care assistance to developing countries, North Korea and overseas South Koreans.

The request submitted to the UN states that the equipment will ship within six months of the sanctions exemption approval.

The UN Security Council sanctions committee approved the exemption for the project on May 22, putting the government's tentative shipping deadline at Nov. 22.

According to the documents, the government plans to transport the medical equipment by sea.

The planned shipment consists of 1,431 pieces of medical equipment across 166 categories, worth a combined $6.75 million.

It will depart from Incheon Port, travel through Dandong, China, and enter North Korea through Nampo Port. Hyundai Asan, a South Korean inter-Korean economic cooperation company, has been tentatively selected as the carrier.

The government set the total transportation cost, including domestic shipping expenses, at $3,500.

Among them, 41 items -- including autoclaves, ambulances, ultralow-temperature freezers, urine analyzers and computed tomography, or CT, devices -- are subject to UN restrictions on transfers to North Korea and require separate authorization.

The government is also considering ways to ensure that the equipment is not diverted from its intended purpose of providing medical services, such as sending a six-member joint monitoring team to North Korea, consisting of three Kofih employees and three outside experts.

If North Korean authorities do not allow South Korean inspectors to enter the country, Seoul has proposed conducting on-site inspections using personnel from third countries such as China or Mongolia or carrying out remote inspections via video link.

The South Korean government said that the North has a considerable number of medical facilities but faces severe shortages of medical equipment and pharmaceuticals; the prolonged border closure during the Covid-19 pandemic reportedly exacerbated vulnerabilities in its health care system.

It also pointed to the location of Kangdong County Hospital on the outskirts of Pyongyang, where access to medical services is more limited than in central areas of the city.

The government believes that supplying the hospital with medical equipment could improve its diagnostic and treatment capabilities and expand access to medical care for vulnerable groups, including pregnant women, newborns, older adults and patients with serious or chronic illnesses.

However, the actual scale and timing of aid have yet to be finalized.

In its response to Rep. Kim, the Unification Ministry said that the current plan is tentative. The government will finalize the project's details only after consulting with North Korea and proceed after completing relevant procedures, including review by the Inter-Korean Exchange and Cooperation Promotion Council.

The government aims to finance the project through the health care cooperation budget under the livelihood cooperation support program of the inter-Korean cooperation fund.

The UN sanctions exemption is valid for nine months from the approval date. If the project is not carried out within that period, the government will review the plan and decide whether to seek an extension of the exemption.

The opposition criticized the timing of the proposed aid.

"At a time when our soldiers have been seriously injured by land mines believed to have been planted by North Korea, we have to ask whether it meets the public's expectations for the government to have already mapped out in detail the equipment that it will provide to North Korea and even how it will be shipped," Kim said, referring to the Sept. 21 land mine explosion in the demilitarized zone that left three South Korean soldiers injured.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff announced on Monday that a probe conducted with the UN Command had concluded that North Korean troops deliberately planted the antipersonnel mines that caused the blast.
