title: Carragher: Swift Man City sanctions need to last 'years and years'
body:
Jamie Carragher believes that sanctions need to be imposed on Man City this season and should have a long-lasting effect.

Last week an independent commission found them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

It was found that City had arranged 'sham' contracts that inflated their revenue by £854 million and decreased their actual expenditure by £66 million.

City have lodged their appeal against the decision, insisting that they are innocent and "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" will exonerate them.

Carragher argues that any potential punishment needs to happen this term, and "should go on for years and years", or else the Premier League season runs the risk of being a "sham".

Carragher: Swift Man City sanctions need to last 'years and years'

"Now that we know that they're guilty, yes, there's an appeal, but now that they've got a big guilty verdict initially, now I don't think anybody wants to wait," he told Sky Sports News at the Legends of Football Awards.

"It has to be done this season, because Man City need to be affected for next season.

"I know the word at the moment is sham; it'll almost make the Premier League of this season, the title to be won would be a sham, if Man City went on to win that league with what we know has gone on.

"So it has to be done this season, and I think the punishment, whatever it should be, I don't think it can be a one-off punishment for one season, because this has gone on for years and years, so I think the punishment should go on for years and years."

Carragher added: "I think it'll be really difficult for City this season now, in terms of going on to achieve anything.

"Of course, there might be sanctions as the season goes on, but I think every away ground that they go to now will be the best atmosphere in that stadium, maybe that season.

"Everyone's baying for blood, unfortunately, for Manchester City right now, or for their players and manager right now, so I think it's going to be very difficult for them to achieve anything."

title: Zelenskyy: High Command sets tasks on electronic warfare, sanctions, supply of long-range drones to AFU
body:
Following a meeting of the High Command, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the assignment of additional tasks for the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) and manufacturers in the field of electronic warfare, the preparation of new sanctions packages against Russia, and key objectives for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones for the coming year.

According to him, detailed reports were presented during the meeting on the capabilities of electronic warfare systems and their use in protecting infrastructure. Zelenskyy said this component of defense accounts for a significant portion of the neutralization of Russian "suicide drones."

"Defense Intelligence of Ukraine also reported on Russia's technological priorities for this year and next, and on the supplies of critical components and equipment that Russia receives for weapons production to meet them," according to a post shared by the president on Facebook.

According to him, based on the findings of the Main Intelligence Agency's report, new sanctions packages will be prepared, and the intelligence agency will submit relevant proposals to the Cabinet of Ministers and the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC).

"We are also working to synchronize our sanctions accross partners' jurisdictions," Zelenskyy said.

In addition, during the meeting, the High Command identified the main tasks for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones for the coming year. The president emphasized that the main criterion in this regard must be Ukraine's ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.

"The key criterion is that we must be able to respond to Russian strikes in kind," Zelenskyy said.

title: IU expands Greek life sanctions as Phi Kappa Psi joins list of fraternities on cease-and-desist
body:
BLOOMINGTON, Ind. -- Indiana University has expanded its disciplinary actions against Greek organizations, with Phi Kappa Psi becoming the latest fraternity placed on cease-and-desist status as of Oct. 6, 2026.

The addition of Phi Kappa Psi brings the number of fraternities under immediate suspension to three in the last month, joining Kappa Sigma and Alpha Epsilon Pi. According to the university's Office of Student Life, the most recent orders follow allegations of hazing and alcohol violations.

Under a cease-and-desist order, all organizational activities -- including social events, recruitment, and chapter meetings -- must stop immediately while university officials conduct a formal investigation.

The latest investigations

The university's "Status of Organizations" dashboard reflects a tightening of oversight on the Bloomington campus:

* Phi Kappa Psi (Indiana Beta chapter): Placed on cease-and-desist for accusations involving hazing and alcohol.

* Kappa Sigma (Nu Beta chapter): Remains on cease-and-desist following September accusations of hazing.

* Alpha Epsilon Pi (Beta Iota chapter): Remains on cease-and-desist following September accusations of hazing.

While specific details of the incidents have not been released, university officials confirmed that the investigations are being handled with "the highest level of urgency."

Broader crackdown on campus

The disciplinary actions extend beyond these three houses. Sigma Alpha Epsilon also recently faced a cease-and-desist order for hazing, while several other organizations remain on long-term probation or suspension:

* Alpha Phi Alpha: On suspension through fall 2026 for hazing and other code of conduct violations.

* Kappa Alpha Psi: On deferred suspension through May 2025.

* Delta Upsilon: Currently under investigation for reported non-compliance with university health and safety policies.

* Sigma Phi Epsilon and Theta Chi: Both remain on disciplinary probation through the end of the academic year.

University and student response

In a statement, Indiana University emphasized its commitment to student safety and a zero-tolerance policy for hazing.

"The safety of our students is our top priority," a university spokesperson said. "We expect all student organizations to uphold the values of Indiana University. When those standards are not met, we will take necessary action to ensure a safe environment."

Students and parents are encouraged to monitor the IU Bloomington Status of Organizations page for real-time updates as these investigations continue.

title: Social Affairs Ministry sanctions 620 employees over online gambling
body:
Jakarta (ANTARA) - The Ministry of Social Affairs has imposed severe disciplinary sanctions on 620 employees within the ministry found to be involved in online gambling.

Minister of Social Affairs Saifullah Yusuf on Tuesday said the sanctions were the result of an in-depth analysis and clarification by the Ministry's Inspectorate General of data on more than 1,900 employees previously received from the Financial Transaction Reports and Analysis Center (PPATK).

The PPATK analysis previously reported that 1,900 employees within the ministry, both central and regional, were suspected of being involved in online gambling transactions, with an average value of Rp4 million (US$217) and a maximum value exceeding Rp2 billion (US$108 thousand).

"Based on the in-depth investigation, 620 employees, or 32.63 percent, are suspected of committing serious disciplinary violations," Yusuf remarked.

He explained that severe sanctions for Government Employees with Employment Agreements (PPPK) include involuntary termination of employment (PHK).

For civil servants, this includes demotion to a lower rank, dismissal from their position to an acting position for 12 months, and involuntary honorable dismissal.

While he did not elaborate, the minister confirmed that his office had issued Ministerial Decree (SK) Number 11/MS/KP.06.08/9/2026 concerning the Imposition of Severe Disciplinary Sanctions on Civil Servants, including dismissal from their position to an acting position for 12 months.

In addition, the ministry also recorded 719 employees (37.84 percent) committing minor disciplinary violations and 561 employees (29.53 percent) committing moderate disciplinary violations.

The level of sanctions imposed is adjusted according to the Minister of Social Affairs Regulation Number 5 of 2023 based on parameters such as transaction intensity, the amount of money used, and the duration of the activity, whether during or after work hours.

"We will continue to strengthen our oversight and will not hesitate to take firm yet measured action if any employees are found to violate their oath of office and code of ethics," Yusuf remarked.

title: Democrats cry foul as U.S. lifts sanctions on Serb nationalist, MAGA-linked firm gets huge Bosnia energy contract
body:
Joanne Stocker is a verification producer for CBS News Confirmed. She was previously chief editor of Kurdistan 24 English and managing editor at The Defense Post. She has combined open-source investigation methods with on-the-ground reporting to cover conflict, terrorism, and misinformation for over 15 years.

London -- The involvement of a small American firm linked to associates of President Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about how the White House could be using its leverage in the fragile Balkan state.

U.S. lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions on Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump was hailed by Dodik after his Serb nationalist party won one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's three presidency seats, which are split between Bosnia's Muslim, Serb and Croat ethnic groups under the country's complex power-sharing electoral system.

"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory ... we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told supporters in a speech, in which he also thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for his support.

Company with links to Trump poised to build gas pipeline

AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by President Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally General Michael Flynn, is close to securing a contract to develop the Southern Interconnection Gas Pipeline.

The pipeline project has been discussed by Bosnian officials for years, but long opposed by Dodik, who has close ties with the Kremlin. But Dodik, whose party has veto power in Bosnia's parliament, said he would not stand in the way of the proposal following the announcement of AAFS' involvement last April. Six months earlier, the Trump administration lifted sanctions against Dodik that were imposed by the U.S. Treasury almost a decade ago.

The pipeline would connect Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia's gas network, allowing Bosnia to import liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its neighbors. The project, which is valued at around $1.7 billion according to the Croatian government, would help make Bosnia and Herzegovina less reliant on Russian gas imports.

On its website, AAFS describes itself as a company focused on "energy security, project structuring, capital alignment, and long-term regional infrastructure development."

The company does not appear to have demonstrable experience in any similar energy projects.

The secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Bosnia's self-governing, Serb-run territory called Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S. brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s.

The sanctions, which included asset freezes and visa bans, were imposed by the Obama administration in 2017. The Biden administration then imposed further sanctions in 2022, accusing Dodik of corruption, including the charge that he had handed government contracts to close business associates in Republika Srpska.

A congressional report published last month by House Democrats, titled "Pay for Play in the Balkans," alleges that those two decisions -- the removal of sanctions on Dodik and his decision to not oppose the pipeline -- are directly linked.

"The Trump administration has used its diplomatic influence and connections with shady characters like Michael Flynn ... to facilitate the concession contract for the SIC [Southern Interconnection Gas pipeline] to AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC, a company owned and operated by Michael Flynn's brother Joseph Flynn and Trump-affiliated lawyer and political activist Jesse Binnall," the report alleges.

AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC did not respond to a CBS News request for comment.

Foreign agent registration filings (FARA) cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, President Trump's former national security adviser, last worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.

Those same filings show that Flynn was paid $100,000 for that work by RRB Strategies, a lobbying firm run by Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor who was convicted in 2011 of 18 counts of corruption and spent nearly eight years in a federal prison before being pardoned by President Trump last year.

Flynn provided strategic advice and counsel, analysis and information research, and introductions to the Republika Srpska government, according to the FARA filings.

Blagoyevich's firm originally signed a contract to "provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska" in March 2025, separate FARA filings reviewed by CBS News show.

CBS News sought comment from email aliases associated with Flynn and Blagojevich, but did not receive any response by the time of publication.

On Nov. 13, 2025, the U.S. Embassy in Sarajevo said in a social media post that Chargé d'Affaires John Ginkel had met Bosnian Prime Minister Nermin Niksic to discuss the gas pipeline project and "to support the importation of U.S. gas through Croatia to consumers in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

One week later, the embassy announced a preliminary agreement for an "American company to develop, build, and manage the pipeline."

Four days after that, on Nov. 24, AAFS Infrastructure & Energy was incorporated in the state of Wyoming.

In January, the U.S Embassy in Sarajevo posted again confirming that a meeting had taken place between AAFS leadership, including Joseph Flynn and Binnall, and top Bosnian officials.

AAFS was then granted the status of lead investor and operator on the proposed natural gas pipeline in legislation passed by Bosnia's parliament in April.

Later that month, the Croatian and Bosnian governments signed a contract to construct the pipeline with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright in attendance for the signing ceremony. At a news conference with Bosnia's energy minister on April 2, Binnall hailed the pipeline project as a "priority" for the Trump administration.

The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.

"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.

A State Department letter published as part of the House Democrat-authored congressional report said the decision to delist Dodik had helped ensure peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The official who wrote the letter, Paul Guaglianone, said lifting sanctions against Dodik had led to Bosnian Serb separatists rolling back policies that would have destabilized Bosnia's government.

The lifting of sanctions "advanced U.S. interests in [Bosnia and Herzegovina] and the Western Balkans. On October 18, the Republika Srpska National Assembly (RSNA) withdrew most of the anti-Dayton legislation it had passed in recent years," the letter read. That legislation had included laws that would have blocked Bosnia's national police and judiciary from having any authority in Republika Srpska.

Political scientist and Balkans foreign policy expert Jasmin Mujanović told CBS News the legislation in question had already been struck down prior to the lifting of the sanctions against Dodik, and he was skeptical of the Trump administration's justifications for the move.

"This package of omnibus secessionist laws that the Serb nationalist authorities and the RS [Republika Srpska] entity in Bosnia had unlawfully voted through in the local assembly had already been struck down by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia Herzegovina," he said.

"If the argument is that the Trump administration nevertheless managed to get Dodik and his people to withdraw the laws, it's still unclear what the significance of that is, or for that matter, why, given that the laws are moot," he said, adding that it that would "result in sanctions relief for an entire regime."

title: European Commission proposes majority voting in EU on sanctions, opening of negotiation clusters
body:
The European Commission has proposed shifting from unanimous voting to qualified majority voting by European Union member states on issues such as sanctions, the opening of negotiation chapters, and interim decisions on enlargement.

These proposals are outlined in the so-called package of documents on the European Union's preparations for future enlargement, specifically in the sections dedicated to improving the governance system for an enlarged Union, the European Commission said on Tuesday.

In particular, the press release notes that, given the current geopolitical conditions, the EU must adapt its governance system to make the decision-making process "swifter and more effective."

"To this end, the Commission will continue to advocate the use of passerelle clauses to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting in key areas such as sanctions, tax fraud and fiscal measures in energy policy," the statement reads.

In addition, the Commission will review existing proposals to determine where enhanced cooperation could help overcome prolonged deadlocks.

In the area of enlargement, the Commission proposes using qualified majority voting to open negotiation chapters and adopt other interim decisions during accession negotiations, which will make the process more dynamic. The Commission also proposes to work with the European Parliament and the Council to explore ways to apply the procedures set out in Article 7 more effectively, particularly with regard to possible timeframes.

The European Commission noted that the annual reports on enlargement and the state of the rule of law will continue to serve as key monitoring tools, with their scope expanded to include other candidate countries as they become ready.

Commenting on the gradual integration of candidate countries into the EU, the Commission is convinced that closer integration should bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses in both the EU and the candidate countries.

title: Man City FFP: Chris Waddle reveals two 'severe' sanctions City should be given after guilty verdict - 'just void it'
body:
Former England international Chris Waddle has revealed how he thinks Manchester City should be punished after the guilty FFP verdict.

Man City face serious sanctions after they were found guilty of breaching Premier League rules between 2009 and 2018.

An independent comission found Man City guilty on 114 of their 115 charges, and their potential sanctions include a fine, transfer ban, points deduction, expulsion and/or being stripped of their Premier League titles.

Enzo Maresca's side have submitted an appeal in an attempt to overturn the initial verdict, but it has been widely reported that they are likely to be unsuccessful.

And given the severity of this case, Man City could be given huge sanctions, and Waddle has explained why they should be relegated from the Premier League.

"I've seen it in France, I've seen it in Italy. We've seen it in other countries where teams have been punished and relegated. Marseille got relegated, so did Juventus," Waddle told talkSPORT Bet.

READ: Top 10 things that make us giddy about Premier League return and Man City's tour of shame

"I feel for the fans, I feel for the players. But let's be perfectly honest, if what they've done is proven, it's cheating. We don't want to see that in the game. We just don't want to see it.

"It's alright having money and competing with everybody else, you might have more money than other clubs and compete on that basis. But to take it to another level, and then another level again is cheating.

"If this is all proven, as it looks like it is going to be, then they've got to be hit severely. It's the owners who should take the punishment, and if it means the club going down, then fans need to blame the owners."

"They should just void it..."

Waddle also thinks that Man City should have their Premier League titles "voided", though he does not think that the titles should be redistributed.

"The fans, for me, and the players have done nothing wrong, but this is a chance now for the Premier League to make a statement to say, 'We are not going to tolerate this'," Waddle continued.

"Now, if it's a soft punishment, other clubs will think, 'You know what? They didn't even get punished properly, why don't we do it?'

"So an example has got to be made. As I say, the fans have done nothing wrong, but you have got to punish people who are not obeying the rules."

He added: "It wasn't down to the players, but you could say they bought these quality players because they were cheating. I understand that.

"But realistically, they should just void it and say there was no winner that year, I don't think the teams that finished in second should get the medals."

title: Israel saved British lives. London rewarded them with sanctions
body:
The Pentagon flew all 12 of its B-1B bombers out of RAF Fairford over the weekend and sent them home. Those are the aircraft that flew America's strikes on Iran, and they left a week after British police arrested five men near the base on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, says there are "strong indications" Tehran was behind it.

Israeli security and intelligence services saw it coming. A senior Israeli official told the Telegraph that Israeli intelligence warned MI5 of an imminent Iranian attack on Fairford, and Benjamin Netanyahu says that without the warning, "It would probably have gone through."

title: Mexico halts fuel shipments to Cuba due to threat of US sanctions -- newspaper
body:
In the first half of the year, the shipments averaged just 900 barrels per day

MEXICO CITY, October 6. /TASS/. Mexico's state-owned oil and gas company Pemex completely halted fuel shipments to Cuba in the third quarter of this year, following a sharp decline in exports during the first half of the year amid the threat of US sanctions, newspaper El Universal reported.

According to a report filed by Pemex with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the company's subsidiary, Servicios Logisticos y Recursos Estrategicos, made no shipments to Cuba during the third quarter. This followed a sharp reduction in exports in the first half of the year, when shipments averaged just 900 barrels per day.

The figures mark a stark contrast with previous years. Cuba received 19,200 barrels per day from Mexico during the first half of 2024 and 19,600 barrels per day during the same period in 2025. In the first half of 2026, however, the figure fell to just 900 barrels per day.

According to El Universal, the decline reflects efforts to avoid US sanctions targeting countries and companies that supply crude oil to Havana.

title: Russian gold floods Hong Kong as sanctions shift bullion trade to Asia: report (GLD:NYSEARCA) | Seeking Alpha
body:
Russian gold is reportedly pouring into Hong Kong at a record pace, highlighting how Western sanctions have rerouted bullion bound for London toward China and other Asian markets.

Hong Kong imported 112.7 tonnes of Russian-origin gold in the first seven

Western sanctions have rerouted Russian gold exports from markets such as London to Hong Kong and other Asian destinations, as Western nations suspended Russian refiners from trading.

Hong Kong offers advantages such as access to Mainland China and circumvents Western sanctions, becoming an important conduit for Russian gold trade.

Russian-origin gold now accounts for almost 15% of Hong Kong's non-monetary gold imports, sharply increasing from 0.6% in 2021.

title: US Increases Pressure on Iran With Sanctions Warning to Foreign Financial Institutions
body:
The U.S. Treasury Department said Iran relies on shadow banking networks to move money through the global financial system.

The United States has warned foreign financial institutions that they could face sanctions if they continue doing business with Iran, as Washington steps up its campaign to cut the country off from the U.S. financial system.

The U.S. Treasury Department said in an Oct. 5 alert that such entities "could be targeted at any time without advance notification" and urged them to end those relationships immediately.

A central theme of Monday's alert is what the Treasury describes as Iran's use of shadow banking networks. According to the department, Iran relies on trusted intermediaries, front companies, and shell companies to disguise financial transactions linked to oil sales and other commodities.

This allows money to move through the international financial system while obscuring its connection to Iran.

The Treasury urged financial institutions to strengthen measures to identify and disrupt such activity. It pointed banks to previous guidance issued by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, including alerts on sanctions evasion, front companies, digital assets, and illicit oil smuggling.

In August, the Treasury proposed revoking Banque Misr UAE's access to U.S. financial institutions. Last month, the United States sanctioned a Turkey-based bank and two of its subsidiaries, and designated one of Russia's largest banks, VTB Bank.

The U.S. government imposed additional sanctions on Tehran on Oct. 1 targeting Iran's automotive and rail industries. The Treasury said the measures built on earlier sanctions targeting individuals and companies involved in Iran's shipping, aviation, technology, gold, and digital asset sectors.

According to the Treasury, Iran has become increasingly dependent on industries such as automotive manufacturing and rail transport after a U.S. military blockade prevented it from exporting oil.

Iranian officials have repeatedly dismissed the sanctions campaign, arguing it will not change Tehran's position.

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi has also criticized Washington's approach.

In a Sept. 8 post on X, he said the United States had imposed sanctions on Iran for nearly five decades before going to war with the country on Israel's behalf. He said Washington had failed to achieve its objectives through sanctions or war.

U.S. Central Command said on Oct. 5 that U.S. forces had redirected 130 ships to ensure compliance with the ongoing U.S. naval blockade against Iran.

title: Iranian students prohibited from taking LSAT in new sanctions by Trump administration
body:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury's latest sanctions on Iran suspended a regulation that, for years, has authorised professional certification and university entrance exams for Iranian nationals.

The Law School Admission Council emailed many Iranian-American students on Sept. 9, saying it was prohibited from providing all services, including the Law School Admission Test to Iranian citizens or residents.

LSAC's prohibition poses a risk to many aspiring Iranian lawyers because all children born to an Iranian father, regardless of the birthplace, automatically receive Iranian citizenship by descent.

"I don't understand why the government is discouraging Iranian-Americans from pursuing law, when we've lived here our whole lives," said a recent Iranian alumnus who requested to remain anonymous. "The administration can't just ban a whole race or ethnicity from taking the LSAT."

This alumnus was not affected by the suspension; they did not identify themself as Iranian when their application on LSAC asked for their ethnicity. They claim that many of their friends who identified themselves as Iranian did have their accounts flagged.

Iranian-American students can work with LSAC to reverse the suspension of their accounts by providing proof of American citizenship, but students without American citizenship may not be able to do so.

Other Iranian students expressed concerns that their career plans could be delayed due to these suspensions.

"I want to apply to a Juris Doctor or Medical Doctor program, but to apply for these programs I need to meet their admission requirements, which includes taking the LSAT," said pre-nursing junior Donya Oufi.

The Trump administration said in a press release that the sanctions against Iran are intended to end what it refers to as the Iranian threat.

But even non-Iranian students worry that these sanctions will set a dangerous precedent that allows the government to control the rights of certain communities.

"I believe that sanctions being used by the government to deny Iranians their right to take the LSAT is a blatant act of racism by the Trump administration and goes against the Constitution," said political science freshman Sanjeev Ganesh. "In no way am I implying that Iranians will be placed in internment camps, but historically, our government has alienated communities based on their country of origin, like Japanese Americans during World War II."

Some political science professors share Ganesh's sentiment, and even say that prohibiting certain citizens from educational services is in violation of the Constitution.

"Assuming that this report is accurate, this is not lawful," said John B. Neibel Professor of Law David Crump. "It might be lawful if it were a law about immigration but not against Iranian-Americans, who presumably are citizens. This would violate the 14th Amendment of the Constitution and the Civil Rights Act of 1968."

Iranian-American lobbies like The National Iranian American Council have challenged LSAC's decision to comply with the U.S's sanctions. The organization said that they wrote a letter to LSAC urging them to not overcomply with the sanctions to restrict the rights of Iranian citizens.

Though it is common for Iranian students to come to the States for educational opportunities, these sanctions will now be halting the career plans of both people of Iranian ethnicity and Iranian citizenship, the alumnus said.

"I have some cousins and relatives in Iran who are extremely smart and would probably have better opportunities by coming to America," the alumnus said. "But unfortunately, these people are unable to do so because something as simple as education is being taken away from them. Even I, who have lived here my whole life, am in fear of whether or not I could pursue my dreams and education after this."

title: Burkina Faso leader Traore risks FIFA sanctions over football intervention - Blueprint Newspapers Limited
body:
Burkina Faso's President, Ibrahim Traoré, has announced plans for his government to intervene directly in the administration of football in the country, despite the possibility of sanctions from FIFA.

Traoré said the government had reached a point where it could no longer remain on the sidelines of football affairs, arguing that the development and proper organisation of the sport had become a priority for his administration.

Traoré insists government must act

The Burkinabe leader said the government was prepared to intervene even if doing so resulted in the country being suspended from international football.

"We have no choice; we have to step in, regardless of whether we get suspended or not," Traoré said.

He explained that the planned intervention would be aimed at improving the organisation of football and creating a stronger environment for players and other stakeholders.

According to him, the government wants to inject fresh energy into the sport by improving infrastructure, supporting players and creating better conditions for football to develop across the country.

"We are going to inject new energy so that people feel more at ease and can give their best," he added.

Move could trigger FIFA sanctions

The proposed government intervention could, however, create a major dispute with FIFA, whose regulations generally protect the independence of national football associations from government interference.

FIFA statutes require member associations to manage their affairs independently and without undue influence from government or other external bodies.

A direct government takeover or significant interference in the administration of the Burkina Faso Football Federation could therefore expose the country to disciplinary measures.

Such measures could include suspension from international football, potentially affecting Burkina Faso's participation in FIFA and other international competitions.

Traoré prioritises football reforms

Despite the potential consequences, Traoré appears prepared to accept the risk as his administration seeks to implement reforms in Burkina Faso's football structure.

The president's position reflects his government's emphasis on strengthening the organisation of the sport and improving conditions for players and other stakeholders.

For football, the proposed changes are expected to focus on administration, infrastructure and support for players, with the ultimate aim of creating an environment where those involved in the sport can perform at their best.

However, how the intervention will be implemented and whether it will lead to a formal response from FIFA remains to be seen.

title: Enforced Disappearances In Pakistan's Balochistan Up 308% Since 2020; ACHR Urges US Sanctions
body:
NEW DELHI: Alleged enforced disappearances in Pakistan's Balochistan province have more than tripled in five years, with 793 cases recorded in the first seven months of 2026 alone, a New Delhi-based rights group said on Monday, as it urged the United States to impose sanctions on those responsible.

The Asian Centre for Human Rights (ACHR), in a report titled "Pakistan's Enforced Disappearances: A Crime Against Humanity Demanding Urgent Global Action", said alleged cases in Balochistan rose by over 308%, from 480 in 2020 to 1,482 in 2025. The 793 cases between January and July this year work out to more than 113 a month, or roughly four a day.

The group has called on Washington to invoke the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act of 2016 against Pakistani officials and security personnel it holds responsible.

According to ACHR's analysis of the 793 cases, the Frontier Corps was responsible for 358, followed by intelligence agencies with 262 and the Counter Terrorism Department with 142. State-sponsored death squads were blamed for 27 cases and the Pakistani Rangers for four.

ACHR pointed to Pakistan's Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances (COIED), set up in March 2011, which it said received 10,973 cases between March 2011 and July 2026, mainly from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, Sindh and Punjab.

In June 2026, the UN Committee against Torture noted that the COIED had "disposed of" more than 9,000 of over 10,000 cases registered between 2010 and August 2025, yet not a single official had been ordered to be prosecuted.

"Such impunity has emboldened the security forces," said Tejang Chakma, ACHR's Research Director.

The report said the Pakistan government has increasingly sought to change the narrative on the issue. On 22 January 2026, Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti declared that the state should no longer be held responsible for cases of "self-imposed disappearance", referring to individuals allegedly choosing to associate voluntarily with militant or separatist organisations.

ACHR also highlighted action against activists. On 22 June 2026, Dr Mahrang Baloch, 33, a prominent voice demanding answers on disappearances in Balochistan, was sentenced to life imprisonment by an anti-terrorism court, along with fellow activist Sibghatullah Shah. They were convicted of terrorism, sedition and murder in connection with the death of a paramilitary soldier during a 2024 protest in Gwadar. Rights advocates have described the charges as politically motivated.

Earlier, on 6 October 2024, Pakistan banned the Pashtun Tahaffuz Movement (PTM) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Amnesty International has described the PTM as a grassroots movement peacefully advocating for the rights of Pashtuns, who it says have long faced harassment and violence from the authorities.

ACHR said the ban and the jailing of Baloch rights defenders have created a climate of fear, making victims' families, journalists and human rights defenders increasingly reluctant to report or document disappearances.

The group cited the US Treasury's 10 December 2021 sanctions under the Global Magnitsky framework on Bangladesh's Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) and seven of its current and former senior officials over serious abuses, including enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.

"The situation of enforced disappearances in Pakistan is equally grave and is worsening by the day," Chakma said, adding that there was a "systematic effort to dilute the narrative, discredit victims and silence those demanding accountability". He noted that enforced disappearance constitutes a crime against humanity under Article 7(1)(i) of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court.

"The continued failure of Pakistan's domestic institutions to prosecute those responsible makes international accountability imperative," Chakma said, urging the US to work with the United Nations (UN) to end the cycle of impunity.

ACHR warned that without immediate international action, mass disappearances, institutional impunity and the suppression of those seeking accountability risk normalising enforced disappearance as an instrument of state repression in Pakistan.

title: US threatens sanctions against banks doing business with Iran - Diaspora Digital Media (DDM News) - Nigeria Breaking News, Africa and World News and Updates
body:
The United States has warned foreign financial institutions that doing business with Iran or its sanctioned banking sector could expose them to penalties from Washington.

The US Treasury Department issued the warning on Monday, urging foreign banks to immediately stop transactions with Iranian financial institutions already under US sanctions.

The Treasury said banks that continue such transactions could be sanctioned without prior notice.

"Foreign financial institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification," the department said.

Washington has intensified its efforts to isolate Iran economically, warning foreign institutions that dealings with the Iranian government could attract secondary sanctions.

The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on Iran's financial, cryptocurrency, rail, automotive and manufacturing sectors.

Two banks, one based in the United Arab Emirates and another in Turkey, have also been sanctioned over their alleged support for Iranian authorities.

According to the Treasury, Iran operates "shadow banking" networks to bypass US sanctions.

The department urged foreign financial institutions to strengthen measures to identify and avoid transactions linked to such networks.

title: Moscow's response to Japan's sanctions to hurt Tokyo's interests -- Russian embassy
body:
The embassy also pointed to a contradiction between "bombastic proclamations about readiness to contribute to a peaceful settlement" voiced by Tokyo and its plans "to promote further defense cooperation with Kiev"

TOKYO, October 6. /TASS/. Moscow will continue to respond to Japan's sanctions by taking systemic countermeasures aimed at hurting Tokyo's interests in areas it finds sensitive, the Russian Embassy in Japan said in a statement.

"We will respond to such steps with systemic countermeasures aimed at hurting Tokyo's interests in areas it finds sensitive," the statement reads. The embassy also pointed to a contradiction between "bombastic proclamations about readiness to contribute to a peaceful settlement" voiced by Tokyo and its plans "to promote further defense cooperation with Kiev." The embassy also warned that full responsibility for "the inevitable negative consequences" would lie with Japan.

Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said earlier, commenting on the new Japanese sanctions, that they proved Tokyo's foreign policy lacked independence.

On October 2, Japan expanded its Russia-related sanctions lists by adding 33 companies and nine individuals from Russia, as well as 35 vessels.

title: Referee Assault: NPFL imposes heavy sanctions on Inter Lagos
body:
The Nigeria Premier Football League, NPFL, has sanctioned Inter Lagos following security breaches during their Matchday 7 game against Katsina United at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena, Onikan, Lagos, on Sunday.

The league body said Inter Lagos failed to provide adequate security for the match, allowing unauthorised persons to enter restricted areas.

The breach reportedly led to an attack on match officials as they left the dressing room and headed to their vehicle after the game.

Following the incident, the NPFL fined Inter Lagos N5.2 million.

The club will also have three points and three goals deducted from its accumulated points and goal tally for assaulting and injuring the first assistant referee.

The NPFL said Inter Lagos has 48 hours from the date of the notice to appeal the sanction.

title: US sanctions halt movement of 50 oil tankers off Iran's coast
body:
Bloomberg: 50 oil tankers stranded near Iran as Washington tightens sanctions on Tehran's oil sector and related financial institutions.

US sanctions imposed on Iran have frozen the movement of 50 oil tankers off the country's coast, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday.

The agency noted that 20 empty Iranian tankers remained off Sri Lanka instead of returning, due to the restrictions. Preliminary tanker tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa indicated that no Iranian crude was loaded from ports during September.

Official statements and tanker tracking data

US Treasury Secretary Scott Beissinger announced on October 1 that Iran did not load any crude oil onto tankers during September. He added that around 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain at sea, most of it en route to China, stressing that Washington is working to cut off Tehran's main source of revenue.

Threat of sanctions on foreign financial institutions

In a related development, the United States threatened to impose sanctions on foreign financial institutions if they conduct any business with Iran or its banking sector. The US Treasury Department said in a statement that financial institutions continuing to cooperate with sanctioned Iranian banks could be targeted at any time without prior notice, urging them to immediately end related activities and relationships.

Escalating US campaign and new sanctions

The United States has intensified its campaign to economically isolate Iran since late August, warning allies of possible sanctions if they continue dealings with Tehran. The US Treasury also announced a new package of sanctions targeting Iran's financial, cryptocurrency, rail, automotive, and manufacturing sectors, along with measures against two banks in the UAE and Turkey accused of assisting Iranian authorities.

title: Zimbabwe: CAF Sanctions Zimbabwe Over Fan Death, Pitch Invasion At National Sports Stadium
body:
Zimbabwe have been ordered to play their next home international match behind closed doors after the Confederation of African Football (CAF) sanctioned the Zimbabwe Football Association (ZIFA) over the death of a fan and pitch invasion after the Warriors' 2-1 defeat to the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The CAF Disciplinary Committee also imposed a fine on ZIFA following the incidents, which occurred at the National Sports Stadium on September 28.

The match marked Zimbabwe's first fixture at the National Sports Stadium since 2021, following renovations aimed at bringing the venue back up to international standards.

However, the return to the refurbished stadium was overshadowed by the fatal incident at Gate 2, where a supporter died during a stampede shortly before the match.

There was also a post-match pitch invasion by fans, an incident that contravenes CAF regulations.

CAF's sanction is a setback for Zimbabwe, which had only recently regained the right to host international matches at the National Sports Stadium after years of renovation work and stadium-related restrictions.

The Warriors' next home international match against Equatorial Guinea will therefore be played without supporters as ZIFA serves the CAF punishment.

title: US Government sanctions two France-based charities for allegedly raising funds for Hamas
body:
The United States issued sanctions against three individuals and two France-based charities that it said were part of a network that raised more than $2 million for the Palestinian armed group Hamas, and announced six arrests.

"These designations expose a sophisticated, multi-year financing architecture that moved more than $2 million to Hamas through deceptive charitable fronts and cryptocurrency channels, demonstrating the organization's persistent ability to adapt its fundraising mechanisms to evade detection," the US Treasury said in a statement.

Those sanctioned include Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq, identified as a Hamas member who oversees the financial network and works with the group's media office.

The US Justice Department said French authorities had also arrested sanctioned individuals Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid, who are linked to the France-based charities Association Baraka and Ensemble C Mieux. Both charities were also sanctioned. A third person, Nordine Barika, was also arrested by French authorities in the case, the DOJ said.

"Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid operate from France, where they run purported charities ostensibly to raise money for humanitarian purposes to aid Gazan civilians," the US Treasury said.

In the United States, authorities arrested three men for their alleged funding of Hamas through the network, the DOJ said. US authorities said the network had raised more than $2 million from 2020 to 2026, of which $1.5 million was raised after the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel.

The Syria (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 were made under the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 ('the Sanctions Act') and provide for the imposition of financial sanctions, including the freezing of funds and economic resources of persons who are or have been involved in repressing the civilian population in Syria or who are or have been involved in supporting or benefitting from the Syrian regime.

title: Sanctions, regulation and prices restrict access to medicines
body:
Having medicines available when we need them is a privilege that can be taken for granted in a relatively wealthy country. But globally, access to medicines is complex and relies on sometimes fragile supply systems.

For example, while medicines are officially exempted from US sanctions on Iran, wider restrictions on air freight and the US blockade of Iran's southern ports have effectively stifled medicine imports, leading to worsening shortages of key treatments and drug ingredients from Europe, India and elsewhere.

With shortages extending to even the most basic drugs, Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, used his visit to India for the Brics emerging economies summit this month to transport several tonnes of pharmaceutical ingredients back to Iran on his private plane, according to Financial Times reporting.

Shortages are one aspect of access, and they affect all healthcare systems to varying extents. But if a medicine is not approved for use in a given country, supply is essentially irrelevant. This is a huge problem in low- and middle-income countries, where there is little incentive for companies to negotiate the fragmented regulatory regimes of multiple countries whose markets are relatively small. Efforts to harmonise regulatory requirements across Africa, for example, are aiming to address some of these issues, with support from various charities, but progress is generally slow.

Perhaps more surprisingly, significant numbers of new medicines - especially cancer and rare disease treatments - are not available in Japan. Many of these medicines' producers have no plans to introduce them there, either. A Nikkei Asia review of found that over half of the 238 new drugs approved by US between 2021 and 2025 were not approved in Japan at the end of August 2026.

While national regulators often approve drugs on different timescales, this disparity is unusually large. Gaining approval in Japan requires clinical trials involving Japanese patients, which means small or mid-sized companies from outside Japan often don't have the resources to prioritise additional country-specific trials, or to negotiate the regulatory and language barriers involved. Licensing development to domestic Japanese companies is an option, but one that is only being exercised for a handful of drugs. The Japanese government has sought to incentivise development of 'high need' drugs that are approved in the US or Europe, but again, progress is slow.

Even if a drug is approved by the regulator, there's no guarantee that healthcare systems will agree to (or be able to) pay for it. This is a chronic issue for low- and middle-income countries - particularly around vaccines and new, long-acting HIV protection that could have enormous impact on the spread of HIV-Aids, but whose rollout is being derailed by cuts in international aid budgets. Closer to home, drug pricing is increasingly being used as a political lever, with companies threatening to withdraw investment unless governments commit to paying more for drugs, while the US government uses threats of import tariffs to coerce companies into agreeing to lower their US prices, and other countries (including the UK) to pay more.

title: Russia blames Euro-Atlantic nations for Japan sanctions over Ukraine
body:
Russia has denounced Japan's new round of "ill-considered" sanctions, accusing countries within the Euro-Atlantic area of inciting Tokyo's animosity.

Japan announced its 27th package of measures on October 2, targeting 33 Russian entities, nine individuals and several companies based abroad.

The measures affected shipping for the first time, with Japanese firms banned from providing key services to designated vessels, including maintenance, chartering and crew employment.

The restrictions extend to the sale or purchase of vessels, repairs, insurance, financing and leasing, and seek to reduce Russia's ability to evade Western oil price caps when exporting crude.

In a statement on Monday, the Russian Foreign Ministry described Japan's reference to the situation in Ukraine as a "clumsy attempt" to justify its "hostile actions."

The spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, called the development "another confirmation that the foreign policy course pursued by Tokyo lacks independence."

The diplomat said the sanctions were dictated by Japan's "reckless solidarity with its partners in the Euro-Atlantic region," who are obsessed with the idea of defeating Russia.

"Sanae Takaichi's government is doing nothing to bring about long-term peace in Ukraine," Zakharova noted. "Instead, it is merely pushing that prospect further away."

Moscow accused Tokyo of breaching bilateral agreements by shunning the 1957 Russia-Japan Trade Treaty, which protects vessels and crews in matters relating to commercial shipping.

"Tokyo's unfriendly moves will not go unanswered," the Vladimir Putin administration asserted, vowing to take proportionate countermeasures aimed at Japan's areas of interest.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary, Minoru Kihara, said the steps taken in response to Russia's aggression against Ukraine "are not something that should be criticised by Moscow."
